  • The facebow relates the maxillary cast to the hinge axis (an arbitrary facebow lands within about 2–5 mm of the true axis; a kinematic facebow finds it). The mandibular cast goes on with an interocclusal record.
  • A protrusive record sets the condylar inclination; lateral records set the Bennett angle. A cast mounted in CR can be closed into MIP, but a cast mounted in MIP can never find CR.

Temporomandibular disorders

  • Muscle disorders are the most common (about half), then intracapsular (joint) disorders (about a third). Okeson's five etiologic factors: occlusal conditions, trauma, emotional stress, deep pain input and parafunction.
  • Occlusion matters in two ways: an acute change (a high crown) triggers protective co-contraction and muscle pain; orthopedic instability (the joints and the teeth not stable at the same time, with a CR-to-MIP discrepancy greater than about 3–4 mm) loads the joint. Bruxism is centrally mediated; occlusion does not start it.
  • A disc displaced with reduction gives a click on opening and often on closing (a reciprocal click); without reduction (closed lock) limits opening to about 25–30 mm with deflection toward the affected side.
  • Treat with reversible care first (counseling, medication, physical therapy, a flat-plane stabilization splint); irreversible care (equilibration, crowns, orthodontics, surgery) only when needed. Prophylactic equilibration is not supported. The rule of thirds: a discrepancy in the first third of the tooth, selective grinding; the middle third, crowns or minor orthodontics; beyond, major orthodontics or surgery.

Trauma, mobility and wear

  • Primary occlusal trauma: excessive force on a normal periodontium. Secondary: normal or excessive force on a reduced periodontium. Signs: increasing mobility, a widened PDL space, fremitus. Trauma does not start gingivitis or periodontitis or cause attachment loss, and it is reversible; adjust the occlusion after the infection is treated.
  • A tooth intrudes about 28 µm under load; an implant moves 2–3 µm (no PDL). Miller's index: 0 none, 1 barely distinguishable, 2 horizontal up to 1 mm, 3 more than 1 mm or vertical (depressible).
  • Wear: attrition (tooth on tooth), abrasion (an outside agent; toothpaste abrasivity matters more than the brush), erosion (acid; palatal surfaces of the maxillary incisors with reflux or bulimia) and abfraction (flexure; not proven clinically).
  • Complete dentures use bilateral balanced or lingualized occlusion (the maxillary lingual cusps in the mandibular fossae), because stability matters most; denture teeth come anatomic (about 30–33°), semi-anatomic or flat (0°).
full.f1-biomol:
What's tested
  • Bond types and their strength, water's properties, pH, buffers and the bicarbonate system
  • Amino acid classes, the side-chain pKa values (histidine near 6), chirality and the four levels of protein structure
  • Collagen: Gly-X-Y, the triple helix, vitamin C–dependent hydroxylation, the synthesis steps inside and outside the cell, and the collagen diseases
  • Hemoglobin: T and R states, cooperativity, the Bohr effect, CO2 and 2,3-BPG, fetal hemoglobin, and myoglobin for contrast
  • Carbohydrates: aldoses and ketoses, epimers and anomers, the disaccharides (sucrose and caries), glycogen, glycoproteins and GAGs
  • Lipids: fatty acids, triglycerides, membrane lipids, cholesterol, lipoproteins, β-oxidation and lipogenesis
  • Nucleic acids: purines and pyrimidines, nucleoside versus nucleotide, base pairing, antiparallel strands, chromatin packing

Chemistry that the rest depends on

Covalent bonds (shared electrons) are the strongest; C–C and C–H are nonpolar, O–H is polar. The noncovalent forces, strongest to weakest, are ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds (a hydrogen on N, O or F attracted to another N, O or F) and van der Waals forces. Everything above a protein's primary structure is held by noncovalent forces, plus covalent disulfide bonds.

Water is polar, so it is a good solvent for polar and charged molecules and a poor one for nonpolar ones. It has a high specific heat (1 cal/g/°C), high surface tension from hydrogen bonding, ice is less dense than liquid water, and it is amphoteric. Blood pH is 7.35–7.45. A buffer resists pH change best when the pH equals its pKa; the bicarbonate system is the main blood buffer.

Amino acids and protein structure

An amino acid has an α carbon carrying an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain (R). At physiological pH it is a zwitterion (NH3+ and COO−). All except glycine are chiral, and proteins use L amino acids (L and D name the configuration, not the direction a molecule turns polarized light). Peptide bonds are planar with partial double-bond character.

GroupAmino acidsSide-chain pKa
Acidic (negative)Aspartate (D), glutamate (E)3.9, 4.3
Basic (positive)Lysine (K), arginine (R), histidine (H)10.5, 12.5, 6.0
Other to knowCysteine (disulfides)8.3

Histidine's pKa near 6 lets it gain or lose a proton near physiological pH, so it buffers and works in active sites (and in hemoglobin's Bohr effect). Only the aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr, Trp) absorb UV at 280 nm. Modified amino acids: hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine (collagen), γ-carboxyglutamate (vitamin K–dependent clotting factors), selenocysteine (selenoenzymes).

  • Primary: the amino acid sequence, joined by peptide bonds.
  • Secondary: backbone hydrogen bonds. The α-helix has 3.6 residues per turn (proline breaks helices); β-sheets are parallel or antiparallel (antiparallel is more stable); β-turns reverse the chain and are rich in proline and glycine.
  • Tertiary: the folded 3D shape, with hydrophobic residues buried inside and polar ones outside. Fibrous proteins (keratin, collagen) are strong and insoluble; globular proteins are soluble with a hydrophobic core.
  • Quaternary: several chains together (hemoglobin is a tetramer), which allows cooperativity and regulation. A single-chain protein has none.

Collagen

The most abundant protein in the body (about a third of it); type I is over 90% (bone, dentin, PDL, skin, tendon). Type II is cartilage, type III is reticular fibers, blood vessels and granulation tissue, type IV is basement membrane. The sequence repeats Gly-X-Y, X and Y often proline and hydroxyproline. Each chain is a left-handed helix; three wind into a right-handed triple helix (tropocollagen, about 300 nm). Glycine is every third residue because only glycine fits in the center of the triple helix.

WhereStepWhat goes wrong
RERPre-pro-α chains made; signal peptide removed
RERHydroxylation of proline and lysine already in the chain by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase (need vitamin C, Fe2+, O2)Scurvy
RERGlycosylation of hydroxylysine; three chains form the procollagen triple helix (disulfides at the propeptides)Osteogenesis imperfecta (faulty type I chains)
Golgi → outPackaged and secreted
Outside the cellProcollagen peptidases cut off the propeptides → tropocollagenSome Ehlers-Danlos types
Outside the cellLysyl oxidase (copper) cross-links fibrilsMenkes disease (copper)

Hydroxyproline's hydrogen bonds stabilize the triple helix, so without vitamin C the helix is weak: scurvy brings bleeding, swollen gums, loose teeth, poor wound healing and petechiae. Fibrils are staggered with 40 nm gaps (hole zones) that give the banded look and are nucleation sites for bone mineral. Osteogenesis imperfecta: brittle bones, blue sclerae, hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta. Ehlers-Danlos: stretchy skin and loose joints.

Hemoglobin

Hemoglobin (α2β2) carries O2 on Fe2+ in heme: four porphyrin nitrogens, a histidine as the fifth ligand, O2 as the sixth. Without O2 the iron sits out of the heme plane; binding pulls it into the plane, breaks salt bridges and shifts the tetramer from the T (tense, deoxy) to the R (relaxed, oxy) state. That makes binding cooperative and the curve sigmoidal, so hemoglobin loads O2 in the lungs and unloads it in tissues. Myoglobin is a monomer (storage) with a hyperbolic curve and higher affinity.

Right shift (lower affinity, more O2 released)Left shift (higher affinity)
↑ H+ (lower pH: the Bohr effect), ↑ CO2, ↑ 2,3-BPG, ↑ temperatureFetal hemoglobin (α2γ2, binds 2,3-BPG poorly), carbon monoxide, ↓ temperature, alkalosis

Most heme is in red blood cells. Sickle cell disease comes from glutamate → valine at position 6 of β-globin (HbS); thalassemias make too little of one chain.

Carbohydrates

Monosaccharides are aldoses (aldehyde) or ketoses (ketone). Epimers differ at one carbon: glucose and galactose at C-4, glucose and mannose at C-2. Ring closure makes a hemiacetal (six-membered pyranose, five-membered furanose) and a new chiral C-1, giving the α and β anomers, which interconvert. Enantiomers are mirror images. Sugars with a free anomeric carbon are reducing sugars. A sugar's carbonyl can join a protein's amino group as a Schiff base (nonenzymatic glycation, the basis of HbA1c).

  • Sucrose (glucose + fructose): the substrate Streptococcus mutans turns into sticky extracellular glucans (dextran) for plaque.
  • Lactose (galactose + glucose), split by lactase; maltose (glucose + glucose), from starch digestion.
  • Glycogen: glucose in α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches (storage). Cellulose: β-1,4 (plants).
  • N-linked glycans go on asparagine in the ER (dolichol carrier); O-linked on serine or threonine in the Golgi. Mannose-6-phosphate sends enzymes to lysosomes.
  • Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs): unbranched repeating disaccharides with an amino sugar; hyaluronic acid, heparin (anticoagulant), chondroitin and keratan sulfate. On a core protein they form proteoglycans, which hold water as the ECM's gel.

Lipids

Mostly hydrocarbon, so they dissolve in nonpolar solvents. Fatty acids: saturated (no double bonds, pack tightly) or unsaturated (cis double bonds kink the chain and lower the melting point). Triglycerides are glycerol with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds: the main energy store, in adipose tissue. Phospholipids are amphipathic and form the bilayer; glycolipids sit on the outer leaflet; cholesterol steadies fluidity; steroids have four fused rings. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from enterocytes through the lymph; LDL carries cholesterol to tissues; HDL brings it back to the liver.

Lipolysis splits triglycerides (lipases). Fatty acids enter the mitochondrion on the carnitine shuttle and undergo β-oxidation in the matrix to acetyl-CoA. Lipogenesis runs in the cytosol of the liver when carbohydrate is plentiful; acetyl-CoA leaves the mitochondrion as citrate.

Nucleic acids

A nucleotide is a pentose, a phosphate and a base; a nucleoside lacks the phosphate. Purines (adenine, guanine) have two rings and break down to uric acid; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have one. Phosphodiester bonds link the 5′ phosphate of one nucleotide to the 3′ OH of the next. The two DNA strands are antiparallel and complementary: A–T with two hydrogen bonds, G–C with three (so GC-rich DNA is harder to separate). DNA wraps around an octamer of histones as the nucleosome, then the 10 nm "beads on a string", the 30 nm fiber and the mitotic chromosome. Bacterial DNA is one circular, supercoiled chromosome in the nucleoid, plus plasmids.
full.f1-cells:
What's tested
  • Prokaryotic versus eukaryotic cells; each organelle's job and its "address tag" (signal peptide, mannose-6-phosphate, ubiquitin, nuclear localization signal)
  • The cytoskeleton, the cell cycle and apoptosis (caspases)
  • Membrane structure, diffusion, osmosis, tonicity and the reflection coefficient
  • Passive, primary active and secondary active transport (cotransport and countertransport)
  • Equilibrium potentials (Nernst), the resting potential and the Na+/K+ pump
  • The phases of the action potential, refractory periods, myelin, and the effect of potassium, tetrodotoxin and local anesthetics
  • Electrical and chemical synapses, the main neurotransmitters, EPSPs and IPSPs, the neuromuscular junction, and the toxins and diseases that act there

Cells and organelles

Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles: a nucleoid, a peptidoglycan wall, often flagella and pili. Eukaryotes (human cells, fungi, parasites) compartmentalize work in membrane-bound organelles. Every cell has a plasma membrane.

OrganelleJobKey fact
NucleusDNA storage, transcriptionDouble membrane continuous with the ER; nuclear pores; big proteins need a nuclear localization signal
Rough ERSecretory, membrane and lysosomal proteinsA signal peptide brings the ribosome to the ER; the signal is cut off inside
Free ribosomesCytosolic and cytoskeletal proteins, and those for mitochondria, peroxisomes and nucleus
Smooth ERLipid synthesis, Ca2+ storageHigh Ca2+ inside
GolgiModifies, sorts and ships proteins (cis → trans)Constitutive (unregulated) or regulated (signal-triggered) secretion
LysosomeAcid hydrolases (pH 4.5–5.0, kept by a proton pump)Enzymes tagged with mannose-6-phosphate
PeroxisomeOxidizes very long-chain fatty acids and toxinsCatalase breaks down H2O2
MitochondrionATP (electron transport on the inner membrane), β-oxidationDouble membrane, its own DNA (inherited from the mother), releases cytochrome c in apoptosis
ProteasomeDegrades proteinsNot membrane-bound; targets are tagged with ubiquitin

Endocytosis takes material in: phagocytosis (pseudopods engulf large particles into phagosomes), pinocytosis (small pits take in fluid) and receptor-mediated endocytosis (ligand-bound receptors in coated pits, as for LDL). Exocytosis sends material out.

The cytoskeleton is held together by noncovalent bonds so it can rebuild quickly. Microtubules (tubulin) are the most rigid: motor-protein highways, the mitotic spindle and the core of cilia and flagella. Actin filaments (microfilaments) support microvilli, the cell surface and cell movement. Intermediate filaments (keratin-related, varying by cell type) are rope-like, take tension and link the nucleus to the membrane. The extracellular matrix (collagen, elastin, proteoglycans, hyaluronic acid, adhesive proteins) attaches through integrins.

The cell cycle: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (checks and repair), M (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis). Apoptosis is programmed, non-inflammatory death carried out by caspases; the plasma membrane goes last. Too much cell death or too little (cancer) causes disease.

Membranes and transport

The fluid mosaic membrane: a phospholipid bilayer with integral (transmembrane) and peripheral proteins, cholesterol (cuts permeability to small molecules), carbohydrates on the outer face only, and lipid rafts rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids. The two leaflets differ in composition.

Diffusion is passive and downhill; for an uncharged solute its rate rises with surface area and gradient and falls with membrane thickness (Fick). Osmosis is water moving toward the side with more osmotically active particles. Osmotic pressure depends on the number of particles (NaCl gives two, glucose one) and on how well they cross, the reflection coefficient σ: 0 means the solute crosses freely and draws no water; 1 means it is impermeant and exerts its full pressure.

  • Hypotonic solution: water enters, the cell swells (and can lyse). Hypertonic: water leaves, the cell shrinks. Isotonic: no change.
MechanismEnergyDirectionExample
Simple diffusionNoneDownhillO2, CO2, steroids
Facilitated (carrier) diffusionNoneDownhill only; saturable, stereospecific, competitiveGLUT transporters
Primary active transportATP directlyUphillNa+/K+ ATPase (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in), Ca2+ ATPase
Secondary active: cotransport (symport)Na+ gradientSolute moves the same way as Na+SGLT (Na+–glucose)
Secondary active: countertransport (antiport)Na+ gradientSolute moves opposite to Na+Na+/Ca2+ exchanger

Epithelial cells sit on a basal lamina, are joined by tight junctions and move solutes in one direction (vectorial transport), through the cells or between them (paracellular).

Membrane potentials

Bulk solutions are electrically neutral; only a thin layer of charge at the membrane is separated (the membrane acts as a capacitor, ion channels as resistors). The equilibrium potential of an ion is the voltage that balances its concentration gradient: E = (61.5/z) log([out]/[in]) at body temperature, so a tenfold gradient gives about 60 mV (the class used ±60 mV). E(K+) is about −90 mV and E(Na+) about +60 mV. At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+ through leak channels, so the resting potential (about −70 mV) sits close to E(K+). The Na+/K+ pump keeps the gradients; its own electrogenic current adds only a few millivolts.

The action potential

  • Threshold (about −55 mV): a stimulus opens enough voltage-gated Na+ channels that Na+ entry depolarizes the membrane further and opens more (positive feedback).
  • Upstroke and overshoot toward E(Na+): about 100 mV above rest. All-or-none: a bigger stimulus doesn't make a bigger action potential.
  • Repolarization: Na+ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ leaves.
  • Afterhyperpolarization: K+ channels are slow to close, so the potential dips below rest.

During the absolute refractory period Na+ channels are inactivated and no stimulus can fire another action potential. In the relative refractory period some Na+ channels are still inactivated and K+ channels are still open, so only a larger-than-normal stimulus works. Myelin speeds conduction: the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next (saltatory conduction); larger diameter also speeds it.

Hyperkalemia depolarizes the resting membrane, which inactivates Na+ channels and lowers excitability (dangerous for the heart). Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from outside, so threshold is never reached. Local anesthetics cross the axon membrane in their uncharged form, then the charged form blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from the cytoplasmic side. In inflamed, acidic tissue more of the drug is charged outside the nerve and less gets in, so the block is weaker.

Synapses and neurotransmitters

A neuron has dendrites (input), a cell body (integration), an axon (conduction) and terminals (output). Electrical synapses pass current through gap junctions: very fast, two-way, mostly excitatory (cardiac and some smooth muscle). Chemical synapses are more common and can excite or inhibit: the action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the terminal, Ca2+ triggers vesicle fusion, transmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptors. Ionotropic receptors are ion channels; metabotropic receptors are G protein–coupled. Small-molecule transmitters are made and packaged in the terminal; neuropeptides are made in the cell body.

EPSPs depolarize (Na+ entry, usually glutamate); IPSPs hyperpolarize (Cl− entry, usually GABA or glycine). Both are graded and local and add up (summation) at the axon hillock.

TransmitterRoleClinical link
Acetylcholine (acetyl-CoA + choline)Neuromuscular junction (nicotinic, a ligand-gated Na+/K+ channel); broken down by acetylcholinesterase, choline recycledBotulinum toxin blocks its release; myasthenia gravis: antibodies against the ACh receptor
GlutamateMain excitatory transmitter of brain and spinal cord (three ionotropic receptors); recycled as glutamine
GABAMain inhibitory transmitter of the brain (ionotropic Cl− channel; metabotropic receptor acting on K+)Benzodiazepines enhance the Cl− channel
GlycineInhibitory in brainstem and spinal cord (Cl− channel)
Norepinephrine, serotonin, dopamineMonoamines, cleared by reuptake transportersCocaine blocks reuptake; SSRIs block the serotonin transporter
full.f1-molbio:
What's tested
  • Replication: semiconservative, leading and lagging strands, the enzymes and their jobs, prokaryotes versus eukaryotes, telomeres and telomerase
  • RNA: how it differs from DNA, the RNA types and their share of cell RNA, ribosome sizes, nucleases
  • Prokaryotic transcription: RNA polymerase subunits (σ), promoters, termination, the lac operon
  • Eukaryotic transcription: the three RNA polymerases, TFIID and the TATA box, enhancers, acetylation and methylation
  • RNA processing: cap, splicing, poly(A) tail, editing, export and decay
  • Translation: tRNA charging, the ribosome's A, P and E sites, factors, wobble, bacterial versus eukaryotic
  • Mendel's laws, modes of inheritance and pedigree risk; types of mutation and the classic mutation diseases
  • Oncogenes, tumor suppressors (two hits), DNA repair genes, benign versus malignant

DNA replication

Replication is semiconservative (each daughter has one old and one new strand) and happens in S phase. It starts at origins (one in bacteria, many in eukaryotes) and runs both ways from each. Polymerases add only to a free 3′-OH, so new DNA grows 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made away from it in short Okazaki fragments, each also built 5′ → 3′.

ProteinJob
Helicase (DnaB)Breaks the hydrogen bonds and opens the fork
Single-strand binding proteinKeeps the separated strands from re-annealing
Topoisomerase (gyrase in bacteria)Relieves the overwinding ahead of the fork (fluoroquinolones block gyrase)
Primase (DnaG)Lays down the RNA primer polymerases need
DNA polymerase III (bacteria)Main replicating enzyme; 3′ → 5′ exonuclease proofreading
DNA polymerase I (bacteria)Removes RNA primers (5′ → 3′ exonuclease) and fills the gaps
DNA ligaseSeals the nicks between Okazaki fragments (phosphodiester bond)

Eukaryotes: many origins, slower (50–100 nucleotides a second versus about 1,000 in bacteria), polymerase α (with primase) starts each fragment, δ and ε do most of the copying and proofread, PCNA is the sliding clamp, RNase H (with a flap nuclease) removes primers. Linear chromosomes lose a little at each end every round, so they end in telomeres (TTAGGG repeats in humans). Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template, extends them; it is active in germ and stem cells and in most cancers.

The nature of RNA

RNA has ribose with a 2′-OH (so dilute base hydrolyzes it, while DNA resists), uses uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded.

RNAShare of cell RNAJob
rRNAAbout 80%Scaffold and catalyst of the ribosome (ribosomes are about two-thirds rRNA)
tRNAAbout 15%Carries one amino acid on its 3′ CCA end; cloverleaf in 2D, L-shaped in 3D
mRNAAbout 2–5%Carries the code; bacterial mRNA lasts minutes
snRNASmallSplicing (in snRNPs)
Small non-coding RNAs (miRNA, siRNA)SmallPost-transcriptional silencing

Ribosomes: bacterial 70S = 30S (16S rRNA) + 50S (23S + 5S); eukaryotic 80S = 40S (18S) + 60S (28S, 5.8S, 5S). Bacterial mRNA is polycistronic (several proteins per message) with no introns; eukaryotic mRNA codes one protein and is spliced.

Prokaryotic transcription

One RNA polymerase makes all RNA. The holoenzyme (α2ββ′σ) starts transcription; σ recognizes the promoter's −35 (TTGACA) and −10 Pribnow box (TATAAT) sequences. β and β′ form the catalytic site; rifampin binds β. RNA polymerase needs no primer, builds 5′ → 3′, opens about 14 bp (closed → open complex), and after 7–12 nucleotides σ leaves and the core enzyme elongates. Termination is rho-dependent (rho, an ATP-dependent helicase) or intrinsic (a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of U's, which pulls the RNA off).

The lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA share one promoter and operator. Negative control: the lacI repressor binds the operator; allolactose (from lactose) pulls it off. Positive control: when glucose is low, cAMP rises and the CAP–cAMP complex binds upstream, bends the DNA and recruits polymerase. Transcription is highest with lactose present and glucose absent; glucose and lactose together give only low expression (catabolite repression).

Eukaryotic transcription

DNA wraps histone octamers (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4; H1 links nucleosomes into the 30 nm fiber). Histones are rich in positive lysine and arginine.

  • RNA polymerase I: the large rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus. II: mRNA (and most snRNA), blocked by α-amanitin. III: tRNA and 5S rRNA.
  • General transcription factors build the pre-initiation complex; TFIID carries the TATA-binding protein, which binds the TATA box about 25 bp upstream.
  • Enhancers bind activators and work at a distance, upstream, downstream or in introns, in either orientation.
  • Histone acetylation loosens chromatin and turns genes on; DNA methylation (at CpG) recruits deacetylases and silences genes.

RNA processing (in the nucleus)

  • 5′ cap: 7-methylguanosine joined by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bond. Needed for export, translation and stability. RNA polymerase I and III products are uncapped.
  • Splicing starts while transcription continues. The spliceosome (snRNPs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) removes introns, which begin with GU and end with AG; the branch-point A attacks the 5′ splice site to form a lariat; the snRNAs catalyze the transesterifications. Alternative splicing gives several proteins from one gene.
  • Poly(A) tail: after the AAUAAA signal the transcript is cut 10–30 nucleotides downstream and poly(A) polymerase adds A's with no template. Poly(A)-binding protein protects the message and helps translation.
  • Editing changes single bases: A → I (ADAR) and C → U (apoB-48 in the gut).

Translation

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach each amino acid to its tRNA's 3′ end using ATP, and an editing site removes a wrong, smaller amino acid: this charging is the main fidelity step. The genetic code has 64 codons: AUG starts (methionine; formyl-Met in bacteria) and UAA, UAG, UGA stop. The code is degenerate, and wobble at the codon's third base lets one tRNA read several codons. The reading frame is kept by starting at AUG and moving exactly three nucleotides each step.

The ribosome has three sites: A (incoming aminoacyl-tRNA), P (the tRNA holding the growing chain) and E (exit). The peptidyl transferase is the large subunit's rRNA, so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

BacteriaEukaryotes
Finding the startShine-Dalgarno sequence pairs with 16S rRNA, about 7 bases before AUGSmall subunit binds the 5′ cap (with the tail's help) and scans to the first AUG
Initiation factorsIF-1, IF-2 (a G protein carrying fMet-tRNA), IF-3Many eIFs
ElongationEF-Tu delivers tRNA, EF-Ts recharges it with GTP, EF-G translocateseEF1A, eEF1B, eEF2 (diphtheria toxin inactivates eEF2)
TerminationRF-1 (UAA, UAG), RF-2 (UAA, UGA), RF-3, ribosome recycling factorOne release factor reads all three stops

Classical genetics

Alleles are versions of a gene; the genotype is the allele combination (homozygous or heterozygous), the phenotype is the trait. Segregation: the two alleles separate into different gametes. Independent assortment: alleles of different (unlinked) genes sort independently. Multiply probabilities for "and", add them for "or". A monohybrid cross of heterozygotes gives 3:1; a dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1.

ModePedigree clueExamples
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; males and females alike; an affected child has an affected parent; 50% risk per childHuntington disease, familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor)
Autosomal recessiveSkips generations; unaffected carrier parents; 25% risk when both carrySickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis
X-linked recessiveMostly males; through carrier mothers; never father to sonHemophilia A (factor VIII)
X-linked dominantAn affected father passes it to all daughters and no sons
Y-linkedFather to every son
MitochondrialMother to all her children; never through the fatherEnergy-failure diseases of muscle and nerve

An unaffected sibling of someone with a recessive disease (both parents carriers) has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

Mutations

  • Point mutations: a transition swaps purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine; a transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine. By effect: silent (same amino acid), missense (another amino acid; sickle cell, Glu → Val), nonsense (premature stop, truncated protein), splice-site.
  • Insertions or deletions: not a multiple of three shifts the frame (frameshift); a multiple of three adds or removes whole amino acids (the common cystic fibrosis mutation removes one phenylalanine).
  • Expanding triplet repeats: more repeats mean earlier, more severe disease in later generations (anticipation): Huntington disease (CAG).
  • Spontaneous mutations come from replication errors; induced ones from chemicals (alkylating and intercalating agents) and radiation (ionizing radiation, including X-rays, breaks the backbone). Somatic mutations affect only the person's own cell line; germline mutations can pass to children.

Genetics of cancer

Cancer is uncontrolled growth from accumulated somatic mutations in cell-cycle genes. Benign tumors are encapsulated, well differentiated, slow and don't metastasize; malignant ones invade, are poorly differentiated, divide often and metastasize. Stages: hyperplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive cancer.

  • Oncogenes: a mutated proto-oncogene (normally pro-growth) becomes overactive ("stepping on the gas"); one mutated copy is enough. Activated by amplification (HER2/ErbB2 in breast cancer), a point mutation that leaves the protein always on (RAS), translocation making a fusion protein (BCR-ABL, chronic myeloid leukemia), or insertion next to a strong promoter.
  • Tumor suppressors ("removing the brakes"): both copies must be lost, Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. RB (retinoblastoma), p53 (stops the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; abnormal in over half of cancers), APC (colon).
  • DNA repair genes: BRCA1/2 (double-strand break repair; inherited as a dominant risk, though each cell still needs a second hit).
  • An inherited first hit is in every cell, so cancer comes earlier and more often. High-risk HPV (types 16 and 18) causes oropharyngeal and cervical cancer: its E6 protein degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB.
  • Cancer cells lose contact inhibition, turn on telomerase, induce angiogenesis (VEGF from oxygen-starved cells) and spread by blood, lymph and nerves.
full.f1-enzhorm:
What's tested
  • Endocrine, paracrine and autocrine signaling; the chemical classes of hormones; how hormones are regulated and measured
  • Peptide hormones: synthesis, transport, cell-surface receptors, the cAMP–PKA and IP3/DAG–Ca2+–PKC pathways, insulin and GLUT4
  • Steroid hormones: cholesterol to pregnenolone, P450 enzymes, carrier proteins, nuclear receptors, the three classes and their disorders; the calcium hormones
  • Metabolism: catabolic versus anabolic, NAD+ versus NADPH, ATP coupling, which tissues burn which fuel
  • Thermodynamics: the three laws, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, exergonic versus endergonic, the ΔH/ΔS table
  • Enzymes: catalytic power, specificity, activation energy, cofactors and coenzymes, the six classes, Km, Vmax, kcat, kcat/Km, bisubstrate reactions, induced fit, and inhibition on a Lineweaver-Burk plot

Hormones: the basics

The endocrine system signals chemically through the blood: slower than the nervous system, but longer lasting. The two overlap (the adrenal medulla releases norepinephrine; the hypothalamus is neural tissue that makes hormones that control the pituitary, the "master" gland). Endocrine hormones travel in blood (growth hormone, insulin), paracrine ones act on neighbors (testosterone from Leydig cells in the testis), autocrine ones act on the cell that made them (estradiol).

  • Chemical classes: amino acid–derived (thyroxine and catecholamines from tyrosine), peptides and proteins (insulin, oxytocin, growth hormone), steroids (from cholesterol), fatty acid–derived (eicosanoids).
  • Regulation: rate of synthesis; rate of release (insulin is biphasic, some hormones pulsatile, cortisol diurnal); half-life (short half-life = tight control); negative feedback (cortisol suppresses ACTH); opposing hormones (insulin versus glucagon); bioavailability (only free hormone acts).
  • Measuring them is hard: tiny blood levels, binding proteins and changing release. Methods: sandwich ELISA (a capture antibody and an enzyme-linked detection antibody) and mass spectrometry (the usual test for testosterone).
PeptideSteroid
Made asPreprohormone → prohormone; stored in granulesMade on demand from cholesterol; not stored
Solubility and transportPolar; small ones travel free, large ones on carriersNonpolar; mostly protein-bound in blood
ReceptorCell surface, second messengersInside the cell; the complex binds DNA (hormone response elements) and changes transcription
SpeedFastSlower, longer lasting
By mouthNo (digested)Often yes

Peptide hormone signaling

G protein–coupled receptors: the hormone changes the receptor's shape, the G protein swaps GDP for GTP, and its α subunit acts on an enzyme.

  • Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A. PKA is two regulatory and two catalytic subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits (four sites in all) and frees the active catalytic ones. Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down (caffeine blocks it). Gs examples: glycogen breakdown in liver, fat breakdown in adipose tissue, water conservation in the kidney (ADH). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (slows the heart).
  • Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP2 into IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the ER) and DAG (with Ca2+ activates protein kinase C).
  • Each step amplifies the signal: one epinephrine molecule releases a flood of glucose from the liver.

Insulin: pancreatic β cells make preproinsulin on the ER; the signal peptide is cut to proinsulin, which the Golgi cleaves to insulin plus C-peptide and packs in granules. Glucose entry raises ATP, and Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis. Its receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase (two α and two β subunits); the cascade moves GLUT4 to the membrane of skeletal muscle and fat cells, so glucose enters and blood glucose falls. Glucagon does the opposite in the liver.

Steroid hormones

Made in the adrenal cortex (glomerulosa: aldosterone; fasciculata: cortisol; reticularis: androgens) and the gonads. The first and rate-limiting step, in mitochondria, cleaves cholesterol's side chain to make pregnenolone. Most steps use cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases, which need O2 and NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway). Carriers: transcortin (corticosteroid-binding globulin) holds about 75% of cortisol and albumin most of the rest; SHBG binds testosterone and estradiol and sets how much is free.

ClassMain hormone and actionsToo muchToo little
GlucocorticoidCortisol (stress): gluconeogenesis and high blood glucose, protein and fat breakdown, immunosuppression, less bone formationCushing syndrome: central obesity, moon face, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, poor healingAddison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency): fatigue, hypotension, hyperpigmentation of skin and oral mucosa from high ACTH; adrenal crisis under stress
MineralocorticoidAldosterone: Na+ (and water) retained, K+ secreted in the distal tubule and collecting duct; raises blood volume and pressureConn syndrome: hypertension with low K+Addison disease: salt loss, high K+, low blood pressure
Sex steroidsTestosterone: muscle, bone density, sex organ maturation. Estrogen: uterus and breast maturation, less bone resorption, more clotting, more HDLAnabolic steroid abuseMenopause: estrogen replacement eases symptoms

Calcium hormones: PTH raises blood Ca2+ (osteoclast resorption through osteoblast signals, kidney Ca2+ reabsorption, more calcitriol); calcitriol (active vitamin D) raises gut absorption of Ca2+ and phosphate; calcitonin from the thyroid lowers Ca2+ by inhibiting osteoclasts. Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, osteocytes signal when to do which.

Metabolism

  • Catabolic pathways break molecules down: oxidative, exergonic, and they reduce NAD+ to NADH. Anabolic pathways build: reductive, endergonic, and they spend NADPH and ATP.
  • ATP hydrolysis (about −7.3 kcal/mol, −30.5 kJ/mol) is coupled to endergonic work: transport, synthesis, contraction, signaling. Each ATP is recycled over a thousand times a day.
  • The liver is the metabolic hub. The brain and red blood cells run almost entirely on glucose (red cells have no mitochondria, so glycolysis only); heart and resting muscle prefer fatty acids.
  • Pathways are controlled by compartments, substrate and product levels, energy charge, enzyme amount and allosteric effectors.

Thermodynamics

Systems are isolated (no exchange), closed (energy only) or open (energy and matter: living cells). First law: energy is conserved. Second law: every real process increases the entropy of the universe. Third law: a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K. Energy units: joules (SI) or calories (1 cal = 4.184 J).

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at constant temperature and pressure. ΔG < 0: exergonic, spontaneous. ΔG > 0: endergonic, needs coupling to an exergonic process. ΔG = 0: equilibrium. ΔG says nothing about speed; ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq links it to the equilibrium constant. Unfolding a protein absorbs heat (ΔH positive) and raises entropy.

ΔHΔSSpontaneous?
− (exothermic)+At every temperature
+−Never
−−Only at low temperature
++Only at high temperature

Enzymes

Enzymes have catalytic power (rates up to about 10^16 times the uncatalyzed rate), specificity (set by the active site's structure) and regulation (substrate and cofactor supply, allosteric control, how much enzyme is made). They lower the activation energy (ΔG‡) by binding the transition state most tightly; they don't change ΔG or the equilibrium. Induced fit (more accurate than lock and key): substrate binding changes the enzyme's shape; in hexokinase two domains close around glucose to form the catalytic site. Enzymes work in a pH range (ionizable side chains) and speed up with temperature until they denature (above about 50 °C).

  • Cofactors are usually metal ions (Mg2+ for hexokinase, K+ for pyruvate kinase, Zn2+ for DNA polymerase). Coenzymes are organic, often from vitamins (NAD+ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, TPP from thiamine), and carry groups or electrons. A tightly bound one is a prosthetic group. Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme.
  • Six classes: oxidoreductases (redox), transferases (move a group), hydrolases (split with water), lyases (add to or form double bonds without water or ATP), isomerases, ligases (join molecules using ATP).
  • Bisubstrate reactions: single-displacement (sequential: both substrates bind before any product leaves; ordered or random, as in creatine kinase) and double-displacement (ping-pong: the first product leaves before the second substrate binds, as in aminotransferases).

Michaelis-Menten: v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Km is the [S] that gives half of Vmax; a low Km means tight binding (high affinity). At low [S] the rate is first order in substrate; at saturating [S] it is zero order and approaches Vmax, which rises with the amount of enzyme. kcat (turnover number) = Vmax / [enzyme]: substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second at saturation. kcat/Km is catalytic efficiency at low [S]; its ceiling is the diffusion limit (about 10^8–10^9 per molar per second). The ES complex reaches a steady state.

Lineweaver-Burk (1/v against 1/[S]): y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km, slope Km/Vmax.

TypeBindsKmVmaxLineweaver-Burk lines
CompetitiveActive site (resembles substrate); overcome by more substrate↑SameCross on the y-axis
Pure noncompetitiveAnother site, E or ES equallySame↓Cross on the x-axis
UncompetitiveES complex only↓↓Parallel
MixedE and ES, unequally↑ or ↓↓Cross off both axes

Examples: methotrexate competes with dihydrofolate at dihydrofolate reductase; statins compete at HMG-CoA reductase. Irreversible inhibitors bind covalently: aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase, organophosphates block acetylcholinesterase. Allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal curves, not Michaelis-Menten.
full.f2-genpath:
What's tested
  • Reversible versus irreversible cell injury, and the nuclear changes of cell death
  • The six necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each one belongs to (coagulative heart and kidney, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas)
  • Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (Fas) pathways, which both end in caspases
  • How cells are injured: ATP loss in hypoxia, free radicals and the enzymes that clear them, reperfusion injury
  • The four adaptations with an example of each, intracellular accumulations, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
  • Acute inflammation (vascular changes, exudate versus transudate, leukocyte recruitment) and chronic inflammation (M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas, repair and scar problems, acute-phase proteins)
  • Neoplasia: naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Cell injury: reversible or not

Reversible injury goes back to normal if the cause is removed. The first sign is cell swelling (the ATP-driven sodium pump fails and water follows sodium in). Others: plasma membrane blebs, dilated ER with ribosomes falling off, swollen mitochondria, fatty change, myelin figures and clumped chromatin. The organ is heavier and firmer.

Irreversible injury ("the point of no return") comes from four failures: mitochondria can't make ATP again, membranes lose integrity, lysosomal enzymes leak and digest the cell, and DNA and chromatin break down. The nucleus shows it: pyknosis (shrinks and darkens), karyorrhexis (fragments) and karyolysis (fades). The changes are seen in order: biochemical (enzymes such as troponin leak into blood), then electron microscopy, then light microscopy, then the gross organ.

Mitochondria are the first organelle hit by hypoxia: less oxidative phosphorylation means less ATP, so the cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, lactic acid builds up and the pH falls (that is what clumps the chromatin).

MechanismKey points
Hypoxia and ischemiaIschemia = blocked blood flow; hypoxia = too little oxygen. ATP falls, protein synthesis stops
Oxidative stressFree radicals (superoxide, hydroxyl radical, peroxynitrite) made faster than removed. Cleared by superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase
Ischemia-reperfusionRestoring blood flow to viable tissue adds injury (radicals, neutrophils), e.g., after a transplant
ToxinsDirect-acting bind a vital molecule; latent ones are converted (often by P450) to reactive metabolites that make radicals
ER stressMisfolded proteins pile up; the unfolded protein response adds chaperones, and if that fails the cell dies by apoptosis
DNA damageRadiation, chemotherapy, radicals. p53 arrests the cycle to repair or triggers apoptosis

Necrosis patterns

PatternWhat it looks likeClassic setting
CoagulativeOutlines kept; pink (eosinophilic) cells with no nucleiInfarct of any solid organ except the brain (heart, kidney, spleen)
LiquefactiveTissue digested to fluid by neutrophil enzymes; pusBacterial or fungal abscess (e.g., dental abscess); brain infarct
CaseousFriable, cheese-like, yellow-white; granuloma; architecture lostTuberculosis
Fat necrosisLipases split fat; fatty acids bind calcium = chalky white saponificationAcute pancreatitis
FibrinoidBright pink fibrin-like material in the vessel wallImmune-complex vasculitis, malignant hypertension
GangrenousClinical term for a limb: dry = coagulative; wet = bacteria added, liquefactiveDiabetic or ischemic foot

Apoptosis

ApoptosisNecrosis
CellShrinks, breaks into apoptotic bodiesSwells, membrane ruptures, contents leak
InflammationNoneYes
WhenPhysiologic (tissue turnover, end of an immune response) or pathologicAlways pathologic
  • Intrinsic (mitochondrial): loss of survival signals, DNA damage or radiation → sensors block BCL2 → mitochondrial channels open → cytochrome c leaks out → caspases.
  • Extrinsic (death receptor): Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell binds Fas on the target cell → death domain adaptors → caspases.
  • Both end in caspase activation. Related forms: autophagy (the cell eats its own organelles in starvation), necroptosis (features of both), pyroptosis (inflammatory, releases IL-1).

Adaptations, accumulations, calcification

AdaptationMeaningPhysiologicPathologic
HypertrophyBigger cells (cells that can't divide)Uterus in pregnancy, weightlifter's muscleHeart muscle in hypertension
HyperplasiaMore cells; stops when the stimulus stopsBreast at puberty, liver after partial removalEndometrium with unopposed estrogen, prostate, HPV warts
AtrophySmaller cells (less workload, nerve, blood, nutrition or hormone; aging)MenopauseBrain in dementia
MetaplasiaOne adult cell type replaced by another, through reprogrammed stem cells—Columnar to squamous in a smoker's bronchus; can lead to cancer
  • Accumulations: lipid (liver steatosis from alcohol, diabetes, obesity), protein, glycogen (storage diseases such as Pompe disease, acid alpha-glucosidase missing), pigments. Endogenous pigments: lipofuscin (wear and tear), melanin, hemosiderin. Exogenous: carbon (anthracosis), tattoo ink.
  • Dystrophic calcification: normal serum calcium, deposits in damaged tissue (atheroma, old heart valves, necrosis).
  • Metastatic calcification: high serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism, bone destruction, vitamin D excess, kidney failure), deposits in normal tissue (vessels, kidneys, lungs, stomach).

Acute inflammation

Causes: infection, necrosis, foreign bodies, immune reactions. Sentinel cells recognize microbes (toll-like receptors), damaged cells (DAMPs) and complement. Vessels: brief vasoconstriction, then histamine vasodilation (heat, redness), then leaky endothelium (fast, short-lived), then stasis. Exudate = high protein and cells (inflammation; pus if full of neutrophils). Transudate = low protein, few cells (high hydrostatic or low oncotic pressure, e.g., heart failure).

  1. Rolling: selectins.
  2. Firm adhesion: integrins (on the leukocyte) binding ICAM-1 and VCAM-1.
  3. Transmigration: PECAM-1 (CD31).
  4. Chemotaxis: chemokines, C5a, leukotriene B4, bacterial products.

Neutrophils dominate early, then macrophages. They kill by phagocytosis (phagosome fuses with lysosome) with reactive oxygen species (NADPH oxidase), nitrogen species and lysosomal enzymes. Outcomes: resolution, scarring, or chronic inflammation. Patterns: serous (blister), fibrinous (body-cavity linings; can leave adhesions), purulent, abscess (pus walled off), ulcer (sloughed surface, common in mucosa).

Chronic inflammation and repair

  • Causes: persistent infection, autoimmune or allergic disease, long toxic exposure. Histology: lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells, tissue destruction and fibrosis (acute = neutrophils, tissue preserved).
  • M1 (classical) macrophages: switched on by microbial products and IFN-γ from CD4 T cells; make ROS, NO, IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-12; kill microbes. M2 (alternative): switched on by IL-4 and IL-13; secrete IL-10 and TGF-β; repair, new vessels, collagen. Eosinophils fight parasites; mast cells act in both acute and chronic inflammation.
  • Granulomas: epithelioid macrophages and giant cells with a lymphocyte rim. Immune granulomas need T cells (caseating in TB; noncaseating in Crohn disease); foreign-body granulomas form around sutures or splinters.
  • Repair: platelet plug → inflammation and proliferation with granulation tissue (new small vessels, fibroblasts, macrophages, little collagen) → remodeling (collagen gives tensile strength). Labile tissues (epithelium, marrow) always divide; stable (liver, kidney, pancreas) wait in G0; permanent (neurons, heart muscle) heal only by scar. First intention = clean apposed edges, little scar; second intention = large gap, more granulation and contraction.
  • Slow healing: infection, protein or vitamin C deficiency, steroids, pressure, poor blood flow (diabetes), foreign bodies. Scar problems: hypertrophic scar (raised, inside the wound, can regress), keloid (grows past the wound edges, doesn't regress), exuberant granulation, contracture.
  • Acute-phase response: fever (pyrogens → IL-1 and TNF → prostaglandins reset the hypothalamus), leukocytosis, and liver proteins: CRP (opsonin; heart-attack risk marker), fibrinogen (raises the sedimentation rate), serum amyloid A (secondary amyloidosis), hepcidin (holds iron: anemia of chronic disease).

Neoplasia

A neoplasm is monoclonal growth that ignores normal controls. Dysplasia is disordered, premalignant growth, usually in epithelium; it may not progress.

TissueBenignMalignant
MesenchymalFibroma, chondroma, lipomaSarcoma: fibrosarcoma, chondrosarcoma
EpithelialAdenoma (gland), papilloma (finger-like)Carcinoma: adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma
Rule breakersMalignant despite "-oma": lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma, hepatoma. Mixed tumors: pleomorphic adenoma, teratoma
FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationWell differentiatedVariable; anaplasia (bizarre nuclei, atypical mitoses, lost polarity)
GrowthSlowUsually faster; may outgrow its blood supply and necrose
InvasionFibrous capsule, pushesInfiltrates
MetastasisNeverThe hallmark: lymphatic, blood, seeding of body cavities
  • Clinical: cachexia; paraneoplastic syndromes (about 10-15% of patients: endocrine, nerve, muscle, blood).
  • Diagnosis: biopsy, exfoliative cytology (Pap smear, brush), fine-needle aspiration. Tumor markers screen or follow a tumor; they don't diagnose it.
  • Grade = differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated). Stage = extent: TNM (tumor size and invasion, nodes, distant metastasis), AJCC I-IV. Stage predicts prognosis better than grade.
full.f2-virology:
What's tested
  • What makes a virus a virus; enveloped versus naked viruses (stability, release by budding or lysis)
  • The Baltimore classes, which viruses bring their own RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, and the six steps of the life cycle
  • The human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: their diseases and where each stays latent
  • HPV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and the poxviruses; the RNA viruses (picornaviruses, coronavirus, measles, RSV, rabies, influenza drift and shift)
  • HIV: structure, entry, life cycle, stages and CD4 counts, tests, drug targets and oral signs
  • Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology
  • The oncogenic viruses and how they drive cancer (E6 and p53, E7 and Rb)

Virus basics

Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: a DNA or RNA genome (never both) in a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope taken from the host membrane. They have no ribosomes and make no energy; they are assembled from parts, not divided, and pass through bacterial filters. Capsids are helical or icosahedral (20 faces). Viral attachment proteins bind host receptors, and the receptors set tropism (HIV gp120 needs CD4).

EnvelopedNaked (non-enveloped)
Survives drying, acid, detergentPoorly: must stay wet; most can't survive the gutWell: survive the gut and stay infectious when dry
SpreadBlood, sex, respiratory dropletsFecal-oral, fomites
ReleaseBudding or exocytosis (cell often survives)Lysis of the host cell
ExamplesHerpesviruses, HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, measles, coronavirusHAV, HEV, HPV, adenovirus, polio, parvovirus
ClassGenomeKey pointExamples
IdsDNAHost RNA polymerase makes mRNAHerpes, adeno, HPV, polyoma, pox
IIssDNANeeds host DNA polymerase; dividing cellsParvovirus B19
IIIdsRNAViral RNA polymeraseRotavirus
IV(+)ssRNAGenome is mRNA, read directly; infectiousPicorna (polio, HAV, coxsackie), corona, HCV, HEV
V(−)ssRNAMust carry its own RdRp; genome not infectiousMeasles, RSV, rabies, influenza
VI(+)ssRNA, retroReverse transcriptase makes DNA that integratesHIV, HTLV-1
VIIPartly dsDNA (gapped)Copies itself through an RNA step with reverse transcriptaseHepatitis B

Life cycle: attachment → entry (naked viruses by endocytosis, enveloped ones by fusion) → uncoating → transcription, replication and translation (every virus uses host ribosomes) → assembly → release. DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus, except the poxviruses, which bring their own enzymes and replicate in the cytoplasm. Most RNA viruses stay in the cytoplasm. Viral growth follows a one-step curve, not exponential growth. Disease comes largely from the immune response (fever, rash, liver damage) plus direct killing of cells.

DNA viruses

  • Herpesviruses: large enveloped dsDNA. Immediate-early, early (DNA polymerase), then late (structural) genes; capsids assemble in the nucleus and bud through the nuclear envelope. The hallmark is latency: the genome sits as a circular episome until it reactivates. Drugs such as acyclovir (a nucleoside analog activated by the viral kinase) stop replication but can't touch latent virus.
  • HPV (papillomavirus): naked, circular dsDNA; warts and cancers; vaccine made from capsid protein. Polyomaviruses: large T antigen binds p53; serious only in the immunocompromised.
  • Adenovirus: naked, linear dsDNA; respiratory illness (military recruits), conjunctivitis ("shipyard eye"), gastroenteritis; tough in pools and on fomites; no antiviral.
  • Poxviruses: large, brick-shaped, cytoplasmic; smallpox (eradicated) and mpox, live vaccinia vaccine. Chickenpox is not a poxvirus.
  • Parvovirus B19: tiny naked ssDNA; grows in erythroid precursors in the marrow; fifth disease (slapped cheeks, rash from the immune response) in children, polyarthritis in adults; no vaccine.
VirusDiseaseLatent in
HHV-1 (HSV-1)Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis, herpes labialis, recurrent intraoral herpes on keratinized mucosaTrigeminal ganglion
HHV-2 (HSV-2)Genital and neonatal herpes (either type can infect either site)Sacral (lumbosacral) ganglia
HHV-3 (VZV)Chickenpox; shingles along one dermatome, one side (V2 or V3 gives oral lesions)Dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia
HHV-4 (EBV)Mononucleosis, oral hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinomaB cells
HHV-5 (CMV)Congenital infection, mono-like illness, retinitis in AIDSMonocytes and lymphocytes
HHV-6, HHV-7Roseola (exanthem subitum)T cells
HHV-8 (KSHV)Kaposi sarcoma (palate, gingiva in AIDS)B cells

Alpha herpesviruses (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV) hide in neurons; beta (CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7) and gamma (EBV, HHV-8) in white cells. HSV hides from immunity by lowering MHC class I; its lesions are intraepithelial vesicles with multinucleated giant cells.

RNA viruses

  • (+)ssRNA: the genome is mRNA, so it is infectious; RdRp is made first, then a (−) antigenome as template; replication in cytoplasmic "factories." Picornaviruses (naked, one polyprotein cut by viral proteases, VPg primer; shut off the host's cap-dependent translation): polio, rhinovirus, coxsackie A (herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease) and HAV. Coronaviruses: largest RNA viruses, enveloped; SARS-CoV-2 spike binds ACE2, cut by TMPRSS2; severe disease from immunothrombosis in the alveoli.
  • (−)ssRNA: all enveloped and helical; bring RdRp in the virion; genes near the start are read most. Measles (paramyxovirus; H and F; syncytia): very contagious, infectious before symptoms; cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, then rash; Koplik spots (blue-white specks on red buccal mucosa) come first; MMR live vaccine. RSV (G and F): bronchiolitis, the top cause of pneumonia in infants; maternal vaccine. Rabies (bullet-shaped rhabdovirus): bite, muscle, then retrograde axonal transport to the brain; Negri bodies; long incubation lets vaccine work after exposure.
  • Influenza (orthomyxovirus, 8 segments): hemagglutinin binds sialic acid (α2,6 in humans, α2,3 in birds); neuraminidase cuts it to release new virus (oseltamivir blocks it). Drift = small mutations, all viruses, yearly epidemics. Shift = segments swapped (reassortment), influenza A only, pandemics. Hemagglutination inhibition tests immunity.

Retroviruses and HIV

Enveloped, two copies of (+)ssRNA. Genes: gag (matrix, capsid p24, nucleocapsid), pol (protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase), env (gp120 binds, gp41 fuses), plus Tat, Rev and accessory proteins. Cycle: gp120 binds CD4 then a coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) → fusion → reverse transcription to DNA (the provirus) → integrase inserts it → host RNA polymerase II transcribes → budding → protease cuts Gag so the particle matures and becomes infectious. Lentiviruses (HIV) have long incubations; the other retrovirus groups can cause cancer.

  • Spread: sex (more with genital lesions), mother to child (mostly at delivery; antiretrovirals prevent most), blood, shared needles. Needlestick risk is about 0.3%, versus about 1.8% for HCV and up to 30% for HBV.
  • Stages: acute (flu-like, rash, sore throat; CD4 drops and partly recovers) → clinical latency (years, CD4 falls, symptoms start below 500) → AIDS at CD4 below 200/µL (or an AIDS-defining illness); 5-10 years untreated.
  • Tests: antibody or antigen-antibody (p24) screening; plasma HIV RNA is the most sensitive and tracks treatment; CD4 count stages the disease.
  • Drugs target entry (CCR5), reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease (maturation) and capsid. Even treated patients carry more heart, liver, kidney and cancer risk; the gut lymphoid tissue never fully recovers.
  • Oral signs: candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), linear gingival erythema, necrotizing periodontal disease, HPV warts. No vaccine: fast mutation, sugar-shielded gp120, latency.

Viral hepatitis

VirusFamily, genomeSpreadChronic?Prevention, treatment
HAVPicornavirus, (+)RNA, nakedFecal-oral (food, daycare)NeverVaccine; immune globulin after exposure; IgM = acute, IgG = past or vaccine
HBVHepadnavirus, partly dsDNA, envelopedBlood, sex, birth; lasts 7 days on surfaces90% of infants, about 5% of adultsVaccine; HBIG plus vaccine after exposure; tenofovir or entecavir suppress
HCVFlavivirus, (+)RNA, envelopedBlood (injection drug use; transfusions before 1992)About 85%No vaccine; direct-acting antivirals cure over 95% in 8-12 weeks
HDVDefective circular RNA; borrows HBsAg coatBloodYes; worst as superinfectionOnly with HBV, so HBV vaccine protects
HEVHepevirus, (+)RNA, nakedFecal-oral (water, undercooked meat)Only if immunocompromisedAbout 20% mortality in pregnancy
PatternHBsAgAnti-HBsAnti-HBc
Vaccinated−+−
Recovered from infection−++ (IgG)
Acute infection+−+ (IgM)
Chronic infection (HBsAg over 6 months)+−+ (IgG)

HBeAg = active replication and high infectivity. HBV isn't directly cytopathic: T cells kill infected hepatocytes. Chronic phases: immune tolerant (HBeAg+, normal liver tests), immune active (raised ALT, treat), inactive, reactivation. Watch for hepatocellular carcinoma even without cirrhosis.

Oncogenic viruses

About 12% of cancers worldwide. Cancer follows years of persistent infection plus other factors; it is a side effect, not part of the virus's cycle.

VirusCancerHow
HPV 16 and 18 (high risk)Cervical, oropharyngeal (tonsil, base of tongue) and anogenital carcinomaE6 + E6AP tag p53 for destruction; E7 binds Rb, freeing E2F. HPV 6 and 11 (low risk): warts, papillomas
EBVBurkitt, Hodgkin, diffuse large B cell lymphoma; nasopharyngeal and gastric carcinomaLatency genes (EBNAs, LMP-1) keep B cells alive and dividing
HBVHepatocellular carcinomaHBx blocks p53 and Rb; chronic inflammation and DNA damage
HCVHepatocellular carcinomaCore, NS3, NS5A hold p53; NS5B degrades Rb; inflammation
HTLV-1Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (CD4 T cells)Retrovirus; spread by breast milk, sex, blood
HHV-8Kaposi sarcomaLatency proteins (LANA, vFLIP)

Proto-oncogenes become oncogenes (gain of function); tumor suppressors lose function: p53 (senses DNA damage, stops the cycle before S phase; mutated in over half of cancers) and Rb (holds E2F to block G1 to S).
full.f2-bacteria:
What's tested
  • Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelopes and why they stain differently; acid-fast and wall-less exceptions
  • Structures outside the wall (capsule, pili, fimbriae, flagella, axial filaments), endospores, plasmids and 70S ribosomes as drug targets
  • Growth (binary fission, the growth curve), oxygen needs and the three ways to make ATP
  • Gene transfer: transformation, transduction and conjugation
  • Steps of pathogenesis, virulence factors, biofilms, and exotoxins versus endotoxin with the classic toxins
  • Staphylococcus (abscess, coagulase, MRSA, toxin syndromes) and Streptococcus (pyogenes, pneumoniae, mutans, viridans)
  • The gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, Vibrio, Salmonella, H. pylori), MacConkey agar, the red complex and the spirochetes

The envelope and the gram stain

Gram stain: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol (decolorizer) → safranin. The alcohol step decides it: a thick peptidoglycan wall holds the violet (gram-positive, purple); a thin wall under an outer membrane lets it wash out, and the counterstain makes it pink (gram-negative). Shape and arrangement (cocci in clusters or chains, rods, spirals) complete the first identification.

FeatureGram-positiveGram-negative
Peptidoglycan (NAG-NAM chains cross-linked by peptides)Thick, outside the one membraneThin, in the periplasm between two membranes
Special moleculesTeichoic and lipoteichoic acids (adhesion; TLR2); M protein in S. pyogenesLipopolysaccharide: lipid A (endotoxin), core, O antigen; porins; lipoproteins
Outer membraneNoneYes: blocks many drugs; efflux pumps add resistance
EndotoxinNoYes (lipid A)
SporesSome rods: Bacillus, ClostridiumNo
  • Exceptions: mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids (acid-fast stain; resist drying, drugs and host defenses); Mycoplasma has no wall (sterols in its membrane); Chlamydia and Rickettsia are obligate intracellular and stain poorly. Archaea differ from bacteria by branched, ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan.
  • Drug targets: wall building has three phases, all blockable. β-lactams block the transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) that cross-link the wall; vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala ends. Resistance: β-lactamase, or PBP2a from the mecA gene (MRSA). 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S) are targets too; DNA itself isn't, but replication enzymes are.
  • The bacterial plasma membrane carries the respiratory chain (ATP is made there) and is negatively charged, so cationic antimicrobial peptides target it. The chromosome is one circular, supercoiled DNA; plasmids carry toxin and resistance genes.

Structures outside the wall

  • Capsule (glycocalyx; tight capsule or loose slime layer): antiphagocytic, aids adherence. S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Klebsiella.
  • Fimbriae and pili (pilin): stick to host cells; the sex (conjugation) pilus links bacteria to pass DNA.
  • Flagella: filament (seen by TLR5), hook, basal body; mono-, amphi-, lopho- or peritrichous. Axial filaments in spirochetes run between the membranes and make the cell corkscrew into tissue.
  • Endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium): dormant, resist heat, drying, disinfectants and antibiotics; germinate when conditions improve. Inclusion bodies store glycogen and other materials.

Growth, metabolism, genetics

Bacteria divide by binary fission (wall remodeling, so β-lactams act here); DNA replication starts at one origin and runs both ways. Growth curve: lag → log (exponential; drugs work best) → stationary → death. Most pathogens like neutral pH (H. pylori survives the stomach) and body temperature (T. pallidum prefers cooler parts of the body).

GroupMetabolismExamples
Obligate aerobeNeeds O2; no fermentationM. tuberculosis, Pseudomonas
Facultative anaerobeRespiration with or without O2, or fermentationE. coli, S. aureus, streptococci
MicroaerophileLow O2H. pylori, B. burgdorferi
Obligate anaerobeO2 is toxic; fermentation and anaerobic respirationBacteroides, Clostridium, Porphyromonas
  • Aerobic respiration: glycolysis, TCA cycle, electron transport; final electron acceptor O2; most ATP (about 38).
  • Anaerobic respiration: same pathways; final acceptor an inorganic or other molecule (nitrate, sulfate, carbonate, fumarate); less ATP.
  • Fermentation: glycolysis only; pyruvate is reduced (lactic acid, ethanol) to regenerate NAD+; 2 ATP.
  • No nucleus, so transcription and translation are coupled, and many ribosomes read one mRNA.
RouteHowPoint to know
TransformationUptake of naked DNANeeds a competent cell; Griffith's pneumococci gained a capsule this way
TransductionDNA carried by a bacteriophageGeneralized: random fragments; specialized: only genes beside the prophage
ConjugationDirect contact through a sex pilusF+ donor to F− recipient; plasmids spread resistance and toxins

Pathogenesis

Commensals (the microbiome, largest in the gut) protect by crowding out pathogens, priming immunity and making vitamins. Opportunists (e.g., Candida) cause disease when defenses drop: children, the elderly, the immunocompromised, after antibiotics. Infections are exogenous (food, water, air, fomites, sex), endogenous (normal flora, reactivation) or nosocomial (a catheter-linked UTI). Routes: contact, droplets, fomites, airborne, fecal-oral, vectors. Endemic = steady low level; epidemic = sudden rise; pandemic = across continents.

  1. Adherence: adhesins, pili and fimbriae, flagella, capsule and biofilm sugars; keeps bacteria from being washed away.
  2. Invasion and damage: toxins and enzymes; secretion systems (mostly gram-negative) inject toxins.
  3. Colonization and spread: biofilms (matrix mostly water; on teeth, lenses, devices; resist drugs and immunity; disperse when nutrients run out) and iron scavenging (siderophores, hemolysins).

Extracellular bacteria must avoid opsonization by antibody and complement; intracellular ones must survive the phagolysosome. Polymicrobial synergy: S. mutans with C. albicans makes more acid and more caries. Antagonism: bacteriocins, hydrogen peroxide, nutrient hoarding, surface blanketing. Antibiotics act only on growing cells, not dormant persisters; alternatives include phage therapy and vaccines.

ExotoxinEndotoxin
SourceSecreted by living gram-positive and gram-negative bacteriaLipid A of LPS, gram-negative only, freed when the cell lyses
ChemistryProteinLipopolysaccharide
HeatMostly labile (staph enterotoxin is an exception)Stable
Toxicity, antigenicityHigh; strongly antigenic, so toxoid vaccines (tetanus)Low; weakly antigenic, no toxoid
EffectSpecific action (A-B toxins, superantigens)Fever, septic shock, DIC (IL-1, TNF)

Gram-positive cocci

  • Staphylococci: clusters, catalase-positive, tough on fomites. S. aureus is coagulase-positive; carried by most people at some point; invades through broken skin or mucosa. Virulence: coagulase (fibrin wall), protein A (binds the Fc of antibody, blocking opsonization), leukocidin (kills neutrophils), hemolysins. When neutrophils can't clear it, the body walls it off: an abscess (liquefactive necrosis in a fibrous capsule) that must be drained, since drugs can't get in. About 90% of strains make β-lactamase; methicillin resists that, but mecA (PBP2a) gives MRSA, treated with vancomycin.
  • S. aureus toxin syndromes: food poisoning (preformed, heat-stable enterotoxin; vomiting within hours), scalded skin syndrome (exfoliative toxins split desmosomes; infants), toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1 superantigen, cytokine storm; hypotension kills).
  • S. epidermidis: coagulase-negative skin flora; biofilm on catheters, prosthetic joints and valves; sepsis, endocarditis.
  • Streptococci: chains, catalase-negative. S. pyogenes (group A): M protein (antiphagocytic), pharyngitis, scarlet fever (pyrogenic exotoxin), necrotizing fasciitis, strep toxic shock, then rheumatic fever (cross-reactive antibodies hit the heart) or glomerulonephritis. S. pneumoniae: lancet-shaped diplococci with a thick capsule; the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, often after a viral infection; lobar consolidation, high fever, productive (rusty) sputum; vaccines cover its capsule types. Viridans streptococci (S. mutans, S. sanguinis, S. mitis): caries and infective endocarditis after bleeding in the mouth. S. mutans is acidogenic and aciduric (works down to about pH 4.4) and its glucosyltransferases build sticky glucans from sucrose.

Gram-negative rods and spirochetes

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa: aerobic non-fermenter, everywhere in the environment, multidrug-resistant; a top nosocomial pathogen (devices, ventilators); cystic fibrosis lungs, burns, contact-lens keratitis; aminoglycosides.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: non-motile, thick capsule, mucoid lactose fermenter; necrotizing pneumonia with abscesses, sepsis, UTI. Acinetobacter: drug-resistant wound infections (war wounds). These are ESKAPE pathogens.
  • Gut: secretory diarrhea comes from toxins that cut sodium absorption and raise chloride secretion; treat with fluids. EHEC O157:H7: Shiga toxin (stops protein synthesis) → bloody diarrhea, hemolytic uremic syndrome (kidney failure). Vibrio cholerae: comma-shaped, salt water and shellfish; cholera toxin raises cAMP → massive watery diarrhea; rehydrate. Salmonella: typhoid (enteric) fever, enterocolitis, bacteremia. H. pylori: helical, flagellated, microaerophilic; ulcers and gastric cancer.
  • Identification: analytical profile strips (biochemical tests, fast species ID) and selective and differential media. MacConkey agar grows only gram-negatives; lactose fermenters are pink (E. coli, Klebsiella), non-fermenters pale (Pseudomonas, Salmonella).
  • Periodontitis: gram-negative subgingival anaerobes; the red complex = Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola. T. denticola (spirochete) damages tissue with proteases and hydrogen sulfide.
  • Borrelia burgdorferi: Lyme disease from ticks; rash, fever, facial palsy, meningitis, recurrent arthritis; early 2-week antibiotic course. Eye infections to know: gonococcal conjunctivitis, trachoma (Chlamydia), Pseudomonas keratitis.
full.f2-fungi:
What's tested
  • The fungal cell (chitin wall, ergosterol membrane) and what antifungals target; yeast, mold and dimorphic forms
  • Endemic mycoses by region (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) versus opportunists (Candida, Aspergillus, Mucor, Cryptococcus); levels of mycoses
  • Tuberculosis: spread, the granuloma, IFN-γ and the macrophage, why treatment takes months; nontuberculous mycobacteria
  • Anaerobes: clinical clues, how to sample, the key organisms (Actinomyces, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Clostridium) and drugs
  • Mycoplasma (no wall), Rickettsia (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Chlamydia (elementary and reticulate bodies), Neisseria (gonorrhea versus meningococcus) and syphilis
  • The five tissue reactions to infection and the lab tests (stains, culture, serology, antigen, skin test, PCR)

Fungi

Fungi are eukaryotes with a cell wall of chitin, glucans and mannoproteins (chitin closest to the membrane) and a membrane made with ergosterol, not cholesterol. They are heterotrophs (saprobic, parasitic or mutualistic; no photosynthesis). Drugs: amphotericin B and nystatin (polyenes) bind ergosterol and punch holes; amphotericin also binds some cholesterol, hence kidney toxicity. Azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, clotrimazole) block ergosterol synthesis; echinocandins block glucan synthesis in the wall.

  • Yeasts: single round cells that bud (blastoconidia). Molds: filaments (hyphae, septate or coenocytic without cross walls) forming a mycelium; reproduce by spores (teleomorph = sexual, anamorph = asexual). Dimorphic fungi switch with temperature: mold in the environment, yeast at body temperature.
  • Levels of mycoses: superficial (outer skin and hair; tinea versicolor, cosmetic), cutaneous (keratin of skin, hair, nails: dermatophytes, ringworm, athlete's foot), subcutaneous (after trauma: sporotrichosis from a thorn; abscesses and ulcers that rarely spread), systemic.
FungusWhere and whoKey points
HistoplasmaOhio and Mississippi River valleys; bird or bat droppings (caves, coops)Inhaled; small yeasts inside macrophages; usually mild, patchy pneumonia; granulomas; CD4 T cells clear it; spreads (oral ulcers) in the immunosuppressed; itraconazole
BlastomycesSame river valleysLungs, then often skin and bone lesions; mixed pus and granulomas; itraconazole
CoccidioidesSouthwest desert ("valley fever")Flu-like, joint pains, skin nodules, sometimes cavities; itraconazole or fluconazole
Candida albicansCommensal everywhere; disease when defenses dropThrush; pseudohyphae; switches shape, adhesins, aspartyl proteinases, biofilm
AspergillusNeutropenia; allergic lungsSeptate hyphae branching at acute angles; invade vessels (infarct, bleeding); allergy without invasion
Mucor, RhizopusDiabetic ketoacidosis, neutropeniaBroad hyphae without septa at right angles; invade vessels; rhinocerebral disease with black palatal necrosis
CryptococcusPigeon droppings; AIDSCapsule; meningitis

Endemic (true) pathogens infect healthy people who breathe in spores, and they are thermally dimorphic. Opportunists infect the immunocompromised, are usually not dimorphic and seldom pass between people. (Histoplasma is a true pathogen that is much worse in the immunosuppressed.) Oral candidiasis: white plaques that wipe off leaving a red base, or red atrophic forms under dentures and in angular cheilitis; risks are antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures, diabetes, dry mouth and HIV. With S. mutans it raises caries risk.

Mycobacteria

  • Acid-fast (mycolic acids, arabinogalactan), obligate aerobes, slow-growing. Koch's postulates were worked out on TB, and TB is still a leading infectious killer.
  • Spread: airborne, person to person; lungs in about 90%. Symptoms: cough (sometimes bloody), fever, night sweats, weight loss, chest pain. One active case can infect 10-15 people a year.
  • Pathogenesis: alveolar macrophages eat the bacilli, which block phagolysosome maturation and grow inside; they later escape by killing the cell (necroptosis). CD4 Th1 cells make IFN-γ (driven by IL-12), which activates macrophages to acidify and make ROS and NO. The result is the caseating granuloma. Defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ loop, HIV, malnutrition, age and immunosuppression allow disease or reactivation of latent infection.
  • Tests: PPD skin test (a delayed-type hypersensitivity), acid-fast smear, culture, PCR.
  • Why treatment takes months, with several drugs at once: bacilli hide in granulomas; the waxy envelope is very poorly permeable (intrinsic resistance); slow, drug-tolerant persisters; and single drugs select resistance (streptomycin alone failed within a year). Penicillins don't work. A vaccine (BCG) exists.
  • Nontuberculous mycobacteria (about 200 kinds) come from the environment, not other people; rising, hard to treat, a problem in cystic fibrosis (M. abscessus; phage therapy has worked).
  • Dental note: active TB means delaying elective care and airborne precautions; oral TB is a chronic painless ulcer, often on the tongue.

Anaerobes

Normal flora on almost every mucosa (mouth, colon, vagina), so infections are endogenous and mixed, often with facultative organisms that use up oxygen or make β-lactamase. Suspect them with foul-smelling discharge, a site near a mucosal surface, gas in tissue, or an abscess. Sample by aspirate or tissue, never a swab, in anaerobic transport; culture on rich media with hemin and vitamin K. A gram stain can't tell anaerobes from aerobes. Treat with drainage plus metronidazole, clindamycin or penicillin G (some Bacteroides and Prevotella make β-lactamase); aminoglycosides don't work on anaerobes.

OrganismGram, shapeHomeDisease
Bacteroides fragilisNegative rodColonMixed abscesses; necrotizing fasciitis
Prevotella, PorphyromonasNegative rodsMouthOdontogenic abscess, periodontitis
FusobacteriumNegative rodMouth, colonF. necrophorum: Lemierre syndrome (sore throat, then septic clot in the internal jugular vein, lung emboli; adolescents); F. nucleatum: linked to preterm birth; with spirochetes, necrotizing gingivitis (Vincent angina)
Actinomyces israeliiPositive branching rodMouthCervicofacial "lumpy jaw" after extraction or trauma; crosses tissue planes; draining sinus tracts with yellow sulfur granules; long course of penicillin; also IUD infections
Cutibacterium acnesPositive rodSkinBiofilm on prosthetic joints and shunts
LactobacillusPositive rodVagina, mouthRarely disease; caries
ClostridiumPositive spore-forming rodsColon, soilSee below
Veillonella, PeptostreptococcusNegative and positive cocciMouth, colonMixed infections
  • C. difficile: pseudomembranous colitis after broad-spectrum antibiotics; toxins A and B; diagnose with PCR or immunoassay, not culture (too slow). Infants carry it without disease (no toxin receptors).
  • C. tetani: wound infection making tetanospasmin (A-B toxin) that blocks GABA and glycine release: spastic paralysis, lockjaw.
  • C. botulinum: toxin blocks acetylcholine release: flaccid paralysis; usually preformed toxin in food (also inhaled, a bioterror agent); infant botulism (honey) and wound botulism make toxin in the body; antitoxin.
  • C. perfringens: gas gangrene (myonecrosis, H2 and CO2 in tissue) from alpha toxin (phospholipase C); also food poisoning.

Mycoplasma and Rickettsia

  • Mycoplasma: smallest free-living bacteria, no cell wall (sterols stiffen the membrane), so β-lactams and vancomycin are useless; use macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones. M. pneumoniae: "walking," atypical pneumonia in children and young adults (peak 5-15 years), droplets, slow onset, dry cough, patchy infiltrates; P1 adhesin binds sialic acid; CARDS toxin strips cilia; can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Bell palsy and cold-agglutinin hemolysis. PCR is the most sensitive test; culture takes weeks. M. genitalium: sexually transmitted urethritis, often silent.
  • Rickettsia: tiny obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria that stain poorly; infect endothelial cells, escape the phagosome and spread on actin tails, causing vasculitis, leaky vessels and possibly DIC. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii, dog and wood ticks): fever, headache, myalgia, then a petechial rash starting at the wrists and ankles that spreads inward and reaches the palms and soles; about 23% fatal untreated. Treat with doxycycline at once; confirmation (rising titers in convalescent serum) comes too late to wait for. Murine typhus (R. typhi, rat fleas) is milder and spares palms and soles.

Chlamydia and Neisseria

  • Chlamydia: obligate intracellular, cannot make its own ATP; gram-negative-type envelope without much peptidoglycan, so penicillins fail. Cycle: the elementary body (infectious) enters by endocytosis → becomes a reticulate body that divides inside an inclusion → turns back into elementary bodies released at about 48-72 hours. C. trachomatis: the most common bacterial STI, mostly silent, causes infertility; serovars A-C trachoma (a leading infectious cause of blindness), L1-L3 lymphogranuloma venereum (painless ulcer, buboes, proctitis). Test with NAAT; treat with doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy). C. pneumoniae: atypical pneumonia; C. psittaci: from bird droppings (psittacosis).
  • Neisseria: gram-negative diplococci, aerobic, oxidase- and catalase-positive, fast-growing, humans only.
N. gonorrhoeaeN. meningitidis
SpreadSex; birth canalRespiratory droplets, saliva; crowding
CapsuleNonePolysaccharide capsule
Key virulencePili that vary their antigens (reinfection, no vaccine)Capsule, endotoxin, IgA protease
DiseaseUrethritis, cervicitis (infertility, ectopic pregnancy), pharyngitis, disseminated arthritis and skin lesions; newborn eye infectionMeningitis and meningococcemia (purpura, shock, limb loss); the only meningitis that causes epidemics; asplenia raises risk
Diagnosis, treatmentNAAT best; ceftriaxone 500 mg onceGram stain and culture; give antibiotics at once; contacts get prophylaxis; vaccines

Syphilis

Treponema pallidum is a spirochete that can't be grown in culture (dark-field or serology: RPR or VDRL, confirmed with a treponemal test).
