Primary: painless, firm chancre (can be on the lip or tongue). Secondary: rash on palms and soles, oral mucous patches. Tertiary: gumma (palatal perforation), aorta, nervous system. Congenital: notched incisors, mulberry molars. Treat with penicillin G.

How tissue reacts, and how the lab finds it

PatternWhat it isExample
SuppurativeNeutrophils and pus; abscessS. aureus, streptococci
Mononuclear, granulomatousMacrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells around a persistent agentTB, Histoplasma

Lab: gram stain; acid-fast for TB; PAS and silver (GMS) show fungi (silver also H. pylori); culture (tell the lab what you suspect); serology shows past exposure, useful for organisms hard to grow (Rickettsia, Mycoplasma, hepatitis viruses); antigen tests (ELISA, immunohistochemistry); skin testing (PPD); PCR/NAAT, the test of choice for genital chlamydia and gonorrhea ("CT/NG").
full.om-caries:
What's tested
  • The order of plaque formation: pellicle, reversible then irreversible attachment of pioneer streptococci, coaggregation (F. nucleatum as the bridge), maturation, dispersal
  • S. mutans virulence: adhesins to salivary Gp340, acid production and acid tolerance, glucosyltransferases (GTFs) that turn sucrose into sticky glucans, stored intracellular polysaccharide
  • Why sucrose is special, and soluble α1,6 versus insoluble α1,3 glucans
  • The Stephan curve, the critical pH of 5.5 and the ecological plaque hypothesis
  • Which organism goes with which lesion (S. mutans, Lactobacillus, Actinomyces, Candida) and fluoride's three actions

The oral microbiome

The mouth holds the body's second largest microbial community, after the gut. It was the first human microbiome to be sequenced, and the results are kept in the Human Oral Microbiome Database (HOMD): about 700 species, with Streptococcus the most abundant genus; only about 58% have formal names and about 26% have never been grown in culture.

  • Microscopy shows shape, not species: a Gram stain gives morphology, fluorescence shows plaque in 2D, confocal laser scanning in 3D, and electron microscopy the ultrastructure.
  • Culture on selective media (does it grow?) and differential media (what does it metabolize?).
  • 16S rRNA sequencing of a housekeeping gene identifies organisms that cannot be cultured; it is reliable but costly, and it is how HOMD was built.

The flora is acquired soon after birth and first resembles the mother's; it drifts away as teeth erupt and solid food starts, and its diversity falls in old age. A sucrose-rich diet favors S. mutans; smoking kills commensals while periodontal pathogens survive it; alcohol-containing mouthwash kills normal flora.

Building the biofilm

Dental plaque is a biofilm: microbes in a matrix of exopolysaccharides (such as glucans), proteins, water, host products and extracellular DNA, which cross-links and strengthens it. Bacteria in a biofilm tolerate antimicrobials far better than free-floating cells.

StageWhat happens
1. Acquired pellicleWithin minutes a film of salivary glycoproteins, mucins, immunoglobulins and enzymes (under 1 µm thick) coats a clean tooth. Gp340 is the key receptor.
2. Reversible attachmentPioneer bacteria carried by saliva are held by weak, long-range forces (van der Waals).
3. Irreversible adhesionAdhesins on the pioneers bind pellicle receptors. The pioneers are commensal Gram-positive streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. oralis, S. mitis) and Actinomyces.
4. CoaggregationSecondary colonizers bind bacteria already attached, often through lectin-like adhesins. F. nucleatum is the bridge between early colonizers and the Gram-negative late colonizers.
5. MaturationThe matrix thickens, oxygen falls and Gram-negative anaerobes such as P. gingivalis (tertiary colonizers) settle in.
6. DispersalCells detach, often by degrading their own adhesins, and seed new sites.

Commensals and how microbes interact

  • Mitis group streptococci make hydrogen peroxide, which keeps competitors down and gives alpha (green) hemolysis.
  • Salivarius group: Gram-positive cocci that dominate the healthy tongue, make bacteriocins (salivaricins) and are not linked to disease.
  • Synergy: C. albicans binds streptococcal adhesins and builds a stronger mixed biofilm. With S. mutans it worsens early childhood caries (more acid); with S. oralis it promotes oral candidiasis.
  • Antagonism: one species suppresses another by making an inhibitor (bacteriocins, H₂O₂), hoarding nutrients, or blanketing the surface so others can't attach. The first colonizer has the advantage.
  • Nitrate–nitrite–nitric oxide pathway: commensals reduce dietary nitrate (leafy greens) to nitrite, which becomes nitric oxide or other products that kill pathogens; NO absorbed systemically helps lower blood pressure.

Systemic links taught: infective endocarditis from oral streptococci entering the blood after dental procedures (antibiotic prophylaxis for the highest-risk heart patients); P. gingivalis gingipains found in Alzheimer brain lesions; F. nucleatum in colorectal cancer and preterm birth (its Fap2 lectin binds tumor cells); S. salivarius and S. parasanguinis as the main streptococci in stable cystic fibrosis lungs.

Caries: which organism, which lesion

LesionMain organismsNote
Smooth-surface and pit-and-fissure enamel cariesS. mutans (and S. sobrinus)Initiates the lesion; usually more than 10% of the flora over early lesions
Deep, cavitated dentin cariesLactobacillusDrives progression, not initiation; thrives at low pH
Root-surface cariesActinomyces (A. viscosus/naeslundii), with S. mutans and lactobacilliOlder patients with recession and dry mouth
Early childhood cariesS. mutans with Candida albicansFrequent sugary drinks; the yeast boosts acid production

ICDAS grades lesions by what you see: codes 1–2 are initial enamel changes (white spots, seen dry or wet), 3–4 moderate (enamel breakdown, or a dentin shadow), and 5–6 extensive (a cavity with visible dentin, the largest reaching toward the pulp). G.V. Black's classes I–VI describe location.

S. mutans: why it causes caries

  • Adhesion: surface proteins anchored to the cell wall by the enzyme sortase bind Gp340 in the pellicle. This first attachment does not need sucrose.
  • Acidogenic: ferments sugars to lactic acid.
  • Aciduric: its acid tolerance response keeps its own pH steady by changing membrane proton permeability and fatty acids and making neutralizing ammonia and CO₂.
  • Glucans from sucrose through GTFs: GtfB makes insoluble α1,3 glucan, GtfC both, GtfD only soluble α1,6 glucan.
  • Intracellular polysaccharide (glycogen-like storage) lets it keep making acid between meals.
  • Bacteriocins (mutacins) suppress competitors.

Evidence for its role: it is nearly always found over small lesions, sound sites usually lack it, and longitudinal studies show it appears before caries develops. Keyes' triad: caries needs a susceptible tooth, fermentable carbohydrate and cariogenic bacteria (and time).

Sucrose, glucans and the Stephan curve

Sucrose is split into glucose and fructose. Inside the cell these are fermented (2 ATP per glucose, lactic acid under anaerobic conditions) or stored. Outside the cell, GTF uses the energy of sucrose's high-energy glycosidic bond to chain glucose into glucans; fructosyltransferase (FTF) makes fructans, which are soluble storage and don't help adhesion.

LinkagePropertyRole
α1,3 (and α1,4)Insoluble, stickyMakes attachment irreversible; the cariogenic matrix
α1,6Soluble, not stickyEnergy storage; little cariogenic effect

Grown on glucose plus fructose alone, S. mutans still grows but cannot clump or stick: without sucrose's bond energy it can't make glucans.

Stephan curve: within minutes of a sugar exposure plaque pH drops below the critical pH of 5.5, where enamel starts to dissolve, then recovers over 30–60 minutes as saliva's bicarbonate buffers it. Frequent exposures keep the plaque acidic longer, so how often matters more than how much.

  • Acidogenic (chemoparasitic) theory: plaque bacteria ferment sugar to acid that dissolves enamel.
  • Ecological plaque hypothesis: frequent sugar keeps the pH low, which kills acid-sensitive commensals and selects acid-tolerant species; low saliva flow makes it worse.
  • Quorum signal autoinducer-2 at high levels inhibits commensals, so an older biofilm drifts toward pathogens.

Prevention and fluoride

  • Cut sucrose (especially how often), lower S. mutans (antimicrobial rinses, sealants), experimental vaccines, and replacement therapy with a strain lacking lactate dehydrogenase.
  • Fluoride works three ways: forms fluorapatite, which resists acid (critical pH about 4.5); promotes remineralization of incipient lesions; and inhibits the bacterial glycolytic enzyme enolase, so less acid and less energy.
  • Fluoride does not inhibit lactobacilli, so its antibacterial effect matters mostly in early, noncavitated lesions dominated by S. mutans.
  • History: McKay and Black linked mottled enamel to fewer caries; Dean found the benefit without mottling at lower levels (about 1 ppm). Community water fluoridation cut caries by about 60%.
full.om-perendo:
What's tested
  • The red complex (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) and its link to deep pockets and bleeding; the orange complex (F. nucleatum) as the bridge that comes first
  • The plaque hypotheses: nonspecific, specific, ecological/keystone (P. gingivalis as the keystone pathogen)
  • P. gingivalis traits and virulence factors (gingipains); A. actinomycetemcomitans and its leukotoxin in molar-incisor (localized aggressive) periodontitis
  • Host response and bone loss: antigen presentation, cytokines, RANKL and osteoclasts; the three routes to systemic disease
  • Pulp infection: routes, dentinal tubule size, the shift to obligate anaerobes, E. faecalis in persistent infection, and which treatment fits which stage

Periodontitis in one paragraph

Periodontitis is chronic, bacteria-driven inflammation that destroys periodontal connective tissue and alveolar bone; bone resorption is its hallmark. It is the main cause of tooth loss in adults and affects about half of adults 30 and older. Caries and gingivitis are driven by supragingival plaque; periodontitis by subgingival plaque.

The plaque hypotheses

HypothesisClaim
NonspecificThe total mass of plaque (a consortium of subgingival bacteria) causes disease, not any single species.
SpecificDisease comes from a shift to particular pathogens that are absent or rare in health. Socransky's 1998 study of over 13,000 subgingival samples grouped them into color-coded complexes.
Ecological / keystoneA synergistic, dysbiotic community causes disease. A low-abundance keystone pathogen (P. gingivalis) remodels a benign community into a destructive one.
  • Red complex: P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola; strongest relationship with pocket depth and bleeding on probing.
  • Orange complex (F. nucleatum, Prevotella intermedia and others) colonizes before the red complex and bridges early colonizers to it.
  • Red complex paradox: red complex organisms are found in healthy mouths, disease can start without them, the flora is more diverse than thought, and P. gingivalis is often scarce in diseased plaque. P. gingivalis is easiest of the three to grow in the lab, not more important.
  • As keystone pathogen, P. gingivalis delays neutrophil recruitment and subverts complement so the whole community overgrows, shifting it toward anaerobes; it cannot cause periodontitis without commensal bacteria.

Two organisms to know cold

P. gingivalisA. actinomycetemcomitans
Shape and oxygenGram-negative, nonmotile rod, obligate anaerobeGram-negative coccobacillus, facultative anaerobe
Lab cluesBlack-pigmented colonies on blood agar; needs iron (hemin); asaccharolytic (ferments amino acids, not sugar)Capnophilic (likes CO₂)
DiseaseChronic (adult) periodontitis; red complexLocalized aggressive periodontitis, now the molar-incisor pattern: teens and young adults, bone loss at first molars and incisors with little plaque
Key virulenceGingipains (arginine- and lysine-specific proteases), fimbriae, LPS, capsule, Ig and complement proteases, collagenaseLeukotoxin A, which kills neutrophils and monocytes; cytolethal distending toxin

P. gingivalis virulence factors by job: colonize (fimbriae, hemagglutinins, outer membrane proteins, vesicles); evade the host (LPS, capsule, Ig and complement proteases); multiply (gingipains, hemolysins for iron); destroy and spread (gingipains, collagenase, trypsin-like and other hydrolytic enzymes). It is a weak trigger of inflammation, which helps it hide. Other members: T. forsythia (proteases), T. denticola (a motile spirochete; hydrogen sulfide).

Host response and bone loss

  • Neutrophils are the first line in the sulcus; neutrophil defects predispose to severe disease.
  • Innate cells capture pathogens and present antigen with costimulatory signals to naive T cells, which release proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17); prostaglandin E₂ and matrix metalloproteinases destroy tissue.
  • Cross talk between immune cells raises RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors; OPG is the decoy that blocks it. More RANKL than OPG means bone resorption. This field is osteoimmunology.

Three links to systemic disease: bacterial dissemination (bacteremia, inhalation, swallowing); dissemination of inflammatory mediators, with trained myelopoiesis (innate immune memory) amplifying later responses; and oropharyngeal aspiration and oro-digestive translocation.

Pulp infection

Pulp necrosis is an anaerobic, polymicrobial, endogenous infection (the patient's own flora). The main cause is pulp exposure: caries, trauma, restorative procedures, attrition or abrasion, a periodontal pocket, or a developmental anomaly. Canal bacteria feed on necrotic pulp, tissue fluid seeping in through the apical and lateral foramina, saliva entering coronally, and each other's products.

  • Routes: from the mouth through dentinal tubules (main route), from the periodontium through lateral or apical foramina, and from the blood through the apex (anachoresis).
  • Tubule size: widest near the pulp (about 2.5 µm), narrowest near enamel or cementum (about 0.9 µm); most oral bacteria are 0.2–0.7 µm, so even the narrow ends admit them. Most are nonmotile and are pushed in by cell division and hydrostatic pressure.
  • Sequence: biofilm on enamel, acid reaches dentin, bacterial products diffuse to the pulp and inflame it, bacteria meet the pulp directly, host and microbes battle, and if the host loses the pulp becomes necrotic and colonized.
  • Ecological shift: crown, aerobes and anaerobes; pulp chamber, facultative bacteria at first; root canal after days or weeks, as oxygen and blood supply go, obligate anaerobes dominate, and they dominate the periapical bone too.
  • E. faecalis: Gram-positive facultative coccus of persistent or failed root canals; drug resistant, survives starvation and calcium hydroxide, invades tubules.
  • In primary molars the infection tends to show at the furcation (accessory canals, large pulp); in permanent teeth, at the apex.

Diagnosis and treatment

Diagnosis weighs severity (reversible or not, necrosis?), duration (acute or chronic), symptoms and vitality, from history, pain features, the exam (discoloration, palpation, percussion, pulp tests, mobility, bite test), swelling or sinus tract, and a periapical radiograph.

  • Pulp polyp (chronic hyperplastic pulpitis): a red, fleshy mass of inflamed pulp filling a large open cavity, bleeds easily, chronic and usually painless; young patients.
  • Space infection of dental origin: spread past the apex into fascial spaces or sinuses; mostly anaerobes; swelling and pain; a true emergency because it can reach the brain.
How far the infection has goneTreatment
Just reached the pulpDirect or indirect pulp cap
Coronal pulp onlyPulpotomy
Into the canals, mature toothPulpectomy (root canal treatment)
Immature tooth, pulp still vitalApexogenesis: keep the pulp alive so the root keeps forming
Immature tooth, pulp necroticApexification (artificial apical barrier, calcium hydroxide or MTA) or a regenerative procedure: disinfect with triple antibiotic paste, induce apical bleeding, seal with MTA or Biodentine
Past the apex, spreadingAntibiotics and drainage or extraction

Regeneration depends on stem cells (DPSCs, SHED, SCAPs, PDLSCs, BMSSCs), a scaffold and signaling molecules. Terms: revascularization restores blood supply to an immature tooth; revitalization is ingrowth of vital tissue unlike the original; regeneration restores the original structure and function.

Virus basics

A virus is packaged nucleic acid that needs a host cell. Steps: receptor-mediated entry, genome replication, translation of viral proteins, packaging into virions, and escape.

The herpesviruses

Large, enveloped, linear dsDNA viruses with an icosahedral capsid and a tegument layer. They replicate and assemble in the nucleus. Infection is lytic (kills the cell, makes lesions) or latent (lifelong); stress, UV light, hormones, other infections or immune suppression reactivate it. All eight human herpesviruses can affect the mouth; PCR tells them apart.

VirusLatencyOral and head-and-neck picture
HSV-1 (and HSV-2)Trigeminal ganglion (HSV-2: sacral)Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis in children; recurrent herpes labialis; herpetic whitlow on a finger. Spread by saliva during lytic shedding. Treat with antivirals (polymerase inhibitors such as acyclovir).
VZV (HHV-3)Sensory (dorsal root and cranial) gangliaChickenpox; shingles in older or immunosuppressed patients: painful unilateral vesicles in one dermatome, stopping at the midline, oral lesions on lip and palate. Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear vesicles) is VZV in the geniculate ganglion. Vaccines exist for both.
EBV (HHV-4)B cells; oral epithelium and tonsilInfectious mononucleosis (saliva, 'kissing disease'); oral hairy leukoplakia; Burkitt lymphoma (with malaria), Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma. About 90% of Americans are seropositive by 25.
CMV (HHV-5)Monocytes, salivary glandSpread by saliva, urine, sex and mother to fetus; congenital infection causes enamel hypoplasia; common in HIV; no vaccine.
HHV-6 and HHV-7Salivary glandsSpread by saliva; no oral lesions; HHV-6 reactivation can cause encephalitis or pneumonitis in the immunosuppressed.
HHV-8 (KSHV)B cellsKaposi sarcoma in immunosuppressed patients: blue-red-purple lesions, classically at the hard–soft palate junction or on the gingiva.

Other DNA viruses

  • HPV: small, nonenveloped, circular dsDNA; replicates in basal squamous cells and assembles as they mature. Spread by direct contact. Oral lesions: squamous papilloma (finger-like, rough surface) and multifocal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck disease), soft painless nodules that regress on their own. About 20% of oral squamous cell carcinomas contain HPV, but tobacco and alcohol are the usual cause in the mouth proper.
  • Mpox: large dsDNA, brick-shaped virion; oral lesions are often the first to appear; a vaccine exists.

RNA viruses

VirusGenomeOral signPrevention
Enteroviruses: coxsackievirus A16 and A6, enterovirus 71(+) ssRNA, nonenveloped, hard to kill; fecal-oralHand, foot and mouth disease; herpangina (vesicles on the soft palate and pillars). Self-limited but very contagious.No vaccine or antiviral
Mumps (paramyxovirus)(−) ssRNAPainful parotid swelling; respiratory spreadHighly effective vaccine
Measles (paramyxovirus)(−) ssRNAKoplik spots: tiny white spots on red buccal mucosa, before the rash; extremely contagiousHighly effective vaccine
Rubella (German, 3-day measles)(+) ssRNA, envelopedRed macules and inflamed tonsils; congenital rubella causes missing teeth and enamel hypoplasiaHighly effective vaccine

Oral infection and cancer

  • Cancer cells divide without control, lose differentiation and contact inhibition, grow new vessels, invade, metastasize, hide from immunity and use nutrients differently.
  • Oncogene activation ('stepping on the gas'): a proto-oncogene gains function; dominant, one copy is enough.
  • Tumor suppressor loss ('removing the brakes'): usually both copies must go. Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: in inherited cancer every cell, gametes included, carries the first hit, and the tumor arises where the second hit happens.
  • About 90% of cancers involve several genes; about 10% are single-gene disorders.
AgentCancer link
HPV-16 and HPV-18Oropharyngeal (tonsil, base of tongue), cervical, anal, penile, vaginal; E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb. All approved vaccines cover 16 and 18.
EBVNasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, gastric cancer; linked to childhood ALL
H. pyloriChronic gastritis and ulcers, the strongest risk for gastric adenocarcinoma; the mouth and tonsils are reservoirs for reinfection
F. nucleatumEnriched in oral and colorectal tumors; enters cells through its FadA adhesin and turns on pro-tumor signaling
P. gingivalisRaises proliferation, invasion and metalloproteinases in oral cancer cells; linked to colorectal and pancreatic cancer
E. faecalisFound in oral cancer tissue; endodontic organism

Head and neck cancers are about 3% of new cancers. Oral and oropharyngeal cancer: twice as common in men, varied in appearance, usually found at stage III or IV; 5-year survival about 64%, and early diagnosis raises it to about 90%. Risk factors: tobacco (about 85% of head and neck cancers, including smokeless and secondhand), alcohol and HPV.
full.ns-anat:
What's tested
  • Glial cells and what each does; neuron shapes and axonal transport
  • Meninges, the dural reflections, herniation, and the three intracranial bleeds (source, space, shape on imaging)
  • The cavernous sinus and what runs in it; CSF flow through the ventricles
  • Lobes, sulci and the key cortical areas (motor, sensory, Broca, Wernicke, visual, auditory)
  • Development: germ layers, neural tube and crest, brain vesicles, neural tube defects and folate
  • Spinal cord levels, horns and funiculi, blood supply and the cord syndromes; spinal reflexes
  • Brainstem parts, the "rule of 4", medial and lateral medullary syndromes
  • Each cranial nerve's job, its parasympathetic ganglion and the lesion sign; thalamic and hypothalamic nuclei

Cells of the nervous system

  • Neurons: most CNS neurons are multipolar; bipolar neurons sit in the retina and olfactory epithelium; pseudounipolar neurons are the sensory neurons of the dorsal root and cranial ganglia. Nissl bodies are the neuron's rough ER. Anterograde transport (kinesin) carries cargo from the soma to the terminal; retrograde transport (dynein) carries it back to the soma, the route rabies, herpes and tetanus toxin use.
  • Astrocytes: the most numerous glia; take up K⁺ and glutamate, help form the blood-brain barrier, regulate blood flow and synapse formation, form the glial scar.
  • Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons (lost in MS); Schwann cells myelinate one PNS axon segment each (lost in Guillain-Barré) and help peripheral nerves regenerate.
  • Microglia: CNS macrophages (from mesoderm, not neural tube). Ependymal cells line the ventricles; the choroid plexus makes CSF. Satellite cells surround cell bodies in PNS ganglia.
  • Nerve wrappings: epineurium (whole nerve), perineurium (each fascicle), endoneurium (each fiber).

Meninges, bleeds and the cavernous sinus

The dura has a periosteal layer (on the skull, sensory supply from CN V, blood from the middle meningeal artery) and a meningeal layer that folds into the falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli and diaphragma sellae, and splits to form the venous sinuses. The tentorium divides the skull into supratentorial (cerebrum) and infratentorial (cerebellum, brainstem) spaces; the brainstem passes through the tentorial notch. Herniation is brain pushed past a dural fold by raised pressure (bleed, tumor, trauma). The arachnoid is avascular; its villi and granulations return CSF to the venous sinuses. The pia follows every gyrus.

BleedSourceSpaceImaging and story
EpiduralMiddle meningeal artery (enters by foramen spinosum)Skull–duraLens-shaped (biconvex); temporal blow, lucid interval
SubduralBridging veinsDura–arachnoidCrescent-shaped; elderly, alcohol use, slower onset
SubarachnoidRuptured berry aneurysm (circle of Willis)Subarachnoid space (CSF)"Worst headache of my life"; blood in the sulci and cisterns

The cavernous sinus sits beside the sella turcica. The internal carotid artery and CN VI run through the sinus itself; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its lateral wall. A spreading infection from the face's "danger triangle" can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, and CN VI is often the first nerve hit (the eye cannot abduct).

Ventricles and cortex

CSF flows: lateral ventricles → interventricular foramen → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures to the subarachnoid space (and the central canal). The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal lobe, the lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes, and the parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal from occipital. White matter: association fibers (front to back, same hemisphere), commissural fibers (side to side, corpus callosum) and projection fibers (up and down, internal capsule).

AreaWhereLesion
Primary motorPrecentral gyrus (frontal)Contralateral weakness
Primary somatosensoryPostcentral gyrus (parietal)Contralateral sensory loss
Broca (speech output)Inferior frontal gyrus, dominant (usually left)Non-fluent aphasia, comprehension kept
Wernicke (comprehension)Posterior superior temporal gyrus, dominantFluent but meaningless speech
Primary visual (V1, area 17)Occipital lobe, calcarine sulcusContralateral visual field loss
Primary auditorySuperior temporal gyrus (Heschl)Hearing processing deficits
Frontal eye fieldsFrontal lobeEyes deviate toward the lesion

Development

  • Gastrulation makes three germ layers; the notochord (mesoderm) induces the overlying ectoderm to become the neural plate by blocking BMP.
  • Neurulation: the plate folds into the neural tube (brain and spinal cord); neural crest cells leave its edges and form the PNS: dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, and in the head much of the face and teeth (odontoblasts, dental pulp).
  • Failure of the anterior neuropore to close gives anencephaly; failure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk.
  • Vesicles: prosencephalon → telencephalon (cerebrum, lateral ventricles) and diencephalon (third ventricle); mesencephalon → midbrain (aqueduct); rhombencephalon → metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla), both on the fourth ventricle.
  • Later steps: neurogenesis and migration (failure: lissencephaly, smooth brain; periventricular heterotopia), synaptogenesis, then apoptosis and pruning, then myelination, which continues into adulthood. Synapse-refinement errors are linked to autism and schizophrenia.

Spinal cord and reflexes

31 segments (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal). The cord ends at about L1–L2 (conus medullaris); below it the cauda equina floats in the lumbar cistern, which is why a lumbar puncture goes in at L3–L5. Enlargements: cervical C5–T1 (arms), lumbosacral L1–S3 (legs). The dorsal horn is sensory, the ventral horn holds lower motor neurons, and the lateral horn (T1–L2) holds sympathetic preganglionic neurons. White matter shrinks toward the sacral cord. Blood: one anterior spinal artery (anterior two thirds: corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) and two posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns); the artery of Adamkiewicz (around T9–T12) feeds the lower cord.

  • Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery): bilateral weakness and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion; vibration and position sense spared.
  • Brown-Séquard (hemisection): ipsilateral weakness and loss of fine touch, vibration and proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting a level or two below.
  • Stretch reflex: monosynaptic; muscle spindle → Ia afferent → alpha motor neuron, with reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist. Golgi tendon organ: Ib afferents sense tension and relax the muscle. Withdrawal reflex: polysynaptic, flexes the stimulated limb and extends the opposite one. Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity. Motor units are recruited smallest (slow) to largest (fast): the size principle.

Brainstem and the rule of 4

Midbrain (from the mesencephalon) has the colliculi (superior: visual reflexes; inferior: auditory), substantia nigra, red nucleus and cerebral peduncles; the pons has the locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) and crossing pontine fibers; the medulla has the pyramids (corticospinal decussation), olives and the area postrema (vomiting center, weak blood-brain barrier). The reticular formation keeps us awake; raphe nuclei make serotonin.

Rule of 4: four nerves above the pons (I–IV), four in the pons (V–VIII), four in the medulla (IX–XII). Four medial "M" structures: motor (corticospinal) tract, medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, motor nuclei III, IV, VI, XII. Four lateral "S" structures: spinocerebellar tract, spinothalamic tract, sensory nucleus of V, sympathetic pathway.

  • Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal or vertebral branches): contralateral weakness and loss of vibration/position sense, tongue deviates toward the lesion (XII).
  • Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome (PICA or vertebral): ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss with contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo, and hoarseness and trouble swallowing (nucleus ambiguus, IX and X).

Cranial nerves

NerveKey jobsLesion sign
III OculomotorMost eye muscles, levator; pupil constriction (ciliary ganglion)Eye "down and out", ptosis, dilated pupil
IV TrochlearSuperior obliqueVertical diplopia, worse going downstairs
V TrigeminalFace sensation; V3 muscles of masticationV3 lesion: jaw deviates toward the lesion
VI AbducensLateral rectusEye cannot abduct
VII FacialFacial expression; taste anterior 2/3; lacrimal (pterygopalatine), submandibular and sublingual (submandibular ganglion)Bell palsy: whole half of face, forehead included
IX GlossopharyngealTaste and sensation posterior 1/3; parotid (otic ganglion); carotid sinus; gag afferentLost gag on that side
X VagusPalate, pharynx, larynx; viscera to the proximal colon; gag efferentUvula deviates away from the lesion; hoarseness
XI AccessorySCM and trapeziusWeak shoulder shrug and head turn
XII HypoglossalTongue musclesTongue deviates toward the lesion

Diencephalon

Thalamus: the relay for every sense except smell. VPL (body) and VPM (face, and taste) → somatosensory cortex; LGN → visual cortex; MGN → auditory cortex; VA/VL carry basal ganglia and cerebellar output to motor cortex; the anterior nucleus is part of the limbic (Papez) circuit. A thalamic stroke (PCA branches) causes contralateral loss of all sensation and can leave thalamic pain. Damage to the dorsomedial thalamus and mammillary bodies with thiamine deficiency gives Wernicke-Korsakoff (confusion, eye-movement palsy, ataxia, then amnesia). Hypothalamus: lateral nucleus hunger, ventromedial satiety, anterior heat loss, posterior heat conservation, suprachiasmatic clock, supraoptic and paraventricular make ADH and oxytocin. Epithalamus: the pineal gland makes melatonin.
full.ns-path:
What's tested
  • The dorsal column–medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways: neurons, where each crosses, what a lesion takes away
  • The trigeminal sensory system: its three nuclei, VPM, the jaw-jerk and corneal reflexes
  • Upper versus lower motor neuron signs; corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts; Guillain-Barré, myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton
  • Cerebellar divisions, peduncles, circuitry and signs (always on the same side)
  • Basal ganglia direct and indirect pathways; Parkinson and Huntington disease
  • Circle of Willis, the ACA, MCA and PCA syndromes, lacunar and brainstem strokes, stroke treatment

The two sensory highways

Somatosensory pathways are three-neuron chains: first-order neuron in a dorsal root or cranial ganglion, second-order neuron in the cord or brainstem (its axon crosses), third-order neuron in the thalamus projecting to the postcentral gyrus through the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

Dorsal column–medial lemniscusSpinothalamic (anterolateral)
CarriesFine touch, vibration, proprioception, two-point discriminationPain, temperature, crude touch
FibersLarge myelinated Aβ (Aα for proprioception)Aδ (fast, sharp) and C (slow, burning)
Second-order neuronNucleus gracilis (legs) and cuneatus (arms), medullaDorsal horn, after Lissauer's tract (1–2 levels up or down)
CrossesMedulla (internal arcuate fibers → medial lemniscus)Spinal cord, anterior white commissure
Cord lesionSame-side loss below the lesionOpposite-side loss starting 1–2 segments below
ThalamusVPLVPL (pain also to intralaminar nuclei)

Receptors: phasic (fast-adapting) ones signal change and vibration; tonic (slow-adapting) ones signal steady pressure. Small receptive fields (fingertips, lips) localize precisely. Pain reaches more than one place: VPL/VPM → S1 and S2 for where and how strong, medial thalamus → insula for the autonomic part, intralaminar nuclei → anterior cingulate for the emotional part.

The trigeminal system (the dental pathway)

  • First-order cell bodies sit in the trigeminal (semilunar) ganglion, with one exception: proprioceptive neurons from the muscles of mastication and the periodontal ligament have their cell bodies in the mesencephalic nucleus, the only primary sensory neurons inside the CNS.
  • Principal (main) sensory nucleus (pons): discriminative touch from the face and teeth, the face's version of the dorsal columns.
  • Spinal trigeminal nucleus (pons down to upper cervical cord): pain and temperature, the face's spinothalamic system. Its descending tract explains why a lateral medullary stroke takes away pain on the same side of the face.
  • Second-order axons cross and ascend as the trigeminothalamic tract to the VPM, then to the face area of the postcentral gyrus (lateral, low on the homunculus).
  • Reflexes: jaw jerk (monosynaptic, mesencephalic nucleus → motor nucleus of V; brisk with an upper motor neuron lesion above the pons); corneal reflex (afferent V1, efferent VII, both eyes blink).

Motor pathways: UMN and LMN

The motor system is a two-neuron chain. The upper motor neuron starts in the primary motor cortex (and premotor areas), runs through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, basilar pons and medullary pyramid. About 90% of corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract (limbs); the rest form the anterior tract (trunk, both sides). The lower motor neuron sits in the ventral horn or a cranial nerve motor nucleus and goes to muscle. Corticobulbar fibers reach the cranial nerve motor nuclei, mostly from both hemispheres; the exceptions are the lower face (VII) and, in many people, the tongue (XII), which get mainly crossed input. So a cortical stroke weakens the contralateral lower face but spares the forehead.

SignUpper motor neuronLower motor neuron
WeaknessSpasticFlaccid
ReflexesHyperreflexia, clonusHyporeflexia or areflexia
BabinskiPresent (big toe goes up, toes fan)Absent (toes go down)
AtrophyMild, from disuseMarked
FasciculationsNoYes
ExamplesStroke, MS, cord injuryPolio, peripheral nerve injury, Bell palsy

A lesion above the decussation (cortex, internal capsule, brainstem) weakens the opposite side; a lesion in the cord weakens the same side. ALS has both UMN and LMN signs. Premotor lesions cause apraxia: strength is normal, but learned movements cannot be planned.

  • Guillain-Barré syndrome: autoimmune attack on peripheral myelin, often after a Campylobacter or viral infection; ascending flaccid weakness and tingling with lost reflexes; can involve the face and breathing. Treated with IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange.
  • Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic ACh receptors; fatigable weakness that worsens through the day, often ptosis, diplopia, and weak chewing and swallowing. Treated with cholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine). Dental: book short morning visits.
  • Lambert-Eaton syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, often with small cell lung cancer; proximal weakness that improves with use.

Cerebellum

  • Vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe): balance and eye movements; damage gives nystagmus and a wide-based, unsteady stance.
  • Spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate zone): posture and tone; damage gives truncal ataxia and gait problems.
  • Cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres): planning skilled limb movement; damage gives limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing) and dysdiadochokinesia (cannot alternate fast movements), and slurred speech.

Peduncles: superior (midbrain, mainly output), middle (pons, input from cortex through the pontine nuclei), inferior (medulla, input from the spinocerebellar tracts and the inferior olive). Cortex layers: molecular, Purkinje, granular. Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex and are inhibitory (GABA), as are basket and stellate cells; mossy fibers, climbing fibers (from the inferior olive) and granule cells are excitatory (glutamate). Deep nuclei: dentate, emboliform and globose (interposed), fastigial. Because the pathway crosses twice (into the cerebellum through the pons, out through the superior peduncle, then back in the pyramids), cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion. Arteries: SCA, AICA, PICA.

Basal ganglia, Parkinson and Huntington

Loop: cortex → striatum (caudate and putamen) → globus pallidus internus/substantia nigra pars reticulata → VA/VL thalamus → cortex. The output (GPi) is inhibitory on the thalamus. The direct pathway inhibits GPi, freeing the thalamus: it promotes movement. The indirect pathway (through GPe and the subthalamic nucleus) strengthens GPi: it inhibits movement. Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta excites the direct pathway through D1 and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2, so both actions promote movement.

  • Parkinson disease (hypokinetic): loss of nigral dopamine neurons with Lewy bodies (α-synuclein). Signs appear after most striatal dopamine is gone: resting tremor ("pill-rolling"), rigidity (cogwheel), bradykinesia, postural instability. Early non-motor signs: lost smell, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder (strongest predictor), depression, orthostatic hypotension. The drugs are in the disease section.
  • Huntington disease (hyperkinetic): autosomal dominant CAG repeat in the HTT gene (chromosome 4); 40 or more repeats always cause disease; repeats lengthen in sperm, so onset comes earlier in the next generation (anticipation, mostly through the father). Loss of GABA neurons in the caudate (indirect pathway) → chorea, with psychiatric change (often first), dementia, dysarthria and dysphagia; death is often from aspiration pneumonia. Chorea is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine) or antipsychotics. A subthalamic nucleus lesion causes hemiballismus on the opposite side.

Cerebral circulation and stroke

Anterior circulation: internal carotid → ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, then ACA and MCA. Posterior circulation: vertebrals (PICA) → basilar (AICA, SCA, pontine branches) → PCA. The circle of Willis joins them through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries; berry aneurysms favor the anterior communicating artery. About 80% of strokes are ischemic and 20% hemorrhagic. Recognize with FAST (face, arm, speech, time).

ArteryTerritorySigns
ACAMedial frontal and parietal (leg area)Contralateral leg weakness and numbness
MCA (most common)Lateral hemisphereContralateral face and arm more than leg; homonymous field cut; aphasia if dominant (left), neglect if non-dominant (right)
PCAOccipital lobe, medial temporal lobe, thalamusContralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing; thalamic sensory loss
Lenticulostriate (MCA)Internal capsule, basal gangliaLacunar stroke: pure motor or pure sensory, no cortical signs; linked to hypertension
Basilar (pons)Basilar ponsLocked-in syndrome: quadriplegia, awake, vertical eye movements kept
PICALateral medullaWallenberg syndrome (crossed pain loss, Horner, hoarseness)

Treatment: for ischemic stroke, IV thrombolysis (tPA) within about 4.5 hours once bleeding is ruled out by CT, and clot retrieval for large-vessel blockage; afterward aspirin or other antiplatelet drugs, anticoagulants for atrial fibrillation, statins and risk-factor control (hypertension is the biggest modifiable one). Dental points: the patient is often on antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs (control bleeding locally instead of stopping them), elective care traditionally waits until the patient is stable, often about 6 months; keep visits short and watch blood pressure.
full.ns-phys:
What's tested
  • Why the resting membrane potential sits near the K⁺ equilibrium potential; the Nernst equation; what changing [K⁺] does
  • The ion channels before, during and after an action potential; refractory periods; myelin and saltatory conduction
  • Electrical versus chemical synapses; Ca²⁺ and vesicle release; ionotropic versus metabotropic receptors; NMDA; EPSPs and IPSPs
  • Local anesthetics: structure and class, mechanism, pKa and onset, lipid solubility and potency, protein binding and duration, metabolism, allergy, toxicity (LAST)
  • General anesthesia: its components, how the drugs act (GABA-A, NMDA), MAC, the levels of sedation

Resting membrane potential

At rest the membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to anything else, so the resting potential (about −65 to −70 mV in a neuron) sits close to EK (about −90 mV). A small Na⁺ leak pulls it a little more positive. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) keeps the gradients; it does not itself create most of the voltage. The Nernst equation gives one ion's equilibrium potential (no net movement): E = (61/z) log([out]/[in]) at body temperature, so a tenfold gradient gives about 60 mV. Raising extracellular K⁺ (hyperkalemia) makes EK less negative and depolarizes the cell. Equal concentrations on both sides give E = 0. The Goldman equation combines all ions by their relative permeability. Typical values: ENa ≈ +60 mV, EK ≈ −90 mV, ECa ≈ +130 mV, ECl ≈ −70 mV.

The action potential

  • Threshold: a stimulus depolarizes the membrane enough to open voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
  • Upstroke: Na⁺ rushes in; the membrane heads toward ENa and overshoots 0 mV.
  • Repolarization: Na⁺ channels inactivate and the slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ leaves.
  • Afterhyperpolarization: K⁺ channels close slowly, so the membrane dips below rest.
  • Absolute refractory period: Na⁺ channels are inactivated; no stimulus can fire the cell. Relative refractory period: a stronger stimulus can.

Passive properties: the membrane is a capacitor (time constant τ = RmCm); the length constant says how far a signal spreads before fading. Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so current runs farther and faster; the action potential regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier, where Na⁺ channels cluster (saltatory conduction). Bigger diameter and more myelin mean faster conduction: Aα (proprioception) > Aβ (touch) > Aδ (sharp pain, cold) > C (unmyelinated, dull pain, warmth). Demyelination (MS in the CNS, Guillain-Barré in the PNS) slows or blocks conduction.

Synapses

Electrical synapses are gap junctions: very fast, two-way, used where cells must fire together. Chemical synapses (the usual kind, a 20–50 nm cleft) work in steps: the action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the terminal, Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion through the SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25), transmitter crosses the cleft and binds receptors, and it is removed by diffusion, reuptake or enzymes (acetylcholinesterase for ACh). Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks ACh release (flaccid paralysis; used cosmetically and for bruxism and spasticity); tetanus toxin blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters glycine and GABA (spastic paralysis, lockjaw). The neuromuscular junction is "fail-safe": one motor neuron action potential always fires the muscle fiber.

  • Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels: fast (nicotinic ACh, AMPA, NMDA, GABA-A, glycine). Metabotropic receptors are G-protein-coupled: slower, longer-lasting (muscarinic ACh, adrenergic, dopamine, most peptide receptors, GABA-B). The receptor, not the transmitter, decides the effect: ACh excites skeletal muscle (nicotinic) but slows the heart (muscarinic).
  • NMDA receptor: a coincidence detector. It needs glutamate (and glycine) plus depolarization to push out its Mg²⁺ block; it lets in Ca²⁺, the trigger for long-term potentiation. Ketamine blocks it.
  • EPSP: depolarization toward threshold (Na⁺ in through mixed cation channels). IPSP: hyperpolarization or clamping toward ECl or EK (GABA-A and glycine open Cl⁻ channels). EPSPs and IPSPs add up in time and space at the axon hillock.
  • Small transmitters (glutamate, GABA, amines, ACh) release with single action potentials; neuropeptides need bursts.
  • Gray type I synapses are asymmetric and excitatory; type II are symmetric and inhibitory.

Local anesthetics

Every local anesthetic has a lipophilic aromatic ring, an intermediate chain (ester or amide link) and a hydrophilic amine. Naming trick: amides have an "i" before "-caine" (lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine, bupivacaine); esters do not (procaine, benzocaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine, cocaine).

Mechanism: the drug is injected as a salt and exists as uncharged base and charged cation. The uncharged base crosses the nerve sheath and membrane; inside, the cation binds the voltage-gated Na⁺ channel from the inner side. The rate of depolarization falls until threshold is never reached, so no action potential is conducted. Resting potential and threshold are unchanged. Binding is use-dependent: open and inactivated channels bind more, so fast-firing nerves block first. Small and myelinated fibers block first (sharp pain, temperature, then touch and pressure, then motor). Block spreads from the outer (mantle) bundles inward to the core, so proximal teeth go numb before distal ones.

PropertyControlsRule
pKaOnsetThe closer the pKa to tissue pH (7.4), the more uncharged base and the faster the onset. Inflamed tissue is acidic, so more drug is trapped as cation and the block can fail.
Lipid solubilityPotencyMore lipid-soluble = more potent (and more toxic): bupivacaine, tetracaine
Protein bindingDurationMore bound = longer: short procaine and chloroprocaine; intermediate lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine; long bupivacaine, ropivacaine, tetracaine
VasoactivityDuration and toxicityMost dilate vessels (cocaine constricts); epinephrine slows uptake, lengthens the block and lowers blood levels
StereochemistryCardiac toxicityR isomers bind cardiac Na⁺ channels more: racemic bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic; ropivacaine is the pure S isomer
  • Esters: hydrolyzed in plasma by pseudocholinesterase; the metabolite PABA causes most true local anesthetic allergies. Patients with atypical pseudocholinesterase have long-lasting effects (and prolonged succinylcholine paralysis).
  • Amides: metabolized in the liver (CYP450); metabolites leave by the kidney. Caution in severe liver disease. True amide allergy is very rare; reactions are usually to the preservative methylparaben or to sodium bisulfite, the antioxidant in cartridges with a vasoconstrictor. No cross-allergy between the classes.
  • Articaine: an amide with a thiophene ring and an ester side chain, so most of it is broken down in plasma (short half-life).
  • Prilocaine (and benzocaine) can cause methemoglobinemia (prilocaine's metabolite is o-toluidine): cyanosis that oxygen does not fix; treated with methylene blue.
  • Dental arithmetic: 2% lidocaine = 20 mg/mL, so a 1.8 mL cartridge holds 36 mg; 1:100,000 epinephrine = 0.01 mg/mL, 0.018 mg per cartridge.

LAST (local anesthetic systemic toxicity), usually from intravascular injection or overdose: the CNS goes first: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness, twitching, then seizures, then CNS depression; at higher levels the heart: hypotension, arrhythmia, arrest. Potency tracks toxicity; acidosis makes it worse. Treatment: stop injecting, airway, oxygen, a benzodiazepine for seizures, and 20% lipid emulsion (the "lipid sink").

General anesthesia

General anesthesia combines unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia and immobility (akinesia), plus control of autonomic reflexes. There is no single "off switch" in the brain; the drugs slow communication between neurons by enhancing inhibition (most act at GABA-A receptors, raising Cl⁻ current: propofol, etomidate, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, volatile agents) or blocking excitation (ketamine and nitrous oxide block NMDA receptors). Arousal (ascending reticular activating system) and awareness (corticothalamic networks) are separate: ketamine disrupts awareness while arousal is preserved ("dissociative"), keeps airway reflexes and breathing, raises blood pressure and can cause emergence hallucinations. Phases: induction, maintenance, emergence.

  • MAC (minimum alveolar concentration): the inhaled concentration at which 50% of patients do not move to a surgical incision. Lower MAC = more potent; potency rises with lipid solubility. Nitrous oxide's MAC is over 100%, so it cannot give general anesthesia alone; it is used for dental sedation and needs 100% oxygen at the end to prevent diffusion hypoxia.
  • Low blood solubility means fast induction and recovery (nitrous oxide, desflurane, sevoflurane).
  • Levels of sedation: minimal (normal response to voice), moderate (purposeful response to voice or light touch; airway kept), deep (purposeful response only to repeated or painful stimuli; airway may need help), general anesthesia (not arousable even by pain).
  • Reversal agents: flumazenil for benzodiazepines, naloxone for opioids.
full.ns-sens:
What's tested
  • Hearing: cochlear fluids, hair-cell transduction, the central pathway (ECOLIMA), tonotopy, sound localization, cochlear implants
  • Taste and smell: nerves for each part of the tongue, the taste pathway, why smell skips the thalamus
  • Vestibular organs and reflexes; the eye-movement systems, extraocular muscles and nerve palsies
  • Visual pathway targets and the visual field defect from each lesion site
  • Sympathetic versus parasympathetic layout and transmitters; the enteric plexuses; the hypothalamus in brief
  • Pain fibers, the spinothalamic route, gate control, descending modulation, peripheral and central sensitization; nociceptive versus neuropathic pain and their drugs
  • Headache and facial pain: upper-half versus lower-half causes, trigeminal neuralgia, migraine, cluster, giant cell arteritis
  • Facial trauma: wound care, graft types, bone-graft healing, superior orbital fissure and orbital apex syndromes

Hearing

The outer ear funnels sound; the middle ear's ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) amplify it by focusing force from the large tympanic membrane onto the small oval window. The stapedius (VII) damps loud sound, so Bell palsy can cause hyperacusis. The cochlea has three chambers: scala vestibuli and scala tympani hold Na⁺-rich perilymph; the scala media holds K⁺-rich endolymph, giving the endocochlear potential. Sound moves the basilar membrane; stereocilia of the inner hair cells bend toward the tallest one (the kinocilium), tip links open mechanically gated channels, K⁺ flows in and depolarizes the cell, Ca²⁺ channels open and glutamate excites spiral ganglion neurons of CN VIII. Tonotopy: the cochlear base codes high pitch, the apex low pitch, and the map is kept up to the cortex. Pathway (ECOLIMA): Eighth nerve → Cochlear nuclei → superior Olive → Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate nucleus → Auditory cortex (Heschl gyrus). Localization: interaural time differences (low pitch, medial superior olive) and intensity differences (high pitch, lateral superior olive). A cochlear implant sits in the scala tympani and stimulates spiral ganglion cells directly, bypassing hair cells.

Taste and smell

RegionTasteGeneral sensation
Anterior 2/3CN VII (chorda tympani, riding the lingual nerve)V3 (lingual nerve)
Posterior 1/3 (incl. circumvallate papillae)CN IXCN IX
Epiglottis, pharynxCN XCN X

Taste fibers go to the nucleus of the solitary tract → VPM → gustatory cortex (anterior insula and frontal operculum), all on the same side. Flavor combines smell (I), taste (VII, IX, X) and texture and temperature (V). Smell is the one sense with no thalamic relay: receptor neurons → olfactory bulb (mitral and tufted cells) → piriform cortex, amygdala and entorhinal cortex, which is why smells call up emotion and memory. Loss of smell (anosmia) follows head trauma that shears the fibers at the cribriform plate, infections and aging, and is an early sign of Parkinson and Alzheimer disease.

Vestibular system and eye movements

Semicircular canals sense rotation (angular acceleration); the otolith organs sense linear acceleration and head tilt: the utricle horizontal, the saccule vertical. Bending toward the kinocilium excites, away inhibits; the two sides work push-pull (turning the head left excites the left horizontal canal). The vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes opposite to the head at the same speed so the image stays still.

  • Eye movement systems: saccades (fast, yoked; frontal eye fields → superior colliculus → PPRF), smooth pursuit, vergence (eyes in opposite directions for near; with accommodation and miosis, the near triad), optokinetic and vestibular (VOR).
  • Muscles: LR6 SO4, the rest CN III. CN III palsy: eye down and out, ptosis, and a dilated pupil when the outer parasympathetic fibers are compressed (aneurysm). CN IV palsy: vertical diplopia, head tilted away. CN VI palsy: eye cannot abduct.
  • MLF lesion (internuclear ophthalmoplegia): on looking to the side, the eye on the lesion side fails to adduct and the other eye shows nystagmus; convergence is spared. Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests MS.

Vision

Photoreceptors (rods for dim light, cones for color) → bipolar cells → ganglion cells, the retina's only output and only cells that fire action potentials. About 90% of ganglion cells go to the LGN → V1 (striate cortex, Brodmann 17) for conscious vision; others go to the superior colliculus (saccades, orienting), pretectum (pupillary light reflex; efferent through Edinger-Westphal and CN III, so light in one eye constricts both pupils), and the suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian clock).

LesionDefect
Optic nerve (before the chiasm)Blindness of that eye only
Optic chiasm (pituitary adenoma)Bitemporal hemianopia
Optic tract or LGNContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Meyer loop (temporal lobe)Contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky")
Parietal optic radiationContralateral inferior quadrantanopia
Occipital cortex (PCA)Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

Autonomic and enteric nervous systems

  • Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (T1–L2 lateral horn), short preganglionic fibers to the chain (paravertebral) or prevertebral ganglia, long postganglionic fibers. Preganglionic ACh on nicotinic receptors; postganglionic norepinephrine on α and β receptors, except sweat glands (ACh, muscarinic). Splanchnic nerves pass the chain without synapsing; the adrenal medulla gets preganglionic fibers directly and releases mostly epinephrine into the blood.
  • Parasympathetic: craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4), long preganglionic fibers to ganglia near or in the organ, short postganglionic fibers, ACh on muscarinic receptors.
  • Saliva: parasympathetic drive gives copious watery saliva; sympathetic gives scant, thick saliva. Anticholinergic drugs cause dry mouth.
  • Enteric nervous system (esophagus to internal anal sphincter, works on its own): myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between the muscle layers for motility; submucosal (Meissner) plexus for secretion and local blood flow.
  • Hypothalamus: supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei make ADH and oxytocin for the posterior pituitary; releasing hormones reach the anterior pituitary by portal veins; arcuate dopamine holds prolactin down; lateral = hunger, ventromedial = satiety.

Pain

Nociceptors are free nerve endings (mechanical, thermal through TRP channels, chemical). Aδ fibers (thin, myelinated) carry fast, sharp, well-localized first pain; C fibers (unmyelinated) carry slow, dull, burning, poorly localized second pain. Transmitters in the dorsal horn: glutamate, substance P, CGRP. Second-order neurons (laminae I, II, V) cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the spinothalamic tract to VPL (face: VPM) for where and how strong, and to intralaminar and medial nuclei → anterior cingulate and insula for the unpleasant, emotional part.

  • Gate control: large Aβ touch fibers excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that damp Aδ and C input; rubbing a bumped elbow helps.
  • Descending modulation: cortex and hypothalamus → periaqueductal gray → rostral ventromedial medulla (serotonin) and locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) → dorsal horn, with endogenous opioids. It can inhibit (placebo, exercise) or facilitate (stress).
  • Peripheral sensitization: the inflammatory "soup" (prostaglandins, bradykinin) lowers nociceptor threshold → primary hyperalgesia at the injury. Central sensitization: dorsal horn neurons become hyperexcitable through NMDA receptors, Ca²⁺ and kinases ("wind-up") → secondary hyperalgesia around the injury and allodynia (pain from touch).

Nociceptive pain comes from tissue damage (surgery, trauma, an abscess), proportional to injury, with inflammation and raised heart rate and cortisol; treated with NSAIDs (COX inhibitors), acetaminophen, corticosteroids and opioids (mu agonists; side effects include respiratory depression, constipation, miosis; naloxone reverses; codeine is a prodrug made active by CYP2D6; tramadol adds serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake block and lowers seizure threshold). Neuropathic pain comes from injury to the nervous system (diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, trigeminal neuralgia, post-stroke pain): burning, shooting, out of proportion, with allodynia; responds poorly to opioids and well to adjuvants: tricyclics (amitriptyline), SNRIs (duloxetine), gabapentin and pregabalin (α2δ Ca²⁺ channel subunit), and carbamazepine (Na⁺ channel block, first line for trigeminal neuralgia).

Headache and facial pain

ConditionWho and whereKey features
Tension-type (most common)Anyone; bilateral band or capPressing, mild to moderate, no nausea, not worse with activity
MigraineYoung women; unilateralPulsating, 4–72 h, nausea, light and sound sensitivity, worse with activity; aura in about 20%; triptans
ClusterMen; around one eyeSevere "boring" pain 15–180 min, same-side tearing, runny nose, Horner signs; restless; clockwork timing; 100% oxygen
Giant cell arteritisOver 50, womenNew headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication (can mimic TMD), high ESR; urgent steroids to save vision
Pseudotumor cerebriYoung obese womenHigh CSF pressure, papilledema, worse lying down or straining
Trigeminal neuralgiaUsually over 50; V2 and V3Seconds of electric-shock pain set off by light touch at trigger zones; normal exam; carbamazepine; under 40 or both sides suggests MS

TMDAdultsJoint tenderness, clicking, limited opening; splints and NSAIDs

"Upper-half" pain (above the eyes) is mostly primary headache, glaucoma, giant cell arteritis or pseudotumor; "lower-half" pain is most often dental, then TMD and burning mouth; sinus disease (overdiagnosed), cardiac pain referred to the jaw, atypical facial pain and trigeminal neuralgia can be either. Red flags: thunderclap onset, new headache after 50, papilledema, fever, visual loss.

Facial trauma and reconstruction

  • Wound care: copious irrigation, exploration, remove debris (road grit tattoos the skin), check the facial nerve, parotid duct and nasolacrimal duct, early debridement, remove only free bone pieces under 1 cm without periosteum, drains for hematoma.
  • Grafts: autograft (same person, the gold standard), allograft (another person), xenograft (another species), alloplast (synthetic). Bone-graft healing: phase I (first 4 weeks) bone made by cells transplanted with the graft, disorganized; phase II (starts about 2 weeks, peaks about 6) bone made by host cells, with resorption and remodeling that continue indefinitely.
  • Orbit: seven bones; the optic nerve lies about 40–45 mm behind the infraorbital rim. Fracture complications: diplopia, enophthalmos, infection, ectropion, rarely blindness.
  • Superior orbital fissure syndrome: a fracture into the fissure injures III, IV, VI and V1 → ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis, a fixed dilated pupil, forehead numbness and lost corneal reflex. Orbital apex syndrome = the same plus blindness (optic nerve).
full.ns-dis:
What's tested
  • Multiple sclerosis: who gets it, its courses, how it is diagnosed (dissemination in time and space, MRI, oligoclonal bands) and treated
  • Seizures: generalized versus focal, absence, automatisms, status epilepticus; antiseizure drugs and their dental side effects
  • Alzheimer disease: plaques and tangles, the stages, other dementias, the drugs; Parkinson drugs and dental care
  • Sleep: stages, obstructive sleep apnea and oral appliances, narcolepsy and cataplexy, the circadian clock
  • Reward and addiction: VTA → nucleus accumbens, how each drug acts, treatments
  • Schizophrenia: symptoms, dopamine pathways, antipsychotics and their side effects; autism in brief
  • Memory and plasticity: declarative versus procedural memory, LTP and LTD; aphasia and neglect

Multiple sclerosis

A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the CNS (white and gray matter) with axon loss. Typical patient: a young adult woman (onset 20–40, about 2:1 female), white, raised far from the equator (risk rises with latitude; vitamin D, smoking and Epstein-Barr virus play a part). Common first events: limb numbness, optic neuritis (painful loss of vision in one eye), double vision (INO), weakness.

  • Courses: relapsing-remitting (most; stable between attacks), secondary progressive (RRMS that turns into steady worsening), primary progressive (worse from the start, more often men and older onset).
  • Diagnosis: a typical demyelinating event plus dissemination in time and space and no better explanation. MRI shows periventricular plaques (gadolinium-enhancing = active, new); CSF shows oligoclonal bands and a raised IgG index; evoked potentials are slowed.
  • Treatment: high-dose IV methylprednisolone to shorten a relapse; long-term disease-modifying immunotherapy to cut relapses and MRI activity; symptom care (bladder, fatigue, spasticity, pain, depression).
  • Dental: trigeminal neuralgia in a patient under 40 or on both sides suggests MS; patients on immunosuppressants or long steroids may need infection precautions; keep visits short and cool.

Seizures and epilepsy

A seizure is one event of excessive synchronized neuronal firing; its signs are stereotyped (the same each time). Epilepsy: at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one with a high risk of more. Generalized-onset seizures start in thalamocortical circuits of both hemispheres (more common in children): tonic-clonic, absence (brief staring with a quick return, 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG), myoclonic, atonic, tonic. Focal-onset seizures start in one area and may spread; awareness may be kept or impaired; automatisms (lip smacking, chewing) point to the temporal lobe. Frontal: motor, brief, nocturnal; parietal: sensory; occipital: visual. Status epilepticus is 5 minutes or more of seizure, or repeated seizures without recovery: an emergency. Mimics include syncope, hypoglycemia and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures. Most patients become seizure-free on the first or second drug; after two failures, a third rarely works, so surgery (for focal epilepsy, 50–75% seizure-free), vagus nerve stimulation or a ketogenic diet are considered.

DrugMain actionDental relevance
PhenytoinNa⁺ channel blockGingival overgrowth (also with cyclosporine and nifedipine); good plaque control
CarbamazepineNa⁺ channel blockFirst line for trigeminal neuralgia; agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (check counts), CYP inducer
