Reproductive pathology

LesionKey facts
CryptorchidismUndescended testis (about 3% of term, 30% of premature boys); body heat stops spermatogenesis. Surgery by about age 1–2 protects fertility; the cancer risk stays
Torsion; epididymitisTorsion: a twisted cord, sudden pain, an emergency. Epididymitis: under 35, gonorrhea or chlamydia; older, E. coli. Orchitis: mumps
Testicular germ cell tumors95% of testicular tumors, men 15–35, a painless mass, cured in over 95%. Seminoma: the most common, no marker usually, radiosensitive. Nonseminomas: embryonal, yolk sac (AFP), choriocarcinoma (hCG), teratoma
BPHNodular hyperplasia of the transition zone around the urethra after 50: urinary obstruction; not premalignant; 5α-reductase inhibitors, alpha-1 blockers
Prostatic adenocarcinomaThe most common cancer in men; the peripheral zone (felt on rectal exam, no early obstruction); PSA; osteoblastic bone metastases; Gleason grade from gland pattern (higher = worse)
Penis and bladderHPV 6 and 11: condyloma; HPV 16 and 18: penile intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous carcinoma (phimosis a risk). Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder: painless hematuria, smoking, dyes; Schistosoma: squamous carcinoma
LesionKey facts
HPV and the cervixHigh-risk HPV 16 and 18 infect the transformation zone (where squamous meets glandular epithelium); koilocytes. Low-grade lesions (CIN1) often regress; high-grade (CIN2–3) progress to squamous carcinoma. Pap and HPV screening and the vaccine prevent it
Condyloma acuminatumHPV 6 and 11: benign warty lesions anywhere on the anogenital tract
VulvaLichen sclerosus: older women, thin white parchment-like skin, a small risk of HPV-negative squamous carcinoma. Lichen simplex chronicus: thick, from scratching. Lichen planus: with oral lace-like white lesions; biopsy fresh tissue for immunofluorescence
VaginaCandida (pseudohyphae, curdy discharge), Trichomonas (sexually transmitted, motile protozoan), atrophic vaginitis after menopause. Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma): grape-like mass in girls under 5
EndometriumEndometrioid carcinoma: unopposed estrogen, obesity, hyperplasia; perimenopausal; less aggressive. Serous and clear cell: older women, not estrogen-related, aggressive. Leiomyoma: the most common uterine tumor, benign
OvaryMost tumors are epithelial; ovarian cancer is often found late and is lethal
BreastInvasive ductal carcinoma most common; DCIS is treated; LCIS marks higher risk; Paget disease of the nipple means a carcinoma beneath; ER, PR and HER2 guide therapy

Sex hormones and the mouth

Puberty and pregnancy exaggerate the gingiva's response to plaque: pregnancy gingivitis (second and third trimesters) and the pyogenic granuloma ("pregnancy tumor"), a red, bleeding, lobulated interdental mass that often shrinks after delivery. The second trimester is the best time for elective care. Menopause brings xerostomia, altered taste, burning mouth and osteoporosis.
full.he-heme:
What's tested
  • Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs; the white cells from most to least common
  • Innate vs adaptive immunity; B, T and NK cells; primary vs secondary lymphoid organs; thymus, lymph node and spleen
  • Anemias: microcytic vs macrocytic, sickle cell, and their oral signs
  • Leukemias: acute vs chronic, myeloid vs lymphoid; AML, ALL, CML, CLL; APL
  • Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin lymphoma; Burkitt, follicular, mantle cell, MALT, diffuse large B-cell, mycosis fungoides; myeloma
  • Oral signs of blood disease and dental management

The blood cells

One pluripotent stem cell gives a myeloid line (red cells, megakaryocytes, granulocytes, monocytes) and a lymphoid line (B, T and NK cells). Red cells are most of the cells; they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide and live about 120 days. Platelets are fragments of marrow megakaryocytes that start clotting. White cells come in two classes and five types, most to least common: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils ("Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas").

CellShareLookJob
Neutrophil50–70%Multilobed nucleus, pale granules (myeloperoxidase, elastase)First line against bacteria; about 10 hours in blood
Lymphocyte20–40%Large round nucleus, thin rim of cytoplasmB cells (antibody), T cells, NK cells
Monocyte2–8%Single kidney-shaped nucleusBecomes the tissue macrophage; presents antigen (MHC II)
Eosinophil1–4%Bilobed nucleus, red granules (major basic protein)Parasites, allergy
BasophilUnder 1%Dark blue-purple granules (histamine, heparin)Allergy and asthma; IgE receptors
  • Innate immunity is what the body simply does: skin and mucosa, low pH, lysozyme and thiocyanate in saliva, complement, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells. Adaptive immunity follows a first contact with an antigen, is specific and has memory: humoral (B cells → plasma cells → antibody) and cellular (T cells).
  • Helper T cells (CD4) see antigen on MHC II and help B cells; cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill cells showing antigen on MHC I. NK cells have no B or T markers: a cell missing MHC I is killed, and in antibody-dependent killing their CD16 binds IgG.
  • Primary lymphoid organs are only the bone marrow (B cells) and the thymus (T cells). Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and MALT (Peyer patches in the ileum).
  • Thymus: behind the manubrium, large in infants, fat by the teens; dense cortex (positive selection), pale medulla with Hassall corpuscles (negative selection); its stroma is epithelioreticular cells (every other lymphoid organ uses reticular cells); most thymocytes die in selection. No thymus (DiGeorge): no T cells, and no parathyroids.
  • Lymph node: afferent lymphatic → subcapsular sinus → trabecular and medullary sinuses → efferent lymphatic. B cells in cortical follicles (germinal centers), T cells in the paracortex (high endothelial venules), plasma cells in the medulla.
  • Spleen: no afferent lymphatics; white pulp (the PALS, T cells around the central arteriole, and B-cell follicles) and red pulp (cords and sinusoids that cull old red cells and hold a third of the platelets). Without a spleen, encapsulated bacteria are the danger.

Anemias

Not taught as a lecture in this course, but tested on boards. Anemia shows in the mouth as pallor, a smooth sore tongue, angular cheilitis and slow healing.

AnemiaLabsClues and oral signs
Iron deficiency (the commonest)Microcytic, hypochromic; ferritin lowChronic blood loss (menses, GI); atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis, spoon nails; Plummer-Vinson (dysphagia, esophageal webs, glossitis) carries a risk of oral and esophageal squamous carcinoma
B12 or folate deficiencyMacrocytic (megaloblastic); hypersegmented neutrophilsBeefy red, painful, smooth tongue, burning mouth, ulcers. B12 adds numbness and gait problems; pernicious anemia = antibodies to intrinsic factor and parietal cells
Sickle cell diseaseHemoglobin S (valine for glutamate at β6); hemolysisPain crises, infections, stroke. Radiograph: "step-ladder" trabeculae, "hair-on-end" skull. Short, stress-free visits; avoid hypoxia and dehydration; treat infection promptly
ThalassemiaMicrocytic with normal or high ironMarrow expansion: "chipmunk" face, maxillary protrusion, hair-on-end skull
Aplastic anemiaPancytopeniaInfections, bleeding, pallor

Leukemias

Neoplastic cells replace the marrow and spill into the blood. Two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature, 20% or more blasts, rapid, fatal in months untreated) or chronic (cells that still mature, insidious, years), and myeloid or lymphoid. The consequences are marrow failure (anemia: fatigue, pallor; low platelets: petechiae and gingival bleeding; low neutrophils: infections and ulcers) and tissue infiltration (bone pain, spleen, liver and nodes, and gingival enlargement, where a dentist may be the first to notice).

WhoKey findings
AMLAdults (median about 65)Myeloblasts with Auer rods. APL: t(15;17) PML-RARA, stuck promyelocytes, DIC can kill, cured by all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic. Acute monocytic leukemia: gums swollen with leukemic cells
ALLChildren (usually 1–5); the most common childhood cancerSmall lymphoblasts, scant cytoplasm, never Auer rods; mostly B-cell; good survival in children
CMLAdultst(9;22) Philadelphia, BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase always on; very high white count with every stage of maturation; big spleen; imatinib
CLL/SLLOver 70Small mature B cells, smudge cells, soccer-ball chromatin; blood = CLL, node = SLL; infections (low antibodies); indolent, largely incurable

Lymphomas

A lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes in nodes, spleen or any lymphoid tissue; the tissue makes the diagnosis (an excised node, fresh for flow cytometry). B symptoms: fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, loss of 10% of body weight in 6 months. A lymphoma node is firm, rubbery, painless and growing; an infected node is tender and soft. 85–90% of lymphoid cancers are B-cell.

HodgkinNon-Hodgkin
SpreadUsually localized; contiguous, node group to the nextUsually widespread; can skip groups
NodesCentral (cervical, mediastinal)Peripheral; often extranodal (including the mouth and Waldeyer ring)
BloodNot involvedCan be involved
CellsA few large Reed-Sternberg cells (prominent nucleoli, often binucleate) among many reactive cells; EBVA monotonous population of one clone
OutcomeOver 80% curedDepends on type: indolent or aggressive
LymphomaKey facts
FollicularIndolent; t(14;18) keeps BCL2 on so cells don't die
Mantle cellt(11;14), cyclin D1; older adults
Marginal zone (MALT)Indolent; tied to chronic inflammation: H. pylori (stomach), Sjögren (salivary glands), Hashimoto (thyroid); the one dentists see most
Diffuse large B-cellThe commonest (about 30%); aggressive, fast; R-CHOP
Burkittt(8;14) MYC; "starry sky"; endemic African form in the jaw of children with EBV; very fast but curable
Mycosis fungoides / SézarySkin T-cell lymphoma (patch, plaque, tumor), indolent; Sézary: red skin all over, nodes, cerebriform cells in blood, aggressive
Extranodal NK/TEBV, necrosis, midline destruction with a perforated palate
Plasma cell myelomaMarrow plasma cells, M-spike; CRAB: high calcium, renal damage, anemia, lytic "punched-out" bone (skull, jaws); amyloid macroglossia; on bisphosphonates, osteonecrosis of the jaw risk

In the dental chair

  • Unexplained gingival enlargement or bleeding, petechiae, pallor, nonhealing ulcers or a firm painless neck node: order a CBC with differential and refer promptly.
  • Before invasive care in leukemia or chemotherapy, get the counts and talk with the oncologist; elective care waits when neutrophils fall below about 1,000/µL or platelets below about 50,000/µL. Clear oral infection before chemotherapy; expect mucositis, candidiasis and herpes during it.
full.mg-giphys:
What's tested
  • The GI hormones: the cell that makes each, what releases it and what it does (gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1, motilin, ghrelin), plus the paracrines (histamine, somatostatin) and neurocrines (VIP, NO, GRP, substance P)
  • Saliva: which gland makes what, isotonic primary saliva made hypotonic by the ducts, and autonomic control
  • Gastric acid: the parietal cell's pump, its three stimulants and its brakes, and the phases of secretion
  • Motility: slow waves, peristalsis vs segmentation, the migrating motor complex, gastric emptying, the colonic reflexes and defecation
  • Pancreatic and biliary secretion: secretin vs CCK, trypsin activation, bile salts and their recycling
  • Digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, protein and fat; where iron, calcium and B12 are absorbed; water and electrolyte transport and the two kinds of diarrhea

How the gut is controlled

The gut has its own nervous system, the enteric nervous system, which can run without the brain: the submucosal (Meissner) plexus controls secretion and blood flow, and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the circular and longitudinal muscle, controls motility. Parasympathetic (vagus, pelvic) input generally speeds digestion; sympathetic input slows it. Chemical messengers act three ways: endocrine (into the blood: gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1, motilin), paracrine (on neighbors: histamine, somatostatin) and neurocrine (released by nerves: VIP, NO, GRP, substance P, enkephalins).

HormoneCell and siteReleased byMain actions
GastrinG cells, gastric antrum (and duodenum)Small peptides and amino acids, distension, vagus via GRP; inhibited by acid (pH < 3) through somatostatin↑ acid secretion; growth of the gastric mucosa (trophic)
CCKI cells, duodenum and jejunumFatty acids, monoglycerides, amino acids and small peptidesGallbladder contraction and sphincter of Oddi relaxation; ↑ pancreatic enzymes; slows gastric emptying
SecretinS cells, duodenumAcid in the duodenum (pH < 4.5), fatty acids↑ pancreatic and biliary HCO3- and water; ↓ gastric acid
GIPK cells, duodenum and jejunumGlucose, amino acids and fat (the only one released by all three)↑ insulin (glucose-dependent); ↓ gastric acid
GLP-1L cells, intestine (mostly ileum and colon)Nutrients in the gut↑ insulin, ↓ glucagon, slows emptying, ↓ appetite (the basis of GLP-1 agonist drugs)
MotilinM cells, upper small intestineFasting, about every 90 minutesStarts the migrating motor complex; erythromycin acts on its receptor
GhrelinStomach (fundus)Fasting; falls after a mealHunger signal to the hypothalamus; ↑ growth hormone

Histamine comes from ECL cells and acts on H2 receptors of parietal cells. Somatostatin from D cells is the universal brake: released when antral pH falls, it inhibits gastrin and acid. VIP and NO relax smooth muscle (they open the LES) and VIP drives intestinal secretion (a VIPoma causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydria). GRP carries the vagal signal to G cells, substance P contracts muscle, and enkephalins slow transit (why opioids constipate).

Saliva

The parotid is the largest gland and is purely serous (amylase); the submandibular makes about 60-70% of resting saliva and is mixed; the sublingual makes about 5% and is mostly mucous. Acinar cells make primary saliva that is isotonic to plasma. The ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, but they let little water through, so final saliva is hypotonic. The faster it flows, the less time the ducts have, so high-flow saliva is closer to plasma and richest in HCO3-. Unusually, both autonomic divisions stimulate saliva: parasympathetic (copious, watery; blocked by atropine) and sympathetic (small volume, protein-rich). Saliva lubricates and buffers, starts starch digestion (α-amylase) and fat digestion (lingual lipase), and defends the mouth (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA, mucins).

Gastric secretion

Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor (the one gastric product we can't live without: it is needed for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum). Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3-; the H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen, Cl- follows through apical channels, and HCO3- leaves into the blood in exchange for Cl- (the "alkaline tide" after a meal). Three stimulants act directly: ACh (M3, Ca2+), gastrin (CCK-B receptor, Ca2+) and histamine (H2, cAMP). Histamine potentiates the other two, which is why an H2 blocker cuts acid from every stimulus; a PPI blocks the final pump, so it works whatever the stimulus. Brakes: somatostatin, prostaglandins, low antral pH and, from the duodenum, secretin and GIP. Chief cells make pepsinogen, which acid turns into pepsin; surface mucous cells make the mucus-bicarbonate layer that keeps the mucosal surface near pH 7.

Phases: the cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste, about 30% of the acid) runs entirely through the vagus (direct ACh on parietal cells plus GRP on G cells), so vagotomy abolishes it; the gastric phase (distension, peptides, about 60%) acts through gastrin and local reflexes; the intestinal phase is small and mostly inhibitory.

Motility

Interstitial cells of Cajal set slow waves, the basic electrical rhythm (about 3/min in the stomach, 12/min in the duodenum). A slow wave alone doesn't contract muscle; contraction happens when spike potentials fire on top of it, and nerves and hormones decide how often that happens. Swallowing is voluntary, then a medullary reflex (soft palate up, epiglottis down, UES relaxes), then primary peristalsis, with secondary peristalsis clearing what's left; the LES relaxes through vagal VIP and NO. In achalasia, those inhibitory myenteric neurons are lost, so the LES can't relax: dysphagia to solids and liquids and a "bird's beak" on barium swallow.

Gastric emptying is fastest for liquids and isotonic chyme and slowest for fat (through CCK); acid, hypertonic chyme and duodenal distension also slow it. In the small intestine, segmentation mixes (contraction in the middle of the bolus) and peristalsis propels (contraction behind, relaxation ahead). Between meals the migrating motor complex (MMC, driven by motilin, about every 90 minutes) sweeps residue and bacteria into the colon; without it, bacteria overgrow. In the colon, haustral contractions mix, and mass movements a few times a day push feces into the rectum. Reflexes: gastrocolic (food in the stomach → colonic mass movements), gastroileal (food in the stomach → ileocecal valve relaxes), and the defecation reflex (rectal stretch → rectum contracts and the involuntary internal anal sphincter relaxes, while the voluntary external sphincter decides when).

Pancreas and bile

Pancreatic acinar cells make enzymes (driven by CCK and ACh); duct cells make HCO3- through CFTR (driven by secretin). Secretin and CCK potentiate each other. Proteases are secreted inactive: brush-border enteropeptidase (enterokinase) turns trypsinogen into trypsin, and trypsin activates the rest (chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase) and more trypsinogen. Amylase and lipase (with colipase) are secreted active. Pepsin is a stomach enzyme, not a pancreatic one.

Hepatocytes make bile acids from cholesterol and conjugate them with glycine or taurine (bile salts); gut bacteria make the secondary ones. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals; CCK empties it. About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by a Na+-coupled transporter and return in portal blood (enterohepatic circulation). Remove or inflame the ileum (Crohn disease) and bile salts are lost: steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and gallstones, with B12 deficiency as well.

NutrientDigested byAbsorbed as / how
CarbohydrateSalivary and pancreatic α-amylase, then brush-border lactase, sucrase, maltaseMonosaccharides only. Glucose and galactose: SGLT1 (Na+-coupled); fructose: GLUT5; all exit by GLUT2
ProteinPepsin, then trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase, brush-border peptidasesAmino acids (Na+-coupled carriers) and di- and tripeptides (PepT1, driven by an H+ gradient)
FatLipase with colipase, after bile salts emulsifyFatty acids and 2-monoglycerides ride micelles to the brush border, are rebuilt into triglyceride and leave as chylomicrons into the lacteals (lymph)
Iron, calciumDuodenum (iron as heme or Fe2+; calcium helped by vitamin D)
Folate / B12Folate in the jejunum; B12 bound to intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum

Water, electrolytes and diarrhea

About 9 L of fluid enter the gut each day (2 L eaten, 7 L secreted): the jejunum absorbs the most, then the ileum, then the colon, leaving about 0.1-0.2 L in stool. Villi absorb; crypts secrete. Na+ is absorbed with glucose and amino acids in the jejunum, as NaCl in the ileum, and through aldosterone-driven ENaC channels in the colon, which also secretes K+ (so diarrhea causes hypokalemia). Crypt cells secrete Cl- through CFTR when cAMP rises. Cholera toxin locks cAMP on, causing a huge secretory diarrhea; oral rehydration works because Na+-glucose cotransport is untouched. Osmotic diarrhea comes from unabsorbed solute (lactase deficiency, magnesium laxatives) and stops with fasting.
full.mg-gianat:
What's tested
  • Foregut, midgut and hindgut: their arteries and boundaries, the stomach's arteries and the main anastomoses
  • Peritoneum: visceral vs parietal pain, referred pain by gut region (appendicitis), retroperitoneal organs, the ligament of Treitz, SMA syndrome
  • Portal-caval anastomoses and what portal hypertension does at each one; the pectinate line
  • Abdominal wall: layers, rectus sheath and the arcuate line, dermatomes, inguinal hernias, diaphragm openings
  • Histology: the four layers, the esophagus, stomach glands and cells, duodenum vs jejunum vs ileum vs colon, oral mucosa, papillae and salivary glands
  • Liver and gallbladder histology: the three lobule models, zones 1-3, sinusoids and their cells

Foregut, midgut, hindgut

RegionArteryExtentPain referred to
ForegutCeliac trunkAbdominal esophagus to the major duodenal papilla (2nd part of duodenum); liver, gallbladder, pancreas (part); spleen is supplied tooEpigastric region
MidgutSuperior mesenteric (SMA)Distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of transverse colonUmbilical region (T10)
HindgutInferior mesenteric (IMA)Distal 1/3 of transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal above the pectinate lineHypogastric (suprapubic) region

Celiac branches: left gastric (lesser curvature, abdominal esophagus), splenic (short gastrics to the fundus, left gastroepiploic to the greater curvature, pancreatic branches) and common hepatic. The common hepatic gives the proper hepatic (right and left hepatic, right gastric, cystic) and the gastroduodenal (right gastroepiploic, superior pancreaticoduodenals). So: lesser curvature = right and left gastric; greater curvature = right and left gastroepiploic; fundus = short gastrics. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery (major bleeding); an anterior one perforates into the peritoneal cavity.

Anastomoses: superior (celiac) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arteries around the head of the pancreas; the marginal artery joining SMA and IMA colic branches; superior epigastric (internal thoracic) with inferior epigastric (external iliac) inside the rectus sheath.

Peritoneum and position

Parietal peritoneum lines the wall and has somatic nerves: sharp, well localized pain. Visceral peritoneum covers organs and has visceral afferents: dull, poorly localized pain referred by region. Appendicitis starts as periumbilical pain (midgut visceral afferents to T10) and moves to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point) once the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum. A mesentery attached to the back wall is a "meso-"; a fold joining two organs or the front wall is a "ligament"; one attached to the stomach is an omentum. The falciform ligament holds the ligamentum teres (old umbilical vein); the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) holds the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, with the epiploic foramen behind it.

Retroperitoneal ("SAD PUCKER"): suprarenal glands, aorta and IVC, duodenum (parts 2-4), pancreas (not the tail), ureters, colon (ascending and descending), kidneys, esophagus, rectum. The transverse and sigmoid colon, jejunum, ileum and stomach are intraperitoneal. The ligament of Treitz at the duodenojejunal flexure divides upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) from lower (bright red blood per rectum). SMA syndrome: the 3rd part of the duodenum is squeezed between the SMA and aorta (often after rapid weight loss). Nutcracker syndrome: the left renal vein is squeezed there instead, backing up the left gonadal vein.

Portal-caval anastomoses

Unpaired gut organs drain to the portal vein, which carries about 75% of the liver's blood (the hepatic artery the rest). When cirrhosis raises portal pressure, blood takes portal-caval shortcuts:

SitePortal sideCaval sideResult
EsophagusLeft gastric veinEsophageal veins to the azygosEsophageal varices (life-threatening hematemesis)
UmbilicusParaumbilical veinsSuperficial epigastric veinsCaput medusae
RectumSuperior rectal veinMiddle and inferior rectal veinsAnorectal varices (often listed as hemorrhoids)

Pectinate line: above it the canal is hindgut (endoderm): superior rectal artery (IMA), portal venous drainage, visceral nerves (painless internal hemorrhoids), adenocarcinoma. Below it, ectoderm: inferior rectal artery (internal iliac via internal pudendal), caval drainage, somatic pudendal nerves (painful external hemorrhoids), lymph to superficial inguinal nodes, squamous cell carcinoma.

Abdominal wall

Superficial to deep: skin, superficial fascia (fatty Camper, membranous Scarpa), external oblique (down and in), internal oblique (up and in), transversus abdominis (horizontal), transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum. Their aponeuroses form the rectus sheath. Above the arcuate line the sheath has anterior and posterior layers; below it all three aponeuroses pass in front, so only transversalis fascia lies behind the rectus. Linea alba is the midline; linea semilunaris is the lateral edge of the rectus. Dermatomes: T4 nipple, T6 xiphoid, T10 umbilicus, L1 groin.

Inguinal canal: from the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (external oblique aponeurosis); it carries the spermatic cord or the round ligament, plus the ilioinguinal nerve. An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through a patent processus vaginalis (congenital, the most common type). A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle (inferior epigastric vessels, rectus edge, inguinal ligament), medial to the vessels, where the transversalis fascia is weak (older men). "MDs don't LIe": Medial = Direct, Lateral = Indirect. Umbilical folds: median (urachus; a patent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus), medial (obliterated umbilical arteries), lateral (inferior epigastric vessels).

Diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3-C5): IVC at T8, esophagus and vagal trunks at T10, aorta, thoracic duct and azygos at T12 ("I 8 10 eggs at 12"). The spleen sits under ribs 9-11 in the left upper quadrant, the organ most often injured in blunt left-side trauma.

GI histology

Four layers everywhere: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa (vessels, Meissner plexus, glands in the esophagus and duodenum), muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal, Auerbach plexus between; the stomach adds an inner oblique layer), and serosa (free organs) or adventitia (fixed ones like the esophagus).

RegionSignature features
EsophagusNonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium; submucosal esophageal glands; muscle skeletal in the upper third, mixed in the middle, smooth in the lower third; abrupt squamous-to-columnar Z-line at the stomach
StomachRugae, gastric pits, no villi. Cardia and pylorus: mucous glands (G cells in the antrum). Fundus and body: oxyntic glands with parietal cells (pink, upper gland: HCl, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (basophilic, gland base: pepsinogen), mucous neck cells, ECL and D cells
DuodenumVilli plus Brunner glands in the submucosa (alkaline mucus); bile and pancreatic ducts open at the major papilla
JejunumTallest plicae circulares and long villi; no Brunner glands; the main site of absorption
IleumPeyer patches (lymphoid follicles) with M cells that sample antigens; most goblet cells of the small intestine
ColonNo villi or plicae; straight crypts full of goblet cells; teniae coli, haustra, epiploic appendages

Small intestine surface area is amplified by plicae circulares (mucosa plus submucosa), villi (mucosa) and microvilli (the brush border, the largest gain). Villi absorb; crypts of Lieberkühn hold stem cells and secrete, with Paneth cells at their base releasing lysozyme and defensins.

Oral mucosa: masticatory (gingiva, hard palate: keratinized or parakeratinized, bound to bone), lining (lips, cheeks, floor of mouth, ventral tongue, soft palate: nonkeratinized), specialized (dorsal tongue). Papillae: filiform (most numerous, keratinized, rasping, no taste buds), fungiform (scattered, taste buds), circumvallate (8-12 in a V, taste buds in the trench, serous von Ebner glands), foliate (lateral). Taste buds have gustatory, supporting and basal (stem) cells. The vermilion has thin keratin and tall vascular papillae (its red color) but no glands.

Salivary glands: acinus → intercalated duct → striated duct (basal mitochondria for ion transport) → excretory ducts; myoepithelial cells squeeze the acini. Serous acini stain dark with round nuclei; mucous ones are pale with flattened basal nuclei; serous demilunes cap mucous tubules. Parotid: all serous. Submandibular: mixed, mostly serous. Sublingual: mostly mucous. Plasma cells make dimeric IgA (J chain); the epithelium carries it into saliva and adds secretory component.

Liver and gallbladder

Three ways to draw the lobule: the classic lobule (hexagon around a central vein, portal triads at the corners; blood flow), the portal lobule (triangle around a triad; bile flow) and the hepatic acinus (diamond between two central veins; the metabolic unit). In the acinus, zone 1 (periportal) gets the most oxygen; zone 3 (centrilobular) gets the least and has the most CYP450, so it is hit first by ischemia, acetaminophen and alcohol. Blood runs from triad to central vein; bile runs the other way, from canaliculi between hepatocytes to the ducts of the triad. Sinusoids have fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium over the space of Disse; Kupffer cells are the resident macrophages; stellate (Ito) cells store vitamin A and, when activated, lay down the collagen of fibrosis. The gallbladder has simple columnar epithelium that concentrates bile, a smooth muscle coat, and no muscularis mucosae or submucosa.
full.mg-gipath:
What's tested
  • Esophagus and stomach: GERD and Barrett esophagus, esophageal cancers, H. pylori and peptic ulcers, NSAID injury, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • Bowel: celiac disease, Crohn disease vs ulcerative colitis, C. difficile colitis, diverticular disease, Hirschsprung disease, colorectal cancer and the polyp syndromes with oral signs
  • Liver: injury patterns, the hepatitis viruses, alcoholic and fatty liver disease, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, acetaminophen, cirrhosis and its complications, jaundice and gallstones
  • The patient with liver disease in the dental chair: bleeding tests, analgesics, infection control
  • GI drugs: PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids, misoprostol and bismuth; antiemetics; antidiarrheals and laxatives; IBD drugs

Esophagus and stomach

GERD is reflux through an incompetent LES (transient relaxations, hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, scleroderma): heartburn, regurgitation, cough and hoarseness, and in the mouth, erosion of the palatal surfaces of the maxillary teeth (bulimia does the same). Long-standing reflux can turn the distal squamous lining into intestinal columnar epithelium with goblet cells, Barrett esophagus, the precursor of adenocarcinoma of the lower esophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus (upper and middle thirds) follows alcohol and tobacco. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting.

H. pylori is a curved, flagellated gram-negative rod whose urease makes ammonia that buffers the acid around it. It causes chronic antral gastritis, about 90% of duodenal ulcers and most gastric ulcers, and raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Duodenal ulcer pain tends to ease with food; gastric ulcer pain worsens with it. Diagnose with a urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy; treat with a PPI plus antibiotics (clarithromycin with amoxicillin or metronidazole), or bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline). NSAIDs are the other main cause: blocking COX-1 removes the prostaglandins that keep mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow up, and the risk climbs with anticoagulants, corticosteroids, SSRIs and age. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a gastrin-secreting tumor (pancreas or duodenum, sometimes with MEN1): severe, multiple or jejunal ulcers and diarrhea, treated with high-dose PPI.

Bowel

Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 carriers: anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA, and a duodenal biopsy with villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes. It causes malabsorption (bulky stools, iron-deficiency anemia), dermatitis herpetiformis and, in the mouth, aphthous ulcers and symmetric enamel defects. Treatment is a gluten-free diet.

Crohn diseaseUlcerative colitis
WhereAnywhere mouth to anus, most often terminal ileum; skip lesionsRectum, spreading continuously up the colon
DepthTransmural: fistulas, strictures, abscessesMucosa and submucosa: crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps
HallmarksNoncaseating granulomas, cobblestone mucosa, creeping fat; smoking worsens itBloody diarrhea, toxic megacolon, primary sclerosing cholangitis; higher colon cancer risk
MouthCobblestoning, linear ulcers, mucosal tags, lip swelling, aphthaeAphthae; pyostomatitis vegetans ("snail-track" pustules)

C. difficile colitis follows antibiotics (clindamycin is the classic one, also cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones) and PPIs: toxins A and B, watery diarrhea, pseudomembranes. Treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin and avoid antimotility drugs. Diverticulosis (outpouchings, mostly sigmoid, low-fiber diets) can bleed painlessly; diverticulitis gives left lower quadrant pain and fever. Hirschsprung disease: neural crest cells fail to reach the distal colon, the aganglionic segment can't relax, and the colon above it dilates (delayed meconium). Colorectal adenocarcinoma is among the top causes of cancer death and usually follows the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC, then KRAS, then p53). Syndromes a dentist may spot first: Gardner syndrome (an APC variant of familial adenomatous polyposis: jaw osteomas, supernumerary and impacted teeth, odontomas, epidermoid cysts; colon cancer is nearly certain without colectomy) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11: hamartomatous polyps and dark macules on the lips and buccal mucosa). GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal (c-KIT).

Liver

Acute hepatitis shows ballooning hepatocytes and apoptotic (Councilman) bodies; chronic hepatitis shows portal inflammation and, with time, bridging fibrosis that ends in cirrhosis: regenerative nodules wrapped in fibrous septa.

VirusSpreadChronic?Notes
A (RNA)Fecal-oralNoVaccine; the most common acute hepatitis
B (DNA)Blood, sex, birthAbout 5% of adults, 90% of newbornsVaccine; HBsAg = infected, anti-HBs = immune, HBeAg = highly infectious; HCC risk
C (RNA)Blood (IV drugs)Most (75-85%)No vaccine; cured by direct-acting antivirals; leading cause of cirrhosis and HCC
DBloodWith BNeeds HBV to replicate
EFecal-oral (water)NoSevere in pregnancy

Alcoholic liver disease runs from reversible steatosis to alcoholic hepatitis (Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophils, AST:ALT above 2) to cirrhosis. Fatty liver disease without alcohol (NAFLD/NASH) tracks obesity, diabetes and the metabolic syndrome. Hemochromatosis (HFE, autosomal recessive) deposits iron in liver, pancreas, heart and skin: cirrhosis, "bronze diabetes," heart failure; treat with phlebotomy. Wilson disease (ATP7B) deposits copper in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), with low ceruloplasmin. Acetaminophen overdose: CYP450 makes the toxic NAPQI, glutathione runs out, zone 3 dies; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione, and chronic alcohol use lowers the safe dose.

Cirrhosis brings portal hypertension (varices, ascites, splenomegaly with low platelets, caput medusae), hepatic encephalopathy (ammonia; treated with lactulose and rifaximin), coagulopathy (the liver makes factors II, VII, IX and X), low albumin, jaundice, spider angiomas and gynecomastia (estrogen isn't cleared) and a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Jaundice appears above about 2-3 mg/dL of bilirubin: unconjugated from hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome; conjugated from obstruction (dark urine, pale stools, itching). Gallstones are mostly cholesterol stones (female, over 40, obesity, pregnancy); pigment stones follow hemolysis. A stone in the cystic duct causes cholecystitis; in the common bile duct, jaundice; at the ampulla, pancreatitis.

The dental patient with liver disease

  • Bleeding: check the PT/INR (clotting factor synthesis) and the platelet count (splenic sequestration) before surgery; use local hemostatic measures.
  • Drugs: acetaminophen at a reduced dose (about 2 g a day at most) is the usual choice; avoid NSAIDs in cirrhosis (bleeding, ulcers, kidney injury); amide local anesthetics such as lidocaine are cleared by the liver, so keep doses modest; sedatives last longer.
  • Infection control: standard precautions and hepatitis B vaccination for the whole team; after a needlestick, HBV transmits far more readily than HCV, and HCV more than HIV.
  • Oral signs: yellow soft palate and floor of mouth, petechiae and gingival bleeding, glossitis, parotid enlargement and xerostomia in alcohol use.

GI drugs

Drug (clue)MechanismKey points
PPIs (-prazole)Irreversibly block H+/K+ ATPase; prodrugs activated in acidMost effective acid suppressors (erosive esophagitis, ulcers, ZE); take 30 min before breakfast; long-term: low B12 and Mg, fractures, C. difficile, pneumonia; rebound acid on stopping
H2 blockers (-tidine)Block histamine at parietal H2 receptorsFaster onset but weaker than PPIs; tolerance; cimetidine inhibits CYP450 and is antiandrogenic (gynecomastia)
AntacidsNeutralize acidFastest relief; Mg causes diarrhea, Al constipation; Ca, Mg, Al bind tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones (separate doses); NaHCO3 alkalosis; calcium carbonate milk-alkali syndrome
MisoprostolPGE1 analogPrevents NSAID ulcers; causes diarrhea; abortifacient, so not in pregnancy
Sucralfate; bismuthCoats the ulcer base; bismuth is also antimicrobialBismuth subsalicylate: traveler's diarrhea, H. pylori; black tongue and stool
5-HT3 antagonists (-setron)Block 5-HT3 in the area postrema and on gut vagal afferentsOndansetron: chemotherapy and postoperative nausea; headache, constipation, QT prolongation
D2 antagonistsBlock D2 in the chemoreceptor trigger zoneMetoclopramide (also 5-HT4 agonist: prokinetic), prochlorperazine, promethazine; extrapyramidal effects (dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia), high prolactin, QT

LaxativesBulk (psyllium), osmotic (PEG, lactulose, Mg salts), stimulant (senna, bisacodyl), softener (docusate)Lactulose also traps ammonia in an acidified colon (encephalopathy); methylnaltrexone for opioid constipation
IBD drugs5-ASA (sulfasalazine, mesalamine); corticosteroids; azathioprine; methotrexate (antifolate); anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab)Steroids induce remission but don't maintain it; methotrexate causes stomatitis (folic acid helps); anti-TNF: screen for TB, infection risk
full.mg-bone:
What's tested
  • Cartilage: the three types, appositional vs interstitial growth, type II collagen and aggrecan, poor repair
  • Bone: matrix (type I collagen, hydroxyapatite), the three cells, the osteoclast's acid machine, M-CSF, RANKL and OPG, why PTH acts on osteoclasts indirectly
  • Intramembranous vs endochondral ossification, the growth plate, remodeling, and calcium control by PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin and FGF-23
  • Bone disorders: osteogenesis imperfecta, achondroplasia, osteopetrosis, cleidocranial dysplasia, Paget disease, osteoporosis, osteomalacia and rickets, with their oral findings
  • Bone drugs: calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonates, denosumab, teriparatide, romosozumab, raloxifene, and medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)

Cartilage

Cartilage is avascular, aneural and alymphatic, fed by diffusion, so it repairs poorly. Chondroblasts from the inner perichondrium add matrix at the surface (appositional growth, girth); chondrocytes inside lacunae divide into isogenous groups (interstitial growth, length). Its matrix is type II collagen plus aggrecan, a bottle-brush proteoglycan on hyaluronan whose negative charge holds water and resists compression. SOX9 is the chondrocyte master gene; collagen hydroxylation needs vitamin C (scurvy).

TypeWhereFeatures
HyalineArticular surfaces, trachea, larynx, fetal skeleton, growth platesMost common; type II collagen; articular cartilage has no perichondrium and can't repair
ElasticExternal ear, epiglottisElastic fibers; has perichondrium
FibrocartilageIntervertebral discs, menisci, pubic symphysis, TMJ discTypes I and II collagen; no perichondrium; resists tension and compression

Bone and its cells

Bone holds 99% of the body's calcium and 85% of its phosphorus. It is about 30% organic (90% of that type I collagen, plus osteocalcin, osteopontin and osteonectin), 50% mineral (hydroxyapatite) and 20% water, and it grows only by apposition. Osteoblasts line bone surfaces, lay down osteoid (unmineralized matrix), make alkaline phosphatase, and end as lining cells, osteocytes or by apoptosis. Osteocytes (90-95% of bone cells) sit in lacunae, talk through canaliculi and sense load; they make sclerostin (brakes bone formation through Wnt) and FGF-23 (wastes phosphate). Osteoclasts come from the monocyte-macrophage line and fuse into giant multinucleated cells. A sealing zone walls off a Howship lacuna; carbonic anhydrase II and an H+ pump at the ruffled border make HCl (pH about 4) that dissolves mineral, and cathepsin K digests the collagen.

Coupling: osteoblasts and osteocytes make M-CSF and RANKL; RANKL binds RANK on precursors and makes osteoclasts. OPG is the osteoblast's decoy receptor that soaks up RANKL. Estrogen raises OPG, lowers RANKL and speeds osteoclast apoptosis, which is why bone loss accelerates after menopause. Osteoclasts have no PTH receptors: PTH acts on osteoblasts, which raise RANKL. Continuous PTH resorbs bone; intermittent PTH builds it.

Bone is laid down first as woven bone, then remodeled into lamellar bone: cortical (osteons around Haversian canals, joined by Volkmann canals) and trabecular. Don't confuse osteon (structural unit) with osteoid (new matrix).

Making bone and controlling calcium

Intramembranous ossification turns mesenchyme straight into bone: the skull vault, maxilla, most of the mandible and most of the clavicle (and an extraction socket heals the same way). Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model: long bones, vertebrae, pelvis, skull base. The growth plate runs reserve → proliferation → hypertrophy → calcification → ossification; estrogen closes it in both sexes. The mandibular condyle has its own secondary cartilage growth site. Remodeling never stops: activation, resorption (weeks), reversal, formation and mineralization (months).

When calcium falls, PTH raises it: bone (through osteoblast RANKL), kidney (keeps calcium, wastes phosphate, switches on 1α-hydroxylase) and gut (through calcitriol). Vitamin D is made in skin by UVB, 25-hydroxylated in the liver and 1α-hydroxylated in the kidney; calcitriol raises gut calcium and phosphate absorption. Calcitonin (thyroid C cells) lowers calcium. FGF-23 from osteocytes wastes phosphate; its excess causes hypophosphatemic rickets, which in the mouth gives large pulp chambers and abscesses of intact teeth.

Hypocalcemia (after parathyroid removal in thyroid surgery, vitamin D deficiency, CKD): perioral tingling, muscle cramps and tetany (Chvostek and Trousseau signs), long QT, cataracts; in children, enamel hypoplasia. Hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism, cancer): stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychiatric moans, constipation and weakness; hyperparathyroidism in the jaws shows loss of the lamina dura and brown tumors. Treat severe hypercalcemia with IV saline, then a bisphosphonate, denosumab or calcitonin.

Bone disorders

DisorderDefectWhat you see
Osteogenesis imperfectaType I collagen (COL1A1/COL1A2, dominant; CRTAP or P3H1, recessive)Too little bone: fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta
AchondroplasiaFGFR3 gain of function (dominant; most new mutations, older fathers)Endochondral growth fails, appositional is normal: short limbs, normal trunk, large head
OsteopetrosisOsteoclasts can't acidify (e.g. carbonic anhydrase II)Dense but brittle bone, marrow failure (anemia, infections), cranial nerve palsies, jaw osteomyelitis after extraction; cured by stem cell transplant
Cleidocranial dysplasiaRUNX2 (needed for osteoblasts)Absent or small clavicles, open fontanelles, many unerupted supernumerary teeth
Paget diseaseChaotic remodeling: osteolytic → mixed → osteoscleroticOver 50; skull, spine, pelvis, femur; very high alkaline phosphatase; mosaic bone; maxilla more than mandible: widening jaw, spacing, dentures stop fitting, "cotton wool" radiopacity, hypercementosis, bleeding at surgery; rarely osteosarcoma
OsteoporosisResorption exceeds formation; bone is normally mineralized but there is less of itPostmenopausal (trabecular: vertebrae, wrist) and senile (hip); DEXA T-score ≤ -2.5; glucocorticoids are the top drug cause
Osteomalacia / ricketsVitamin D deficiency: osteoid isn't mineralizedLow calcium and phosphate, high PTH and alkaline phosphatase; rickets: bowed legs, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, delayed eruption, enamel hypoplasia

Fracture repair: hematoma, then a soft procallus (about week 1), a bony callus of woven bone (weeks 2-3), bridging, and remodeling. Osteoporosis in the dental patient means thinner alveolar bone, more ridge resorption after extraction, and patients on antiresorptives.

Bone drugs

DrugMechanismKey points
Calcium, vitamin DSupplementsCarbonate needs stomach acid (take with food); citrate absorbs without it; separate calcium by about 4 hours from tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine and bisphosphonates
Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate oral; zoledronic acid IV)Pyrophosphate analogs that bind hydroxyapatite; resorbing osteoclasts take them up; nitrogen-containing ones block farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (mevalonate pathway) and the cell diesFirst line for osteoporosis; also Paget, bone metastases, hypercalcemia of malignancy. Oral: empty stomach, plain water, upright 30 minutes (esophagitis). Stay in bone for years. Risks: MRONJ, atypical femur fractures, hypocalcemia
DenosumabMonoclonal antibody to RANKLInjected every 6 months; doesn't stay in bone, so stopping it brings rebound loss and vertebral fractures; hypocalcemia; MRONJ risk similar to or higher than bisphosphonates
Teriparatide (abaloparatide)Intermittent PTH-receptor activation: anabolicDaily injection, about 2 years (osteosarcoma in rats); can raise calcium; avoid in Paget disease, prior skeletal radiation and open growth plates; the osteoporosis drug not linked to MRONJ
RomosozumabAntibody to sclerostin: builds bone and slows resorption12 months; boxed warning for MI and stroke
RaloxifeneSERM: estrogen agonist in bone, antagonist in breastFewer vertebral fractures and breast cancers; raises clot risk
Calcitonin (salmon)Inhibits osteoclastsWeak; Paget disease, hypercalcemia

MRONJ

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw is exposed jawbone for more than 8 weeks in a patient on an antiresorptive (or antiangiogenic) drug who has had no jaw radiation. Antiresorptives stop the remodeling that repairs everyday microdamage, and the jaws carry heavy loads. The risk is highest with high-dose IV therapy for cancer (about 1-5%), far lower with oral drugs for osteoporosis, and rises with longer use, extractions and other bone surgery (the usual trigger), periodontal disease, steroids, diabetes and smoking; the mandible is hit more than the maxilla. Prevent it: finish extractions and remove infection before the drug starts, keep hygiene excellent, use atraumatic technique, and in high-risk patients prefer endodontics over extraction. Talk to the physician about timing; stopping the drug for surgery is not a settled practice.
full.et-ada:
What's tested
  • The five principles in Code order, their one-word meanings and the duty each states: patient autonomy (1), nonmaleficence (2), beneficence (3), justice (4), veracity (5)
  • Naming the principle and Code section a scenario turns on, and the ethical answer
  • How the Code is built: principles (aspirational), the Code of Professional Conduct (binding on members) and advisory opinions (interpretations); ethics versus law
  • The classic cases: records and transfer, impaired colleagues, abandonment, postexposure duties, abuse reporting, patient selection and HIV, emergency care, justifiable criticism, split fees, amalgam removal, insurance and fees, advertising and specialty claims

How the Code is built

The ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct has three parts:

  • Principles of Ethics: five aspirational goals that justify the rest. They can overlap and compete, so at times they must be balanced.
  • Code of Professional Conduct: specific conduct that is required or forbidden, adopted by the ADA House of Delegates. It is binding on ADA members, and a violation can bring censure, suspension or expulsion.
  • Advisory opinions: the Council on Ethics, Bylaws and Judicial Affairs' interpretations of the Code in specific situations.

Ethics and law are related but not the same: ethical duties often go beyond legal ones. A complaint about a member goes first to the local (component) or state (constituent) dental society. Bioethics' usual four principles (Beauchamp and Childress) are autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice; the ADA adds veracity.

SectionPrincipleIn a wordThe duty
1Patient autonomySelf-governanceRespect the patient's right to self-determination and confidentiality
2NonmaleficenceDo no harmRefrain from harming the patient
3BeneficenceDo goodPromote the patient's welfare
4JusticeFairnessTreat people fairly
5VeracityTruthfulnessCommunicate truthfully

Section 1: Patient autonomy

  • 1.A Patient involvement: tell the patient the proposed treatment and the reasonable alternatives in a way that lets them take part in the decision. This is the Code's basis for informed consent.
  • 1.B Patient records: keep records confidential. When the patient or the patient's new dentist asks, provide the information that will help future treatment, including copies of radiographs, free or for a nominal cost, whether or not the account is paid in full.
  • Sensitive information (HIV status, chemical dependency, sexual orientation) needs the patient's written permission before it is forwarded, unless you know the law allows it. If you must consult another practitioner and the patient can't stay anonymous, ask the patient first.

Section 2: Nonmaleficence

  • 2.A Education: keep knowledge and skills current. 2.B Consultation and referral: refer when the patient will benefit from someone's special skills; the specialist returns the patient to the referring dentist. A second opinion should come from someone with no stake in the treatment that follows.
  • 2.C Auxiliaries: delegate only duties that can legally be delegated, to qualified staff, and supervise them.
  • 2.D Personal impairment: practicing while impaired by alcohol or drugs is unethical. Urge an impaired colleague to seek treatment; with first-hand knowledge that a colleague is practicing impaired, report it to the dental society's professional assistance committee. A dentist with a disease that could endanger patients limits their practice on a physician's advice.
  • 2.E Postexposure: whatever the dentist's own status, tell an exposed patient at once of the need for postexposure evaluation and refer them; if the dentist is the source, share their status with the evaluating practitioner and be tested.
  • 2.F Patient abandonment: once treatment has started, don't stop it without adequate notice and a chance to find another dentist, and don't let the patient's oral health be jeopardized meanwhile.
  • 2.G Personal relationships: avoid relationships with patients that could impair judgment or exploit their trust.

Section 3: Beneficence

  • 3.A Community service, 3.B Governance (every profession regulates itself, so dentists join a professional society and follow its ethics), 3.C sharing research results, and 3.D patents never used to restrict research or practice.
  • 3.E Abuse and neglect: know the signs and report suspected cases to the proper authorities as state law requires. If an adult asks you not to report and the law doesn't require it, respect the wish and, with permission, look for other help.
  • 3.F Professional demeanor: dentists lead the team, and disruptive behavior undermines care and trust.
  • During a public health emergency, the duty to the public may outweigh a patient's request for elective care (3.A.1).

Section 4: Justice

  • 4.A Patient selection: dentists may use reasonable discretion, but may not refuse a patient because of race, creed, color, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin or disability. A patient with HIV, HBV or HCV is treated on the same basis as anyone else: refer only if another practitioner's skills or equipment are needed, and consult the physician if treatment might seriously compromise the patient's health.
  • 4.B Emergency service: make reasonable arrangements for the emergency care of patients of record, and of patients not of record who contact you in an emergency; afterward, return them to their regular dentist unless they prefer otherwise.
  • 4.C Justifiable criticism: tell patients their present oral health status without disparaging prior work, and check with the previous dentist where possible; a difference of opinion is not mistreatment. Report gross or continual faulty treatment to the reviewing agency the local or state society designates.
  • 4.D Expert testimony is allowed, but a fee that depends on the case's outcome is unethical.
  • 4.E Rebates and split fees are forbidden, including paying a marketer, social-coupon company or influencer a percentage of the fees collected.

Section 5: Veracity

  • 5.A Representation of care: removing sound amalgams from a non-allergic patient to rid the body of "toxins," at the dentist's recommendation, is unethical, and so is any claim to cure disease without scientific support.
  • 5.B Representation of fees: waiving a copayment without telling the insurer is overbilling; raising a fee because the patient has insurance is unethical; the full fee is the fee charged a patient without benefits. Reporting wrong treatment dates, misdescribing a procedure and recommending unnecessary services are all false representations.
  • 5.C Conflicts of interest: disclose a financial tie to a company whose product you present. 5.D: report a serious adverse drug or device reaction to the FDA; when selling products, verify the claims yourself and disclose your financial incentive.
  • 5.F Advertising is allowed unless it is false or misleading in a material respect (unsubstantiated claims of superior quality, results you can't promise). Advertising an HIV-negative test needs a statement that it can't guarantee current status.
  • 5.G Name of practice: a departing dentist's name may stay for up to one year. 5.H and 5.I: announce as a specialist only in a recognized specialty for which you are educated; a general dentist may list services such as implants or orthodontics but must say they are provided by a general dentist.

Working a scenario

Ask which duty is at stake and name its principle: a patient's choice or privacy (autonomy), a risk of harm (nonmaleficence), the patient's or the public's welfare (beneficence), fair treatment and dealings with colleagues (justice), or honesty in records, claims and advertising (veracity). Principles are prima facie duties that sometimes have to be weighed against each other, but the Code's specific rules (records released whether or not the bill is paid, no split fees) are not optional.

ScenarioPrincipleThe answer
A new dentist asks for records; the patient owes moneyAutonomy (1.B)Send copies anyway, free or at nominal cost
A colleague practices while impairedNonmaleficence (2.D)Urge treatment; report to the professional assistance committee
You want to dismiss a patient midway through a bridgeNonmaleficence (2.F)Adequate notice and time to find another dentist
A patient with HIV asks to become your patientJustice (4.A)Accept and treat on the same basis as others
A stranger calls with facial swelling on a weekendJustice (4.B)Arrange emergency care, then return them to their dentist
A new patient has poor crowns from another dentistJustice (4.C)Explain the findings without disparaging; report only gross or continual faulty work
A coupon site keeps half of each feeJustice (4.E)Fee splitting: not allowed
Copay waived without telling the insurerVeracity (5.B)Overbilling
full.et-pro:
What's tested
  • Informed consent: what must be disclosed, the reasonable-patient standard (Canterbury v. Spence), decision-making capacity, informed refusal and implied consent
  • Who consents for a minor or for an adult who lacks capacity
  • Confidentiality and HIPAA: what's protected, when you may share without authorization, the patient's rights, and the duty to warn (Tarasoff)
  • Records and the medical history: what to record and how to correct an entry
  • The duty to report suspected child abuse and neglect and its signs; disclosing errors; whistle-blowing
  • Infection control and bloodborne pathogens as professional duties: standard precautions, OSHA's rules, transmission risks and what to do after an exposure
  • Ethical reasoning: valid and sound arguments, the common fallacies and the main moral theories

Informed consent

Consent is a conversation, not a signature: the signed form only documents it. Valid consent needs a patient with capacity who understands and chooses freely after hearing the diagnosis; the nature and purpose of the proposed treatment; its benefits and material risks; the reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, and their risks; and the prognosis and costs, with a chance to ask questions.

Three court cases built it. Schloendorff (1914): every adult of sound mind has the right to decide what is done to their own body. Salgo (1957): the first use of the words "informed consent." Canterbury v. Spence (1972): disclose every risk that a reasonable person in the patient's position would find significant to the decision (the reasonable-patient standard), not just what other doctors customarily disclose.

  • Capacity is a clinical judgment, made decision by decision; competence is a legal finding by a court. Capacity means the patient can understand the information, appreciate that it applies to them, reason about the options and express a choice. Agreeing with the dentist is not one of them.
  • Informed refusal: a patient with capacity may refuse; explain the consequences, document the refusal and have it signed. But a patient can't require care below the standard of care: if a patient refuses the radiographs needed to diagnose, the dentist may decline that treatment.
  • Implied consent: a patient who opens for an examination implies consent to it, and an emergency in an unconscious patient implies consent to lifesaving care.
  • Mill's harm principle allows limiting liberty only to prevent harm to others. Paternalism, overriding a competent, informed adult for their own good (a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood), isn't justified: give your recommendation and reasons, then respect the choice.

Minors and patients who can't consent

  • For a minor, a parent or legal guardian consents. A grandparent, babysitter or stepparent can't, unless they are the legal guardian or hold written authorization. After a divorce, a parent with legal custody consents.
  • An emancipated minor (married, in the military, or self-supporting and living independently) consents for themselves. State law sets the details: Alabama's age of majority is 19, and Alabama lets a minor 14 or older consent to their own dental care.
  • Seek a child's assent (agreement) as well, but it doesn't replace the parent's consent. For an adult without capacity, a court-appointed guardian or a health care power of attorney consents.

Confidentiality and HIPAA

Confidentiality respects autonomy and an implied promise (deontological reasons) and lets patients disclose what the dentist needs to know (consequentialist reasons). HIPAA (1996):

  • The Privacy Rule protects protected health information (PHI), any individually identifiable health information, whether spoken, on paper or electronic. The Security Rule covers electronic PHI, and the Breach Notification Rule says when patients must be told of a breach.
  • PHI may be shared without written authorization for treatment, payment and health care operations, and where the law requires it (abuse reports, public health, court orders). Other uses, such as marketing or a patient's photo on social media, need written authorization.
  • The minimum necessary standard limits what is shared to what the purpose needs; it doesn't apply to sharing for treatment.
  • Patients receive a Notice of Privacy Practices and may see and get a copy of their records (within 30 days, for a reasonable cost-based fee), ask for corrections and get an accounting of disclosures. Discuss patients only with those caring for them, never in public spaces.

Tarasoff (1976): a therapist had a duty to protect an identifiable person whom his patient had threatened to kill. Confidentiality gives way to a serious, foreseeable threat to someone else.

Records and the medical history

  • The record is a legal document: medical history, findings, diagnosis, consent and refusal, treatment, prescriptions and communications.
  • Never erase, alter or backdate. Correct a paper entry with a single line, dated and initialed, so the original stays readable; in an electronic record, add a dated addendum.
  • The dentist owns the original, and the patient is entitled to a copy. Review the medical history at every visit and update it fully at least once a year.

The duty to report

  • Child abuse and neglect: dentists are mandated reporters in every state. Report a reasonable suspicion (proof isn't needed) to child protective services or the police. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability, and in most states failing to report is itself an offense.
  • More than half of physical abuse injuries are to the head, face, mouth or neck. Warning signs: bruises in different stages of healing, a torn labial frenum, bruises on the cheeks or ears, a story that doesn't fit the injury or keeps changing, delay in seeking care, and untreated disease the caregiver knows about (neglect).
  • Most states also require reports of elder or vulnerable-adult abuse; for a competent adult, follow the law and the patient's wishes (Code 3.E).
  • Errors: disclose them, since not disclosing is almost never justified. Disclosure keeps future consent informed and builds trust, and the fiduciary relationship demands it. A bad outcome isn't always bad work.
  • Whistle-blowing is permissible when serious harm is at stake, you have told your supervisors and nothing was done; it becomes obligatory when you also have documentation and good reason to think going public will prevent the harm. Use internal routes first.

Infection control as a professional duty

  • Standard precautions (CDC, 1996) apply to every patient, whatever their infection status. They grew out of universal precautions (1985), which treated blood and certain body fluids as infectious. In dentistry, saliva counts as potentially infectious material.
  • OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard: a written exposure control plan; engineering controls (sharps containers, self-sheathing needles) and work-practice controls (no two-handed recapping); PPE at no cost; the hepatitis B vaccine offered free within 10 working days of assignment (a refusal is signed); free, confidential follow-up after an exposure; and yearly training.
  • Risk of infection after a needlestick from an infected source: HBV about 30% (6–30%), HCV about 2%, HIV about 0.3%. HBV survives on dry surfaces for at least a week. There is a vaccine for HBV, but none for HCV or HIV.
  • After an exposure: wash with soap and water (flush the eyes or mouth with water), don't squeeze the wound or use bleach, report at once, and test the source with consent. HIV prophylaxis starts as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72.

Thinking it through: arguments and theories

  • An argument offers premises as reasons for a conclusion. A deductive argument is valid when true premises would guarantee the conclusion, and sound when it is valid and its premises are true. An inductive argument is strong or weak; a strong one with true premises is cogent. Validity is about structure, not truth.
  • Valid forms: modus ponens (if p then q; p; so q) and modus tollens (if p then q; not q; so not p). Invalid: affirming the consequent (q; so p) and denying the antecedent (not p; so not q).
FallacyWhat it does
Straw manDistorts a view to attack it more easily
Ad hominemRejects a claim because of who made it
Appeal to ignoranceTrue because not proven false, or false because not proven true
Begging the questionUses the conclusion as its own support
Slippery slopeClaims one step will inevitably lead to disaster
TheoryWhat makes an act right
Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill)Consequences: the greatest good for all affected (act or rule versions)
Kantian deontologyDuty and motive: act only on rules you could make universal; treat people as ends, never merely as means
Principlism (Ross; Beauchamp and Childress)Prima facie duties, weighed case by case
Virtue ethicsCharacter: what a good person would do
Ethics of careRelationships and responsibilities to particular people
full.eb-ask:
What's tested
  • The 5 A's in order (ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess) and what each step does
  • Building a PICO(T) question and picking P, I, C, O and T out of a case; background versus foreground questions; the four kinds of clinical question and the design that best answers each
  • Where to search: TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library
  • Naming the design from a short description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good and bad at
  • The evidence pyramid, and literature review versus systematic review versus meta-analysis versus clinical practice guideline (GRADE, AGREE)
  • Efficacy versus effectiveness, the study-context continuum, practice-based research networks and the three gaps between evidence and practice

The 5 A's

Evidence-based dentistry combines the best available research with the dentist's clinical expertise and the patient's needs and values. It runs as five steps, always in this order.

StepWhat you do
1. AskTurn the patient's problem into a focused, answerable question (PICO).
2. AcquireSearch for the best evidence: TRIP, PubMed, Cochrane.
3. AppraiseJudge it: is the design the strongest one for this question, is the study valid, are the results important?
4. ApplyCombine the evidence with your expertise and the patient's values, and decide together.
5. AssessCheck the result: did it work, did the patient follow through, what would you change next time?

Apply and assess are the pair people mix up: apply is using the evidence with this patient; assess is looking back at how it went.

Asking: PICO(T)

  • P (patient, population or problem): the few characteristics that matter (age, condition), neither so broad that it means nothing nor so narrow that no study fits.
  • I (intervention or exposure): the treatment, test or risk factor you are asking about.
  • C (comparison): ideally one alternative, such as standard care, a placebo or no treatment. It is sometimes only implied.
  • O (outcome): specific and measurable (new caries, pain score, implant survival), never "better care".
  • T (time): optional in the question and easy to forget, but every study answering it needs a time frame.

Template: "In [P], does [I], compared with [C], change [O] over [T]?" For example: "In children with primary teeth, does fluoride toothpaste, compared with non-fluoride toothpaste, lower caries incidence over one year?" A classic mistake is a population that makes the comparison impossible, such as comparing smokers with nonsmokers in a population defined as smokers.

BackgroundForeground
AsksGeneral knowledge about one condition or treatment (who, what, when, why, how)A comparison of two or more options for a specific patient or problem
Example"What are the side effects of ibuprofen?""After third-molar extraction, is ibuprofen plus acetaminophen as good as an opioid for pain?"
PICO?No: a textbook or review answers itYes
Question typeAsks aboutBest design
TherapyWhich treatment does more good than harmRandomized controlled trial
DiagnosisHow well a test identifies a diseaseCross-sectional comparison against a reference (gold) standard
PrognosisThe likely course of a disease, or what predicts itCohort
Etiology or harmCauses and risk factors; harm from an exposure or treatmentCohort or case-control (assigning a harm would be unethical)

Acquiring: where to search

  • TRIP first: one search returns guidelines, systematic reviews and primary studies, sorted by level of evidence.
  • PubMed (MEDLINE, from the National Library of Medicine) next: the largest biomedical database. Clinical Queries filters it by question type (therapy, diagnosis, etiology, prognosis) and pulls out systematic reviews.
  • Cochrane Library: rigorous systematic reviews, mostly of randomized trials.
  • Also: journals through the UAB library, the ADA's clinical practice guidelines and evidence-based journals. Expert opinion is the last resort.

Study designs

The first split is who decides the exposure. In an experimental study the investigator assigns it; in an observational study the investigator only watches exposures people already have. Observational studies are descriptive (no comparison group: case reports and series) or analytic (a comparison: ecological, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort).

DesignHow it worksGood forWeak spots
Case report or seriesOne unusual patient, or several with the same condition or treatment, describedNew diseases and side effects; ideas for trialsNo comparison group; the lowest inferential power of human studies
Ecological (correlational)Compares averages of groups (cities, countries)Cheap; uses existing dataEcological fallacy: the exposed people may not be the ones with the outcome
Cross-sectionalA snapshot: exposure and outcome measured at the same time in the same people, often by surveyPrevalence; quick and cheapNo time order, so no cause and effect
Case-controlStarts with the outcome: cases with the disease and controls without, then looks back for exposuresRare diseases, long latency, many risk factors at once; quick and cheapRecall and selection bias; poor for rare exposures; no incidence; gives an odds ratio
CohortStarts with the exposure: exposed and unexposed people followed for the outcome (prospective, or retrospective from records)Time order; incidence and relative risk; rare exposures; several outcomes of one exposureSlow and costly; loss to follow-up; poor for rare diseases
Controlled trialThe investigator allocates people to treatment or control without randomizingThe investigator controls the exposureAllocation can be biased
Randomized controlled trialRandom allocation to treatment or control, followed forwardThe only true experiment: randomization balances known and unknown factors, so it best shows cause and effectCostly; can't test a harmful exposure; strict entry rules limit whom it applies to

Clues in a stem: "looked back" from a disease is case-control; "followed" exposed and unexposed people is cohort; "surveyed once" is cross-sectional; cities or countries is ecological; "randomly assigned" is an RCT.

The evidence pyramid

From bottom to top, as the course draws it: animal and lab studies; case reports, case series and expert opinion; ecological; cross-sectional; case-control; cohort; randomized controlled trials; systematic reviews and meta-analyses; clinical practice guidelines. Higher means stronger evidence for a clinical decision, if the study is done well. Two twists: lab and animal studies control every variable, so they have the greatest inferential power (rigor) when done properly, yet they sit at the bottom because they apply least to patients. And many published pyramids put systematic reviews at the very top, where the course puts guidelines, which build their recommendations on those reviews.

Pre-appraised (filtered) evidence

Literature reviewSystematic reviewMeta-analysisClinical practice guideline
Summarizes the evidence?MaybeYesYesYes
Methods section?No: a narrative; the author picks the studiesYes: a full, reproducible search and a quality grade for each studyYes: a systematic review plus a summary statistic pooling the studies' dataYes: integrates the evidence to approach a clinical problem
Whose view?The author'sCollects and grades the evidenceCollects, grades and combines itEvidence, plus expert opinion where evidence is missing or weak
  • GRADE rates the certainty of a body of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low; risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness (surrogate outcomes), imprecision and publication bias rate it down.
  • AGREE (Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation) judges the quality of clinical practice guidelines.
  • Reporting checklists: CONSORT for randomized trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for systematic reviews.
  • A forest plot shows each study as a square (bigger means more weight) on a line (its 95% confidence interval). The diamond at the bottom is the pooled result: its center is the estimate and its tips the 95% CI. A diamond that crosses the line of no effect (1 for a ratio) is not significant.

From research to practice

Study contexts run along a continuum: lab research (the treatment isn't ready for humans), clinical trials in academic settings (not ready for everyday patients; they test efficacy), practice-based research (not yet ready for all practices; it tests effectiveness) and community-based research (outside the health care system).

EfficacyEffectiveness
AsksDoes it work under ideal conditions?Does it work in the real world?
SettingAn academic health center, usually an RCTEveryday practices
PatientsHighly selectedTypical
CliniciansHighly trained, with no time or cost limitsTypical, with the usual time and money limits

A practice-based research network (PBRN) is a group of dental practices that join to answer research questions in daily practice, where most people get their care; a national dental PBRN has run since 2005.

GapWhat's wrongWhat closes it
Knowledge gapThe evidence doesn't exist yetEfficacy and effectiveness studies
Knowing gapThe evidence exists, but clinicians don't know itDissemination science
Knowing-to-doing gapClinicians know it but don't use it (patient acceptance, habit, cost)Implementation science

The "magic pill" example: if about half drop out at each step (hear of it, try it, prescribe it, the patient accepts it, the patient keeps taking it), very few patients end up helped.
full.eb-appraise:
What's tested
  • Internal versus external validity, and the three threats to validity: bias, confounding and chance
  • The kinds of bias and what randomization, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis do about them; what to check in an RCT
  • Standardization versus calibration, inter- versus intra-examiner reliability, precision versus accuracy, incidence versus prevalence
  • Types of data, mean versus median, and standard deviation
  • Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a 2×2 table, and which one a screening or a confirming test needs
  • Relative risk, odds ratio, absolute risk and the number needed to treat; reading a ratio with its 95% confidence interval
  • p-values, type I and II errors, power, and statistical versus clinical significance

Is the study valid?

Internal validityExternal validity
AsksWas the study well designed, run and analyzed?Was the study population well defined, and enrolled with that definition in mind?
MeansThe findings are believable for the people studiedThe findings apply (generalize) to your patients

Three things threaten validity: bias, any systematic error that skews the estimate of the link between exposure and outcome (a bigger sample doesn't fix it); confounding, a third factor tied to both the exposure and the outcome (studying soda and caries without accounting for oral hygiene); and chance, random variation in who was sampled (handled by sample size and statistics).

BiasWhat happensTypical design
SelectionThe way people are chosen makes the groups unlike each other or unlike the population (recruiting in a park for an exercise study)Any, especially case-control
RecallCases remember past exposures differently from controlsCase-control
Attrition (loss to follow-up)Those who drop out differ from those who stayCohort, RCT
Self-report (social desirability)People underreport smoking or overreport flossingSurveys, cross-sectional
Measurement (observer)An examiner who knows the group scores it differentlyUnblinded trials
PublicationPositive results are published more often than negative onesSystematic reviews (search the gray literature)

Confounding is controlled by randomization (the only method that also balances unknown factors), restriction, matching, stratification and statistical adjustment.

Appraising a randomized trial

  • Randomization done properly (for example, computer-generated and concealed), not circumvented, with the groups balanced at baseline.
  • Blinding (masking): in a double-blind trial neither the participants nor the clinicians and assessors know who got what. The groups must be treated alike apart from the intervention.
  • Intention-to-treat analysis: everyone is analyzed in the group they were randomized to, whether or not they finished or followed the treatment, which keeps randomization's balance. A per-protocol analysis counts only those who completed the treatment as planned and can overstate the benefit.
  • Subgroups planned at the start; a subgroup found afterward (reporting only the women because it worked better in them) is a red flag.
  • Sample size calculated beforehand, the trial registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and reported by CONSORT (enrollment, allocation, follow-up, analysis).
  • Applicability: patient-important outcomes rather than surrogate outcomes (a plaque index in place of tooth loss), an effect large enough to matter, long enough follow-up, benefits and harms both reported, good compliance, and participants like your patients.

Measuring well

  • Standardization: every examiner uses the same criteria, instruments and procedure. Calibration: examiners score the same patients and train until their scores agree; it takes longer.
  • Reliability (repeatability): inter-examiner, different examiners get the same score; intra-examiner, the same examiner gets the same score on the same patient at different times; test-retest, the same person answers the same questionnaire again 1–2 weeks later.
  • Precision is repeatability (reliability); accuracy is closeness to the truth (validity). An examiner who always records the same wrong probing depth is precise but not accurate.
  • Incidence is new cases over a period among people at risk (it needs follow-up: a cohort); prevalence is all existing cases at one time (a cross-sectional study).
  • A census measures everyone, so no inference is needed; a sample measures some and relies on statistics.

Data and the center

TypeWhat it isExamplesUsual graph
