QuantitativeNumbers you can add or subtractAge, blood pressure, millimeters of bone lossHistogram, box plot
BinaryTwo categoriesDisease or no disease, treatment or controlBar chart
NominalNamed categories with no orderBlood type, occupationBar chart
OrdinalCategories with a rankCancer stage, light/moderate/heavy smokerBar chart

The mean is pulled by outliers; the median (the middle value) is the better center for skewed data. The standard deviation measures spread around the mean, and two data sets with the same mean can have very different SDs. In a normal curve about 68% of values fall within 1 SD and 95% within 2. A correlation coefficient runs from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive); correlation doesn't prove cause.

Diagnostic tests

Disease presentDisease absent
Test positiveTrue positive (a)False positive (b)
Test negativeFalse negative (c)True negative (d)
  • Sensitivity = a/(a+c): of the people with the disease, the share who test positive (the true positive rate). A highly sensitive test misses few cases, so a negative result rules the disease out (SnNout). Screening tests need it.
  • Specificity = d/(b+d): of the people without the disease, the share who test negative (the true negative rate). A highly specific test has few false positives, so a positive result rules the disease in (SpPin). Use it to confirm before an irreversible step such as an extraction.
  • PPV = a/(a+b) and NPV = d/(c+d). Predictive values change with prevalence: where a disease is rarer, PPV falls and NPV rises. Sensitivity and specificity don't change with prevalence.
  • Moving a test's cutoff to catch more disease raises sensitivity and lowers specificity. That is why the class notes say a highly sensitive test "can lead to false positives": the false positives come from the specificity it gives up.

Example: a caries device tested on 100 decayed and 100 sound teeth is positive on 90 decayed and 20 sound teeth. Sensitivity 90/100 = 90%; specificity 80/100 = 80%; PPV 90/110 = 82%; NPV 80/90 = 89%.

Risk and the size of an effect

  • Absolute risk = events ÷ people in the group; odds = events ÷ non-events (200 of 600 with arthritis: risk 0.33, odds 0.5).
  • Relative risk (risk ratio) = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed, from cohorts and RCTs. 1 means no difference, above 1 a harmful effect, below 1 a protective one (0.87 means 13% lower risk). A hazard ratio reads the same way over time.
  • Odds ratio = (a×d)/(b×c), the measure from case-control studies; it approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare.
  • Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control risk − treated risk, and NNT = 1/ARR, rounded up (NNH for a harm). Caries in 25% of controls and 15% of treated children: ARR 10%, NNT 10, though the relative risk reduction is 40%.
  • The lecture's pain NNT is how many patients must take an analgesic for one more to get at least 50% pain relief over 4–6 hours than with placebo: 1 is perfect and lower is better. Ibuprofen with acetaminophen (about 1.5) beats oxycodone 5 mg (about 5.5).
  • Relative risk can mislead when the event is rare: armor that makes you "8 times less likely" to be hit by a meteorite changes almost nothing in absolute terms.

Significance and errors

  • The p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if there were truly no difference. Below the chosen alpha (usually 0.05) the result is statistically significant. It doesn't measure how big or important the effect is.
  • The 95% confidence interval is the range of plausible true values. For a ratio, an interval that includes 1 is not significant (HR 0.92, CI 0.83–1.02); for a difference, one that includes 0. A narrower interval is a more precise estimate.
  • Type I error (alpha): a false positive, finding a difference that isn't real. Type II error (beta): a false negative, missing a real difference, most likely in a small study.
  • Power = 1 − beta (usually set at 80%), the chance of detecting a real difference. A larger sample, a bigger true difference, less variability and more accurate measurement raise it; a stricter alpha lowers it.
  • Statistical is not clinical significance: a huge trial can make a trivial difference significant. Judge the size of the effect, its interval, and whether it matters to patients.

plain.hn-neck:
What's tested
  • How spinal nerves and the two autonomic systems are laid out
  • Horner syndrome
  • What lives in the posterior and anterior triangles
  • The root of the neck, the thyroid and the nerves at risk in thyroid surgery
  • Neck fascia and how infection spreads

Each spinal nerve has a sensory back root and a motor front root. The sympathetic system starts in the spinal cord from T1 to L2; nerves for the head relay in the superior cervical ganglion and ride along the carotid arteries. The parasympathetic system leaves with cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and the sacral cord; its head relay stations are the ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular and otic ganglia.

If the neck's sympathetic chain is cut or squeezed (for example by a lung-top tumor), you get Horner syndrome: a slightly droopy eyelid, a small pupil, and a face that is dry and flushed on that side.

The posterior triangle sits between the SCM, the trapezius and the clavicle. Its most famous content is CN XI, lying just under the fascia: cut it and the patient can't shrug. The skin nerves of the cervical plexus come out at the middle of the SCM's back edge; the great auricular nerve covers the skin over the angle of the jaw.

The anterior triangle holds the strap muscles, the carotid sheath (carotid artery inside, internal jugular vein outside, vagus behind), the carotid sinus (blood pressure sensor) and body (oxygen sensor), and the external carotid's eight branches. The hyoid is at C3 and the cricoid at C6.

At the root of the neck, the subclavian artery is split into three parts by the anterior scalene. The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) runs down that muscle to the diaphragm. The thoracic duct empties where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.

In thyroid surgery, the nerve near the superior thyroid artery (external laryngeal) controls pitch, and the nerve near the inferior thyroid artery (recurrent laryngeal) controls most of the voice box; injuring it makes the voice hoarse. Removing the parathyroids by mistake drops calcium and causes muscle spasms.

Neck fascia forms tubes and spaces. The spaces behind the pharynx can carry an infection from a tooth or tonsil down into the chest.
plain.hn-skull:
What's tested
  • The bones and weak spots of the skull
  • What passes through the main skull openings
  • Dural sinuses and the cavernous sinus
  • Head bleeds
  • What each cranial nerve does and how it fails

The braincase is 8 bones; the face is built from the rest. The pterion, on the side of the head, is thin bone over the middle meningeal artery. A hard blow there can tear the artery and cause an epidural bleed: lens-shaped on CT, often with a period of feeling fine before the patient crashes.

Learn the openings in pairs: V2 through the foramen rotundum, V3 through the foramen ovale, the middle meningeal artery through the foramen spinosum; III, IV, V1 and VI through the superior orbital fissure; VII and VIII into the internal acoustic meatus; IX, X and XI through the jugular foramen; XII through its own canal.

Venous blood collects in the dural sinuses and leaves through the internal jugular vein. The cavernous sinus, next to the pituitary, holds the internal carotid and CN VI, with III, IV, V1 and V2 in its wall. Infection from the face or teeth can reach it; the first sign is often an eye that can't look outward (CN VI).

A subdural bleed comes from torn bridging veins (crescent shape, often older people after a small fall). A subarachnoid bleed comes from a burst aneurysm and gives a sudden, terrible headache.

Cranial nerve signs to know: the tongue points toward a bad XII; the uvula points away from a bad X; a bad III gives a droopy lid, a big pupil and an eye turned down and out; Bell palsy (VII nerve) paralyzes the whole half-face, but a stroke spares the forehead.

Two reflexes tie nerves together: touching the cornea is felt by V1 and answered by VII (blink); touching the throat is felt by IX and answered by X (gag).
plain.hn-face:
What's tested
  • The orbit and its fractures
  • How the eye muscles and pupil are controlled
  • Face muscles and facial nerve palsy
  • The danger triangle and the scalp
  • Tears and the parotid gland

The orbit's floor is the weakest wall. A punch to the eye can blow it out into the maxillary sinus, trapping the inferior rectus (the patient can't look up and sees double) and numbing the cheek.

Eye muscles: LR6, SO4, all the rest III. The superior oblique is tested by looking down and in. CN III also opens the eyelid and shrinks the pupil; the sympathetics widen the pupil. For close work, the ciliary muscle tightens and the lens gets rounder. Fluid made in the eye drains at the angle into the canal of Schlemm; when it can't, pressure rises (glaucoma).

All face muscles belong to VII, which splits into five branches inside the parotid. Feeling on the face comes from V1, V2 and V3. In Bell palsy the whole half-face is weak, forehead too. A dental block placed too far back can do this for a few hours.

Face veins around the nose link to the veins of the eye and on to the cavernous sinus, so infections in the danger triangle are serious. In the scalp, the loose layer under the aponeurosis is where blood and pus spread.

Tears come from a gland at the upper outer corner, run to the inner corner and drain into the nose (inferior meatus). The nerve signal for tears comes from VII and relays in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

The parotid is wrapped in tight fascia. The facial nerve runs through it but does not control it; spit from the parotid is driven by IX through the otic ganglion and the auriculotemporal nerve. Its duct opens opposite the upper second molar. After parotid surgery some people sweat on the cheek when they eat (Frey syndrome).
plain.hn-itf:
What's tested
  • What is in the infratemporal fossa
  • The four chewing muscles
  • V3 and its branches, and the blocks dentists give
  • The maxillary artery and the pterygoid plexus
  • How the TMJ moves and dislocates

The infratemporal fossa is the space behind and inside the ramus. It holds the two pterygoid muscles, the maxillary artery, the pterygoid venous plexus and V3, which enters from the foramen ovale.

Chewing muscles all come from arch 1 and all use V3. Three close the jaw (temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid). The lateral pterygoid pulls the jaw forward and opens it. If V3 is cut on one side, the jaw swings toward that side when the mouth opens.

V3's front branch is mostly motor, except the buccal nerve to the cheek. The back branch gives the auriculotemporal nerve (temple, ear, TMJ), the lingual nerve (tongue feeling; it picks up the chorda tympani for taste) and the inferior alveolar nerve (lower teeth, then the mental nerve to the lip and chin).

An inferior alveolar block puts anesthetic in the space between the ramus and the medial pterygoid. It misses the buccal nerve. Too far back reaches the parotid and the facial nerve. A posterior superior alveolar block too deep can hit the pterygoid plexus and cause a sudden bruise-like swelling.

The maxillary artery has three parts: the first gives the middle meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries, the second feeds the chewing muscles, the third gives the arteries for the upper teeth, palate and nose. The pterygoid plexus links to the cavernous sinus, a path for dental infection.

The TMJ has a disc that makes two joints: the lower one hinges, the upper one slides. It dislocates forward, in front of the articular eminence, usually from a big yawn. The joint is fed by the auriculotemporal nerve, which also supplies the ear canal, so a sore TMJ often feels like an earache.
plain.hn-phx:
What's tested
  • What each pharyngeal arch and pouch builds
  • How the lip and palate form and how clefts happen
  • Neck cysts from development
  • The muscles and nerves of the pharynx and larynx
  • The parts of the ear and kinds of hearing loss

Each pharyngeal arch brings its own nerve: arch 1 is V (chewing muscles, malleus, incus), arch 2 is VII (face muscles, stapes, styloid), arch 3 is IX (stylopharyngeus), arches 4 and 6 are X (pharynx, palate and larynx). Pouch 3 makes the thymus and the lower parathyroids; pouch 4 makes the upper parathyroids.

The upper lip's middle (philtrum) and the front of the palate come from the joined medial nasal prominences. If the maxillary prominence doesn't meet them, you get a cleft lip. If the two palatal shelves don't meet each other, you get a cleft palate.

A lump on the side of the neck in front of the SCM may be a lateral cervical cyst, left over from the cervical sinus. A lump in the midline that rises when the tongue sticks out is a thyroglossal duct cyst, left along the path the thyroid took down from the tongue.

In the pharynx, the vagus moves every muscle except the stylopharyngeus (IX). IX feels the gag; X answers it. A fish bone stuck in the piriform recess can injure the nerve that lets the larynx feel food (internal laryngeal).

In the larynx, the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs every muscle except the cricothyroid. Only the posterior cricoarytenoid opens the vocal folds, so losing both recurrent nerves closes the airway. Emergency airway: cut through the cricothyroid ligament.

In the ear, the stapes sits in the oval window. The stapedius (VII) damps loud sound; without it, normal sounds hurt. Children get ear infections because their auditory tube is short and flat. Hearing loss is conductive (outer or middle ear) or sensorineural (cochlea or nerve).
plain.hn-oral:
What's tested
  • The openings of the pterygopalatine fossa
  • Where the sinuses drain and why the maxillary sinus matters to dentists
  • Nerves of the palate and tongue
  • The salivary glands
  • Where infections and lymph from the mouth go

The pterygopalatine fossa is a crossroads behind the upper jaw. V2 enters from the skull and sends branches to the upper teeth, palate, nose and face. Its ganglion relays signals from VII for tears and for nose and palate glands.

Most sinuses drain into the middle meatus. The tear duct drains into the inferior meatus. The maxillary sinus drains from high up, so it gets infected easily, and its floor sits on the roots of the upper back teeth: an extraction can leave a hole into the sinus, and sinusitis can feel like a toothache. Most nosebleeds start on the front of the septum.

For the palate, the greater palatine nerve covers the back of the hard palate and the nasopalatine nerve covers the front, behind the incisors. All soft palate muscles are run by X except the tensor veli palatini (V3).

For the tongue: front two-thirds feel through V3 and taste through VII (chorda tympani); back third feels and tastes through IX; XII moves it (except palatoglossus, X).

The submandibular gland makes most resting saliva and most salivary stones; its duct opens under the tongue. VII drives it and the sublingual gland; IX drives the parotid.

Lymph from the tongue tip and lower front teeth goes to the submental nodes; most other teeth drain to the submandibular nodes; everything ends in the deep cervical chain. A lower tooth whose root tip is below the mylohyoid line spreads infection under the jaw (submandibular space); above it, into the floor of the mouth (sublingual space). Both sides at once is Ludwig angina, an airway emergency.
plain.da-numbering:
What's tested
  • Writing any tooth in Universal, Palmer and FDI
  • When teeth come in, and in what order
  • When teeth start to harden and when roots finish
  • How baby teeth differ from adult teeth

Naming teeth

Universal numbers adult teeth 1 to 32, starting at the upper right third molar and going around to the lower right third molar. Baby teeth use letters A to T the same way. FDI uses two digits: the quadrant (1 upper right, 2 upper left, 3 lower left, 4 lower right; 5 to 8 for baby teeth), then the tooth counted from the midline. So #8 is 11, #19 is 36, #30 is 46, and baby tooth A is 55. Palmer uses a bracket for the quadrant and counts 1 to 8 (A to E for baby teeth) from the midline.

When teeth come in

Baby teeth: central incisors, lateral incisors, first molars, canines, then second molars, from about 6 months to 2 years. The lower teeth usually come first. Adult teeth: the first molars and lower central incisors arrive at about 6. The upper order is 6-1-2-4-5-3-7-8, so the upper canine comes after the premolars, at 11–12, and is the anterior tooth most likely to get stuck. The lower order is 6-1-2-3-4-5-7-8. The first adult tooth to replace a baby tooth is the lower central incisor. Adult molars replace nothing, so they are not "succedaneous".

Hardening and roots

Baby teeth start hardening before birth (about 4–6 months in the womb). The adult first molar starts at birth. Cusp tips and incisal edges harden first, and crowns before roots. An adult root finishes 2–3 years after the tooth comes in; baby roots finish by about age 3.

Baby versus adult teeth

Baby teeth are smaller and whiter, with thin enamel, big pulps and high pulp horns. Their crowns are short and bulge at the neck (cervical ridges), and their molar roots spread wide to leave room for the premolars. A few are one of a kind: the upper central is wider than it is tall, the upper canine has its longer slope on the mesial, and the lower first molar has a big transverse ridge and a bulge at the mesiobuccal. The second baby molars look like the adult first molars.
plain.da-anterior:
What's tested
  • Where the bulge of each surface is
  • Where teeth touch, and the exceptions
  • Telling the incisors apart
  • Upper versus lower canine

Bulges and contacts

Every tooth's facial bulge is in the cervical third. On the tongue side, front teeth bulge in the cervical third and back teeth in the middle third. A crown that is too bulky lets food skip the gum and collects plaque; one that is too flat pushes food into the gum. Teeth touch lower (more cervically) the farther back they are, and each tooth touches its back neighbor lower than its front one. The exceptions are the lower central incisor (both contacts level), the lower first premolar and the baby upper canine. The gap on the tongue side between teeth is bigger than on the cheek side. The CEJ dips most on the mesial of the central incisors.

Incisors

The upper central is the biggest incisor, with a sharp mesial corner and a rounded distal one. The upper lateral is a smaller, rounder copy with a deep lingual fossa; it can have a groove running onto the root that traps plaque, and it often comes in peg-shaped or not at all. The lower central is the smallest adult tooth and nearly symmetric. The lower lateral is a bit bigger, with its incisal edge twisted toward the distolingual.

Canines

The upper canine is the longest tooth with the longest root, a sharp cusp, a short mesial slope and a strong lingual ridge. The lower canine has the longest crown, a long distal slope, a smooth lingual side, and a mesial outline that runs straight into the root; its root can split in two. The upper canine is the last front tooth to come in, so it is the one that gets stuck. Its long root in thick bone also makes it the best tooth to guide the jaw sideways.
plain.da-posterior:
What's tested
  • Which premolar or molar is which
  • How many roots and canals each has
  • First versus second molars

Premolars

The upper first premolar is the one with two roots and a dip (concavity) on its mesial side. The upper second premolar has one root and two cusps of about the same height. The lower first premolar looks like a small canine: a big buccal cusp, a tiny lingual cusp, a crown leaning to the tongue, and a mesial marginal ridge lower than the distal one, which no other back tooth has. The lower second premolar usually has three cusps in a Y pattern with a pit in the middle; with two cusps its grooves look like an H or a U. Lower premolars lean toward the tongue; upper premolars sit straight over their roots.

Upper molars

The upper first molar is the biggest upper tooth. Its cusps from biggest to smallest are mesiolingual, mesiobuccal, distobuccal and distolingual, and the Carabelli cusp sits on the mesiolingual. A ridge (the oblique ridge) runs from the distobuccal to the mesiolingual cusp. It is the only molar wider on the tongue side. It has three roots: palatal longest, then mesiobuccal, then distobuccal. The mesiobuccal root usually holds two canals, so look for four. Its lingual groove and pit are where decay starts. The second molar has a smaller (or missing) distolingual cusp and roots that sit closer together.

Lower molars

The lower first molar has five cusps (three buccal, two lingual) and two buccal grooves; the distal cusp is the smallest. The lower second molar has four cusps in a plus-sign pattern. Both have two roots, mesial and distal; the mesial root is wider, more curved, and holds two canals. Lower molars lean toward the tongue, and their roots lean toward the distal, which helps you tell right from left on an extracted tooth.
plain.da-anomalies:
What's tested
  • Naming an anomaly from a description
  • Fusion versus gemination versus concrescence
  • Inherited versus acquired enamel and dentin defects
  • Types of wear
  • Tooth identification

Too few, too many, in the wrong place

Third molars are the teeth most often missing, then upper laterals and lower second premolars. Missing all teeth goes with ectodermal dysplasia. An extra tooth between the upper centrals is a mesiodens. Third molars and upper canines get impacted most.

Odd shapes

Gemination is one tooth trying to split: count it as one and the count is normal. Fusion is two teeth joined by dentin: count it as one and you are one short. Concrescence is two teeth joined only by cementum. A peg lateral is a small upper lateral. Notched incisors and many-cusped molars point to congenital syphilis. A talon cusp is a claw off the cingulum. Dens in dente is enamel folded into the tooth, usually an upper lateral. Taurodontism is a tall pulp chamber with the furcation pushed down. An enamel pearl at a furcation leaves a pocket.

Enamel and dentin defects

Inherited defects hit every tooth in both sets: amelogenesis imperfecta (bad enamel) and dentinogenesis imperfecta (bluish teeth, chipping enamel, pulps filled in). Fluoride causes white to brown mottling, tetracycline causes gray bands, and an infected baby tooth can spoil the one adult tooth below it (Turner tooth).

Wear

Attrition is tooth against tooth, abrasion is something else rubbing (hard brushing), erosion is acid (vomiting wears the inside of the upper front teeth), and abfraction is a V-shaped notch at the gumline from flexing.

Naming a tooth

Count the cusps for the class, use the roots and tilt for the arch, find the mesial landmark, then hold the face toward you with the mesial at the midline: that side is the patient's side. When two answers seem to fit, the root count and the crown's tilt usually decide it.
plain.da-occlusion:
What's tested
  • Angle Class I, II and III
  • Which cusps hold the bite
  • CR, MIP and CO
  • Canine guidance and group function, and bad contacts
  • What makes cusps taller or shorter

The basics

The upper tongue-side cusps and the lower cheek-side cusps are the "centric" cusps: they hold the bite height and land in the opposing grooves. The other cusps are sharper and guide and protect the cheek and tongue. Seen from the side, the lower teeth follow the curve of Spee; seen from the front, the curve of Wilson. Every tooth meets two opposing teeth except the lower central incisor and the upper third molar.

Angle classes

Class I (most people): the upper first molar's mesiobuccal cusp sits in the lower first molar's buccal groove. Class II: the lower jaw sits back. In division 1 the upper incisors flare forward; in division 2 the upper centrals tip back with a deep bite. Class III: the lower jaw sits forward.

CR, MIP and CO

Centric relation is a joint position: condyles up and forward against the eminences, discs in place. It does not depend on the teeth. MIP is where the teeth fit together best. Centric occlusion is the tooth contact you get with the condyles in CR. Most people (about 9 in 10) slide about 1 mm from CR contact into MIP.

Guidance

The ideal: all back teeth touch evenly when you close, forces go down the long axis, and when the jaw slides sideways or forward the front teeth separate the back teeth at once. Canine guidance means only the canines touch going sideways; they have the longest roots and quiet the closing muscles. Group function shares the guidance among the canine and premolars on the working side. A back-tooth contact on the nonworking side is the worst interference. Full dentures use balanced occlusion instead.

Cusp height

A steep joint path and a deep overbite allow tall cusps. A big overjet, a sharp curve of Spee and more sideways shift of the jaw call for short cusps. The front teeth can be changed by the dentist; the joint cannot.
plain.da-tmj:
What's tested
  • The joint's parts
  • Which muscles move the jaw
  • How far the jaw opens, and how
  • Articulators and the facebow
  • Jaw pain, loose teeth and wear

The joint

The jaw joint both hinges and slides. A disc sits between the condyle and the skull. Its middle is thin and has no blood vessels or nerves. Behind it, the retrodiscal tissue has both, so that is where pain comes from; its upper layer is elastic and pulls the disc back. Hinging happens below the disc and sliding above it. The temporomandibular ligament's outer part stops the pure hinge at about 20–25 mm; its inner part keeps the condyle from being pushed back.

Muscles

The temporalis, masseter and medial pterygoid close. The lower lateral pterygoid and the muscles under the chin open and push the jaw forward. To move the jaw right, the right temporalis and masseter pull while the left lateral and medial pterygoids push.

Movement

The jaw hinges for the first 20–25 mm and then slides forward to open 40–60 mm. In a side movement, the condyle on the side you move toward spins; the other one swings forward, down and in. The whole jaw may also shift sideways (Bennett movement).

Articulators

An articulator holds models and copies jaw movement. A facebow places the upper model in relation to the hinge axis. Models mounted in centric relation can find the bite, but models mounted in the bite can't find centric relation.

Problems

Most jaw pain is in the muscles. Stress, injury, other pain, clenching and grinding, and bite problems all play a part. Grinding starts in the brain, not in the bite. Start with reversible care such as a flat splint. Heavy bite forces can loosen a tooth but do not cause gum disease. Wear comes from teeth rubbing, brushing with gritty toothpaste, acid, and perhaps flexing.
plain.f1-biomol:
What's tested
  • Bonds, water, pH and buffers
  • Amino acids and the four levels of protein structure
  • Collagen and vitamin C; hemoglobin's oxygen binding
  • Sugars, fats and DNA's building blocks

The short version

Covalent bonds share electrons and are the strongest. Ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are weaker and hold a protein's folded shape. Blood stays between pH 7.35 and 7.45, mostly thanks to the bicarbonate buffer.

Proteins are chains of amino acids. The order is the primary structure. Local coils and sheets held by hydrogen bonds are secondary structure. The whole folded shape is tertiary, with oily parts tucked inside. Several chains working together is quaternary, as in hemoglobin. Histidine is the amino acid whose side chain can pick up or drop a proton right around body pH.

Collagen is the body's most common protein, and type I (bone, dentin, skin) is most of it. Every third amino acid is glycine, the only one small enough for the center of the triple rope. Enzymes inside the cell add OH groups to proline and lysine, and those enzymes need vitamin C. No vitamin C means weak collagen: bleeding gums, loose teeth and wounds that won't heal (scurvy). Outside the cell the ends are trimmed and the fibers are cross-linked by a copper enzyme.

Hemoglobin has four chains. When one grabs oxygen, the others grab it more easily, so the binding curve is S-shaped. Acid, carbon dioxide, heat and 2,3-BPG make it let go of oxygen in working tissues. Fetal hemoglobin holds oxygen tighter so the baby can take it from the mother. Myoglobin, in muscle, is a single chain that just stores oxygen.

Sugars: glucose and galactose differ at one carbon (C-4). Sucrose is table sugar, glucose plus fructose, and it is what cavity bacteria use to make sticky plaque. Glycogen is the body's branched glucose store.

Fats: a triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids. Double bonds put kinks in fatty acids and keep fats liquid. Phospholipids make the cell membrane, and cholesterol keeps it from getting too stiff or too runny. Fatty acids are burned inside mitochondria.

DNA: purines (A, G) have two rings, pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one. A pairs with T using two hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C using three. The two strands run in opposite directions and wrap around histone spools.
plain.f1-cells:
What's tested
  • What each organelle does
  • How things cross the membrane
  • How a nerve fires and how drugs and toxins stop it
  • How synapses pass the signal on

The short version

Bacteria have no nucleus and no inner compartments; our cells do. The rough ER makes proteins that will be secreted or put in the membrane, the Golgi ships them, lysosomes digest things in acid (their enzymes carry a mannose-6-phosphate tag), and the proteasome chews up proteins marked with ubiquitin. Mitochondria make ATP and have their own DNA from the mother. Microtubules build the spindle and the inside of cilia; actin lets cells change shape; intermediate filaments are tough ropes. Caspases carry out tidy, planned cell death (apoptosis).

Things cross the membrane downhill on their own (diffusion), downhill through a carrier (facilitated diffusion), uphill using ATP directly (the Na+/K+ pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in), or uphill by riding along with Na+ as it flows in (secondary active transport). Water moves toward more dissolved particles: in a dilute (hypotonic) bath a cell swells, in a concentrated one it shrinks.

A resting nerve is about −70 mV inside, close to potassium's balance point, because potassium leaks out. When a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium channels fly open and sodium rushes in: the spike. Then sodium channels shut themselves off and potassium channels open to bring the voltage back down, and a little below. Right after a spike the nerve can't fire again at all, then only with a bigger push. Myelin makes the signal jump from gap to gap, much faster.

Local anesthetics slip into the nerve and plug sodium channels from the inside. In infected, acidic tissue less of the drug can get in, so numbing is harder. High blood potassium also stalls sodium channels.

At a chemical synapse, calcium entering the nerve ending releases the transmitter. Glutamate excites; GABA and glycine calm things down. At muscle, acetylcholine opens channels to start contraction. Botulinum toxin stops acetylcholine from being released, and in myasthenia gravis the body makes antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, so muscles tire quickly.
plain.f1-molbio:
What's tested
  • How DNA is copied, read into RNA and translated into protein
  • How genes are inherited and how to read a family tree
  • What kinds of mutations there are and which genes cause cancer

The short version

Copying DNA: helicase unzips it, primase lays a short RNA starter, DNA polymerase adds new letters, always building in the 5′ to 3′ direction. One strand is made in one long piece; the other in short Okazaki pieces that ligase glues together. Each new DNA keeps one old strand. Chromosome tips (telomeres) shrink each time, except where telomerase rebuilds them, as in stem cells and most cancers.

RNA has an extra OH on its sugar and uracil in place of thymine. Most of a cell's RNA is ribosomal. In bacteria, the σ part of RNA polymerase finds the start signal. The lac operon is switched on fully only when lactose is around and glucose is not.

In our cells, RNA polymerase II makes messenger RNA. The message gets a cap on the front, its introns cut out (they start with GU and end with AG) and a poly(A) tail on the back that isn't copied from DNA. Acetylated histones open DNA up for reading; methylated DNA is shut off.

Translation: each tRNA carries one amino acid and matches a three-letter codon. AUG starts, UAA, UAG and UGA stop. The ribosome's own RNA makes the peptide bonds. Bacteria line up the ribosome with a Shine-Dalgarno sequence; our ribosomes slide from the cap to the first AUG.

Inheritance: dominant traits show up in every generation; recessive ones skip generations and need two copies. X-linked recessive diseases such as hemophilia A hit boys through carrier mothers. If your brother has a recessive disease and you don't, your chance of being a carrier is 2 in 3.

Mutations: a single-letter change can be silent, swap an amino acid (sickle cell), or make an early stop. Adding or losing letters in numbers that aren't multiples of three scrambles everything after (frameshift). Growing repeats, as in Huntington disease, get worse each generation.

Cancer genes: oncogenes are stuck gas pedals (one bad copy is enough). Tumor suppressors such as p53 and RB are brakes, and both copies have to be lost. BRCA1 and BRCA2 repair broken DNA. HPV causes throat cancer by knocking out p53 and RB.
plain.f1-enzhorm:
What's tested
  • How peptide and steroid hormones reach and act on cells
  • Insulin, cortisol, aldosterone and the calcium hormones
  • Which reactions release energy and which need it
  • How enzymes speed reactions, and what Km, Vmax and the inhibitor types mean

The short version

Peptide hormones (like insulin) dissolve in blood, can't get through the membrane, and so bind receptors on the outside of the cell. The signal is passed on inside by messengers such as cAMP (which turns on protein kinase A) or IP3 and calcium. They can't be swallowed as pills because the gut digests them. Insulin's receptor is a tyrosine kinase, and its job is to move GLUT4 glucose doors to the surface of muscle and fat cells.

Steroid hormones are made from cholesterol (first step: pregnenolone), ride on carrier proteins in the blood, slip through the membrane and switch genes on or off inside the nucleus. Cortisol raises blood sugar and calms the immune system; too much is Cushing syndrome. Aldosterone holds on to salt and water; too much is Conn syndrome (high blood pressure, low potassium). In Addison disease the adrenal glands fail: low blood pressure, tiredness and dark patches in the mouth from high ACTH.

PTH raises blood calcium, active vitamin D helps the gut absorb it, and calcitonin lowers it by slowing osteoclasts.

Energy: breaking things down (catabolism) releases energy and uses NAD+; building things (anabolism) costs energy and uses NADPH. A reaction happens on its own when ΔG is negative, but that says nothing about how fast. Brain and red blood cells live on glucose.

Enzymes speed reactions by lowering the energy hill, not by changing where the reaction ends up. Km is the substrate level that gives half the top speed; a small Km means the enzyme grabs its substrate tightly. Vmax is the top speed. A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and fights for the active site: Km goes up, Vmax stays (more substrate wins). A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere: Vmax drops, Km stays. An uncompetitive one binds only the enzyme–substrate pair and lowers both.
plain.f2-genpath:
What's tested
  • Reversible versus irreversible cell injury, and the nuclear changes of cell death
  • The six necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each one belongs to (coagulative heart and kidney, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas)
  • Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (Fas) pathways, which both end in caspases
  • How cells are injured: ATP loss in hypoxia, free radicals and the enzymes that clear them, reperfusion injury
  • The four adaptations with an example of each, intracellular accumulations, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
  • Acute inflammation (vascular changes, exudate versus transudate, leukocyte recruitment) and chronic inflammation (M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas, repair and scar problems, acute-phase proteins)
  • Neoplasia: naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Injured cells first swell. If the cause stops, they recover (reversible). If the mitochondria, membranes, lysosomes or DNA fail, the cell dies. A dying nucleus shrinks (pyknosis), breaks up (karyorrhexis) or fades (karyolysis).

Necrosis is messy death with inflammation. Learn the pattern with its place: coagulative in heart or kidney infarcts (ghost cells), liquefactive in abscesses and the brain (pus), caseous in TB (cheesy granuloma), fat necrosis in pancreatitis (chalky calcium soaps), fibrinoid in damaged vessel walls. Apoptosis is tidy, programmed death with no inflammation. The intrinsic path releases cytochrome c from mitochondria; the extrinsic path uses Fas ligand on a T cell binding Fas. Both switch on caspases.

Free radicals hurt cells; superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase clear them. Bringing blood back to an ischemic organ can add injury (reperfusion).

Adaptations: bigger cells (hypertrophy), more cells (hyperplasia), smaller cells (atrophy), or a switch of cell type (metaplasia, like a smoker's bronchus turning squamous). Calcium in damaged tissue with normal blood calcium is dystrophic; calcium in normal tissue because blood calcium is high is metastatic.

Acute inflammation: histamine widens vessels, protein-rich exudate leaks out, and neutrophils roll (selectins), stick (integrins), squeeze through (PECAM-1) and follow chemokines. Chronic inflammation brings macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells. M1 macrophages kill; M2 macrophages (IL-4, IL-13) heal with IL-10 and TGF-β. Granulomas wall off things the body can't clear, like TB.

Healing: granulation tissue (new vessels and fibroblasts) fills the wound, then collagen gives strength. Neurons and heart muscle can't regrow, so they scar. A keloid grows past the wound edges; a hypertrophic scar stays inside them. Infection, steroids, poor nutrition (vitamin C) and diabetes slow healing.

Tumors: benign ones end in "-oma" (lipoma, adenoma). Malignant epithelial tumors are carcinomas, malignant connective-tissue tumors are sarcomas, and melanoma and lymphoma are malignant despite their names. Metastasis proves malignancy. Grade is how abnormal the cells look; stage (TNM) is how far it has spread, and stage matters more for prognosis.
plain.f2-virology:
What's tested
  • What makes a virus a virus; enveloped versus naked viruses (stability, release by budding or lysis)
  • The Baltimore classes, which viruses bring their own RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, and the six steps of the life cycle
  • The human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: their diseases and where each stays latent
  • HPV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and the poxviruses; the RNA viruses (picornaviruses, coronavirus, measles, RSV, rabies, influenza drift and shift)
  • HIV: structure, entry, life cycle, stages and CD4 counts, tests, drug targets and oral signs
  • Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology
  • The oncogenic viruses and how they drive cancer (E6 and p53, E7 and Rb)

Viruses are genes in a protein shell that can only copy themselves inside a cell. Some wear a fatty envelope; these break down when dry and spread by blood, sex or droplets. Naked viruses (hepatitis A, HPV, polio) are tough and spread by the fecal-oral route or surfaces.

DNA viruses copy themselves in the nucleus (poxviruses are the exception). Retroviruses (HIV) and hepatitis B use reverse transcriptase. Negative-sense RNA viruses (measles, rabies, influenza) must bring their own RNA polymerase.

Herpesviruses never leave. HSV-1 (cold sores, herpetic gingivostomatitis) hides in the trigeminal ganglion, HSV-2 in the sacral ganglia, VZV (chickenpox, then shingles) in sensory ganglia, EBV (mono, oral hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt lymphoma) in B cells, CMV in white cells, HHV-6 and 7 cause roseola, and HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma.

Other favorites: coxsackie A causes herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease; measles shows Koplik spots inside the cheek before the rash; rabies climbs nerves to the brain (Negri bodies); influenza changes a little every year (drift, all strains) and sometimes swaps whole segments (shift, influenza A only), which causes pandemics.

HIV binds CD4 and then CCR5 or CXCR4, turns its RNA into DNA and inserts it into our DNA. AIDS means a CD4 count under 200. Viral RNA testing is the most sensitive test. In the mouth look for candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia and Kaposi sarcoma.

Hepatitis: A and E are fecal-oral and don't become chronic (E is dangerous in pregnancy). B, C and D are bloodborne and can become chronic. C becomes chronic in most people but is now curable; B has a vaccine; D needs B to exist. For hepatitis B: surface antibody alone means vaccinated, surface antigen means infected, IgM core antibody means acute infection.

Cancer viruses: HPV 16 and 18 (cervical and oropharyngeal cancer; E6 removes p53, E7 blocks Rb), EBV (lymphomas, nasopharyngeal cancer), HBV and HCV (liver cancer), HTLV-1 (T-cell leukemia) and HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma).
plain.f2-bacteria:
What's tested
  • Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelopes and why they stain differently; acid-fast and wall-less exceptions
  • Structures outside the wall (capsule, pili, fimbriae, flagella, axial filaments), endospores, plasmids and 70S ribosomes as drug targets
  • Growth (binary fission, the growth curve), oxygen needs and the three ways to make ATP
  • Gene transfer: transformation, transduction and conjugation
  • Steps of pathogenesis, virulence factors, biofilms, and exotoxins versus endotoxin with the classic toxins
  • Staphylococcus (abscess, coagulase, MRSA, toxin syndromes) and Streptococcus (pyogenes, pneumoniae, mutans, viridans)
  • The gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, Vibrio, Salmonella, H. pylori), MacConkey agar, the red complex and the spirochetes

The gram stain sorts bacteria by their wall. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick wall that keeps the purple dye. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane; the alcohol washes the purple out and they stain pink. Only gram-negatives have endotoxin (lipid A in LPS). Mycobacteria have waxy walls (acid-fast), and Mycoplasma has no wall at all.

Penicillins block wall cross-linking; MRSA resists them with an altered binding protein (PBP2a, from mecA). Capsules stop phagocytosis, pili help bacteria stick and share DNA, flagella and axial filaments move them, and spores (only Bacillus and Clostridium) survive heat and disinfectants.

Bacteria split in two and grow fastest in the log phase. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen as the last electron acceptor, anaerobic respiration uses something like nitrate or sulfate, and fermentation makes only 2 ATP. Bacteria swap genes by taking up naked DNA (transformation), through viruses (transduction) or through a sex pilus (conjugation), which is how drug resistance spreads.

Toxins: exotoxins are proteins made by both groups, very potent, and can become vaccines (toxoids). Endotoxin is part of the gram-negative wall, heat-stable, and causes fever and septic shock. Cholera toxin causes watery diarrhea, Shiga toxin bloody diarrhea and kidney failure, tetanus toxin spastic paralysis and botulinum toxin floppy paralysis.

S. aureus (clusters, coagulase-positive) makes abscesses that need draining, food poisoning, scalded skin and toxic shock. S. epidermidis grows as biofilm on implants. S. pyogenes causes strep throat and flesh-eating infections. S. pneumoniae, protected by its capsule, is the top cause of community pneumonia. S. mutans makes acid and sticky glucans from sugar, causing caries.

Gram-negatives: Pseudomonas (hospital, burns, contact lenses, very drug-resistant), Klebsiella (capsule, pneumonia), EHEC, Vibrio, Salmonella and H. pylori. The red complex of periodontitis is P. gingivalis, T. forsythia and T. denticola.
plain.f2-fungi:
What's tested
  • The fungal cell (chitin wall, ergosterol membrane) and what antifungals target; yeast, mold and dimorphic forms
  • Endemic mycoses by region (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) versus opportunists (Candida, Aspergillus, Mucor, Cryptococcus); levels of mycoses
  • Tuberculosis: spread, the granuloma, IFN-γ and the macrophage, why treatment takes months; nontuberculous mycobacteria
  • Anaerobes: clinical clues, how to sample, the key organisms (Actinomyces, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Clostridium) and drugs
  • Mycoplasma (no wall), Rickettsia (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Chlamydia (elementary and reticulate bodies), Neisseria (gonorrhea versus meningococcus) and syphilis
  • The five tissue reactions to infection and the lab tests (stains, culture, serology, antigen, skin test, PCR)

Fungi have a chitin wall and ergosterol (not cholesterol) in their membrane, so antifungals target ergosterol. Yeasts are single budding cells; molds grow as hyphae. Dimorphic fungi are molds outside and yeasts in the body. Histoplasma (bird and bat droppings, river valleys) and Blastomyces live in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys; Coccidioides in the Southwest desert. Opportunists hit weak hosts: Candida (thrush that wipes off), Aspergillus and Mucor (invade vessels; Mucor in diabetic ketoacidosis can blacken the palate), Cryptococcus (meningitis in AIDS).

Tuberculosis spreads through the air. It hides in macrophages until T cells make IFN-γ, and the fight builds a cheesy (caseating) granuloma. Its waxy, acid-fast wall, its slow growth and its hiding place mean months of several drugs. Other mycobacteria come from the environment, not from people.

Anaerobes are normal mouth and gut flora. Think of them with foul pus, gas or an abscess near a mucosa. Collect pus with a needle, not a swab, drain it, and use metronidazole, clindamycin or penicillin. Actinomyces gives a jaw swelling with draining tracts and yellow "sulfur granules" after an extraction. Fusobacterium necrophorum gives Lemierre syndrome (a clot in the jugular vein after a sore throat). Tetanus toxin causes spasms and lockjaw; botulinum toxin causes floppy paralysis; C. perfringens causes gas gangrene; C. difficile causes colitis after antibiotics.

Mycoplasma has no wall, so penicillins don't work on its walking pneumonia. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (ticks) starts with a rash on the wrists and ankles; give doxycycline right away. Chlamydia lives inside cells (elementary body infects, reticulate body divides), is the most common bacterial STI and is found by NAAT. Gonorrhea has no capsule and keeps changing its pili, so there is no vaccine; meningococcus has a capsule, spreads by droplets and needs antibiotics at once. Syphilis starts as a painless chancre and is treated with penicillin.
plain.om-caries:
What's tested
  • The order of plaque formation: pellicle, reversible then irreversible attachment of pioneer streptococci, coaggregation (F. nucleatum as the bridge), maturation, dispersal
  • S. mutans virulence: adhesins to salivary Gp340, acid production and acid tolerance, glucosyltransferases (GTFs) that turn sucrose into sticky glucans, stored intracellular polysaccharide
  • Why sucrose is special, and soluble α1,6 versus insoluble α1,3 glucans
  • The Stephan curve, the critical pH of 5.5 and the ecological plaque hypothesis
  • Which organism goes with which lesion (S. mutans, Lactobacillus, Actinomyces, Candida) and fluoride's three actions

The big picture

Your mouth has about 700 kinds of microbes, and streptococci are the most common. Many can't be grown in a dish, so they are found by reading their 16S rRNA genes.

How plaque builds

First a thin film from saliva (the pellicle) coats a clean tooth. Friendly Gram-positive streptococci stick to it, loosely at first and then firmly. Other bacteria then stick to them; F. nucleatum is the bridge that lets the harmful Gram-negative anaerobes like P. gingivalis join later. The finished plaque is a biofilm, which shrugs off antimicrobials better than loose bacteria do.

Why S. mutans causes cavities

  • It sticks to the pellicle protein Gp340.
  • It makes lactic acid and survives in it.
  • It uses sucrose to build sticky, insoluble glucans with its GTF enzymes. Only sucrose has the high-energy bond it needs, so on glucose and fructose alone it can't stick.
  • It stores sugar inside the cell to keep making acid later.

Acid and the Stephan curve

After sugar, plaque pH falls below 5.5 within minutes and enamel starts to dissolve; saliva's bicarbonate brings it back up over about half an hour to an hour. Snacking often keeps the pH low, which favors acid-loving bacteria (the ecological plaque hypothesis).

Who goes with which cavity

  • S. mutans starts enamel caries.
  • Lactobacillus pushes deep, cavitated dentin caries.
  • Actinomyces goes with root caries.
  • S. mutans plus Candida drives early childhood caries.

Fluoride

Fluoride makes enamel tougher (fluorapatite), helps early lesions remineralize and blocks the bacterial enzyme enolase. It doesn't stop lactobacilli, so it helps most before a lesion cavitates.
plain.om-perendo:
What's tested
  • The red complex (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) and its link to deep pockets and bleeding; the orange complex (F. nucleatum) as the bridge that comes first
  • The plaque hypotheses: nonspecific, specific, ecological/keystone (P. gingivalis as the keystone pathogen)
  • P. gingivalis traits and virulence factors (gingipains); A. actinomycetemcomitans and its leukotoxin in molar-incisor (localized aggressive) periodontitis
  • Host response and bone loss: antigen presentation, cytokines, RANKL and osteoclasts; the three routes to systemic disease
  • Pulp infection: routes, dentinal tubule size, the shift to obligate anaerobes, E. faecalis in persistent infection, and which treatment fits which stage

Gum disease bugs

Periodontitis is long-running inflammation under the gumline that eats away the bone holding the teeth. The red complex (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) shows up in deep, bleeding pockets. The orange complex, with F. nucleatum, moves in first and acts as the bridge.

Today's view is the keystone idea: P. gingivalis is rare, but it confuses the immune system so the whole community grows out of control. It can't do it alone; it needs the other bacteria.

  • P. gingivalis: Gram-negative anaerobic rod, black colonies, needs iron, eats proteins instead of sugar, makes gingipain enzymes.
  • A. actinomycetemcomitans: the bug of aggressive disease in teens around first molars and incisors; its leukotoxin kills white cells.

Why bone is lost

Immune cells present the bacteria to T cells, which pour out inflammatory signals. These raise RANKL, which switches on osteoclasts; OPG is the brake. The inflammation and bacteria can also travel through the blood, the lungs and the gut, which ties gum disease to other illnesses.

Infected pulp

Bacteria mostly reach the pulp through the dentinal tubules, which are widest next to the pulp. Early on, bacteria that can live with or without oxygen win; once the pulp dies, strict anaerobes take over. E. faecalis is the tough survivor in root canals that fail.

Treatment by stage

  • Pulp barely reached: pulp cap.
  • Only the top of the pulp: pulpotomy.
  • Into the canals: root canal (pulpectomy).
  • Young tooth with an open apex: apexogenesis if the pulp is alive, apexification or regenerative endodontics if it's dead.
  • Spreading past the apex: antibiotics and extraction or drainage.

A pulp polyp is a red, bleeding, painless mass of pulp growing out of a big cavity in a young patient.
plain.om-viral:
What's tested
  • Culture media (blood agar, Rogosa SL, mitis-salivarius, Gold's agar) and Gram/colony features of common oral organisms
  • The herpesviruses: latency sites, oral signs and cancers (HSV-1, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6/7, HHV-8)
  • HPV: papillomas, Heck disease, HPV-16/18 in oropharyngeal cancer, E6 and E7
  • RNA viruses with oral signs: coxsackievirus (hand, foot and mouth; herpangina), mumps, measles (Koplik spots), rubella
  • Cancer basics (oncogenes, tumor suppressors, two-hit) and bacteria tied to cancer (F. nucleatum, P. gingivalis, H. pylori)

Growing oral bacteria

Blood agar grows almost everything. Rogosa agar picks out lactobacilli, mitis-salivarius agar picks out streptococci, and Gold's agar (with extra sucrose and bacitracin) picks out S. mutans. S. mutans colonies look rough and frosted with a shiny glucan drop on top; S. salivarius looks like a big gumdrop.

Herpes family

  • HSV-1 hides in the trigeminal ganglion. First infection in a child: sore, swollen gums with blisters. Later: cold sores. On a finger: herpetic whitlow.
  • VZV causes chickenpox, then later shingles: a painful one-sided band of blisters that stops at the midline.
  • EBV causes mono and is tied to Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer.
  • CMV passed to a fetus can leave thin enamel.
  • HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma: purple patches on the palate in people with weak immunity.

HPV

HPV makes small warty growths (papillomas) and Heck disease. Types 16 and 18 cause throat (oropharyngeal) cancer by switching off p53 (E6) and Rb (E7). Vaccines cover them.

RNA viruses

Coxsackie causes hand, foot and mouth disease and herpangina; mumps swells the parotids; measles gives Koplik spots inside the cheek; rubella in pregnancy can leave the baby with enamel defects or missing teeth.

Infection and cancer

Oncogenes are a stuck gas pedal (one bad copy is enough); tumor suppressors are lost brakes (usually both copies). Tobacco, alcohol and HPV are the big risks for mouth and throat cancer. F. nucleatum and P. gingivalis are found in tumors, and the mouth can reinfect the stomach with H. pylori.
plain.ns-anat:
What's tested
  • What each glial cell does
  • The three brain bleeds and the cavernous sinus
  • Ventricles, lobes and the main cortical areas
  • Neural tube, neural crest and their birth defects
  • Spinal cord layout, blood supply, cord syndromes and reflexes
  • Brainstem "rule of 4" and the cranial nerve lesion signs

Cells. Neurons carry signals. Astrocytes are the helpers: they clean up potassium and glutamate and help build the blood-brain barrier. Oligodendrocytes wrap CNS axons in myelin (MS attacks them); Schwann cells do it in the PNS (Guillain-Barré attacks them). Microglia are the brain's immune cells.

Bleeds. Epidural = artery (middle meningeal), lens shape, often after a blow to the temple with a lucid interval. Subdural = veins (bridging veins), crescent shape, often older people. Subarachnoid = aneurysm, sudden "worst headache". In the cavernous sinus, the carotid artery and CN VI run through the middle, and III, IV, V1 and V2 run in the wall.

Brain layout. CSF goes lateral ventricles → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle → out. The central sulcus splits the motor strip (in front) from the sensory strip (behind). Broca (front, left) makes speech; Wernicke (temporal, left) understands it.

Development. The neural tube becomes the brain and cord; the neural crest becomes the peripheral nerves, ganglia, adrenal medulla and much of the face and teeth. If the top of the tube does not close: anencephaly. If the bottom does not close: spina bifida. Folic acid prevents both.

Spinal cord. It ends at about L1–L2, so needles go in lower. Front of the cord (anterior spinal artery) carries movement and pain; the back (posterior spinal arteries) carries fine touch and position sense. Cut half the cord and you lose movement and fine touch on the same side but pain and temperature on the other side. The knee-jerk is a one-synapse reflex.

Brainstem. Nerves I–IV sit above the pons, V–VIII in the pons, IX–XII in the medulla. Medial structures are motor; lateral ones are sensory and sympathetic. A PICA stroke (lateral medulla) numbs pain and temperature on the same side of the face and the opposite side of the body, with hoarseness and Horner syndrome.

Cranial nerve signs. The tongue (XII) and the jaw (V3) point toward the bad side; the uvula (X) points away. CN III palsy: eye down and out with a droopy lid and big pupil. Bell palsy (VII) droops the whole half of the face.
plain.ns-path:
What's tested
  • Fine touch versus pain pathways and where each crosses
  • The trigeminal pathway for the face and teeth
  • Upper versus lower motor neuron signs, and three nerve-muscle diseases
  • Cerebellum and basal ganglia problems
  • Which artery causes which stroke

Two sensory routes. Fine touch, vibration and position sense go up the back of the cord on the same side and cross in the medulla. Pain and temperature cross right away in the cord and go up the other side. So a half-cord injury loses fine touch on the same side and pain on the opposite side.

The face. Face and tooth sensation travels on CN V. Touch goes to the main sensory nucleus in the pons; pain and temperature go down to the spinal trigeminal nucleus; jaw-muscle and PDL position sense uses the mesencephalic nucleus, whose cell bodies are oddly inside the brain. All of it relays in the VPM of the thalamus.

Movement. Upper motor neurons run from the cortex and cross in the medulla. Damage gives stiff (spastic) weakness, brisk reflexes and an up-going big toe. Lower motor neurons run from the cord to the muscle; damage gives floppy weakness, lost reflexes, wasting and twitching. Guillain-Barré is weakness that climbs from the feet after an infection. Myasthenia gravis is weakness that gets worse with use (blocked ACh receptors). Lambert-Eaton gets better with use and goes with lung cancer.

Cerebellum. Problems show on the same side: clumsy reaching, shaking near the target, wobbly walking. Basal ganglia. Dopamine helps movement. Parkinson disease loses dopamine: slow, stiff, shaky at rest. Huntington disease is an inherited repeat that causes dance-like movements, mood change and dementia.

Strokes. ACA: opposite leg. MCA: opposite face and arm, plus language trouble on the left side or neglect on the right side. PCA: half the visual field. Small deep (lacunar) strokes give pure weakness or pure numbness. Clot-busting drugs work only in the first hours.
plain.ns-phys:
What's tested
  • Why the inside of a neuron is negative at rest
  • What each channel does during an action potential, and why myelin speeds things up
  • How a synapse releases transmitter, and the main receptor types
  • How local anesthetics work and what changes their onset, strength and duration
  • How general anesthetics and sedation levels work

Resting voltage. At rest, potassium leaks out of the cell much more easily than anything else, so the inside sits near potassium's own voltage, about −70 mV. Add potassium outside the cell and the cell becomes less negative.

The spike. Sodium channels open and sodium rushes in (the upswing). Then sodium channels shut themselves off and potassium channels open, bringing the voltage back down. While sodium channels are shut off, the cell cannot fire again. Myelin lets the signal jump from node to node, so thick, myelinated fibers are fastest.

Synapses. The spike opens calcium channels; calcium makes vesicles fuse and dump transmitter. Fast receptors are channels; slow receptors use G proteins. The NMDA receptor opens only with both glutamate and a depolarized cell. Botulinum toxin stops ACh release.

Local anesthetics plug sodium channels from the inside. The uncharged form gets into the nerve; the charged form does the blocking. A pKa near body pH means fast onset; infected (acidic) tissue slows or stops it. More fat-soluble = stronger; more protein-bound = longer. Esters break down in the blood and make PABA (allergy); amides break down in the liver. Too much drug in the blood affects the brain first (tingling lips, ringing ears, seizures) and then the heart. Treat with oxygen, seizure control and lipid emulsion. A lidocaine cartridge holds 36 mg.

General anesthesia means asleep, no memory, no pain and no movement. Most drugs boost GABA (inhibition); ketamine blocks NMDA. MAC tells you potency: lower MAC, stronger gas. Moderate sedation: the patient still answers when you talk to them.
plain.ns-sens:
What's tested
  • How we hear, taste, smell and balance
  • Eye muscles, eye-nerve palsies and visual field cuts
  • Sympathetic versus parasympathetic
  • How pain travels and how drugs treat it
  • Face and head pain, and facial fracture basics

Hearing. The middle-ear bones boost sound. In the cochlea, bending hair cells lets potassium in, which fires CN VIII. The base of the cochlea hears high notes, the tip low notes. The route is ECOLIMA: eighth nerve, cochlear nucleus, olive, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate, auditory cortex.

Taste and smell. Front of tongue: taste by VII, feeling by V3. Back of tongue: both by IX. Taste relays through the VPM of the thalamus. Smell is the only sense that skips the thalamus and goes straight to the piriform cortex and memory areas.

Balance and eyes. Canals sense turning; utricle and saccule sense straight-line movement and tilt. LR is CN VI, SO is CN IV, the rest are CN III. A pituitary tumor presses the chiasm and takes away both outer visual fields. A temporal lobe lesion takes the upper corner ("pie in the sky").

Autonomic. Sympathetic nerves start at T1–L2 and mostly use norepinephrine. Parasympathetic nerves start in the brainstem and sacral cord and use ACh. Parasympathetic stimulation makes lots of watery saliva.

Pain. Fast sharp pain rides Aδ fibers; slow aching pain rides C fibers. Rubbing the area helps by "closing the gate". The brain can turn pain down from the PAG. Injury makes nerves more sensitive (hyperalgesia) and can make touch hurt (allodynia). Tissue pain responds to NSAIDs and opioids; nerve pain responds better to gabapentin, tricyclics and carbamazepine.

Face pain. Trigeminal neuralgia is seconds of electric pain from a light touch; carbamazepine treats it. Pain in the lower face is most often dental. Jaw pain on chewing in an older person can be giant cell arteritis, an emergency for vision. Facial fractures. A fracture into the superior orbital fissure freezes the eye and numbs the forehead; add blindness and it is orbital apex syndrome.
plain.ns-dis:
What's tested
  • MS: who, which kinds, how it is found and treated
  • Seizure types, emergencies and drug side effects in the mouth
  • Alzheimer and Parkinson disease, their drugs and dental care
  • Sleep apnea, narcolepsy and the body clock
  • How addictive drugs work; schizophrenia and its drugs
  • How memories are made

MS strips myelin in the brain and spinal cord, usually in young women. It comes and goes in attacks at different times and places. MRI shows plaques; spinal fluid shows oligoclonal bands. Steroids shorten attacks. Trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult should make you think of MS.

Seizures look the same every time. Absence seizures are brief stares in children. Lip smacking and chewing suggest a temporal lobe seizure. Five minutes or more is an emergency: call for help and give a benzodiazepine such as midazolam. Phenytoin overgrows the gums; carbamazepine treats trigeminal neuralgia but can lower white cells; valproate can cause bleeding.

Alzheimer disease starts with forgetting new things. Amyloid plaques sit outside cells and tau tangles inside. Drugs (donepezil, memantine) help for a while but do not cure. Parkinson drugs replace or protect dopamine (levodopa with carbidopa). Patients get dizzy standing up, so sit them up slowly.

Sleep. Deep sleep comes early in the night, REM later. Sleep apnea: snoring, pauses in breathing and daytime sleepiness, mostly with obesity. CPAP is first line; a dental appliance that moves the jaw forward helps milder cases or people who cannot use CPAP. Narcolepsy: falling asleep in the day and going limp when laughing (cataplexy). The body clock (SCN) is set by morning light.

Addiction. Every addictive drug raises dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake; no epinephrine within 24 hours of cocaine. Schizophrenia needs 6 months of illness; drugs block D2 receptors. Older drugs cause movement side effects, including lip and tongue movements (tardive dyskinesia); clozapine can wipe out white cells.

Memory. The hippocampus files new facts; the cerebellum and striatum hold skills. Learning strengthens synapses through NMDA receptors, calcium and extra AMPA receptors (LTP).
plain.rn-filtration:
What's tested
  • What the kidneys do and where they sit
  • The parts of a nephron and the filter that keeps protein in the blood
  • How the bladder fills and empties
  • How much blood the kidneys get, how much they filter, and what speeds or slows filtering
  • Clearance and the markers inulin, creatinine and PAH
  • Where the body's water is, and what happens when you lose or gain fluid

The kidneys clean the blood, keep water, salt, potassium and acid in balance, set blood pressure, and make three hormones: erythropoietin (for red cells), active vitamin D, and renin.

Where they are

They sit behind the peritoneum at about T12 to L3. The right one is lower because the liver sits above it. Blood goes in through the afferent arteriole to the glomerulus and leaves through the efferent arteriole. Urine runs from the papilla to the calyces, the pelvis, the ureter and the bladder.

The filter

The glomerulus filters plasma through three layers: leaky endothelium, a negatively charged basement membrane, and podocyte feet. Big, negative proteins like albumin stay in the blood. Near the glomerulus, the macula densa tastes the salt in the tubule and the JG cells release renin.

The bladder

Sympathetic nerves hold urine in (detrusor relaxed, internal sphincter closed). Parasympathetic nerves from S2–S4 empty it (detrusor contracts). The pudendal nerve keeps the external sphincter shut until you choose to go.

Filtering

The kidneys get about a fifth of the cardiac output and filter about 125 mL a minute, 180 L a day. About 20% of the plasma that arrives is filtered. Squeezing the efferent arteriole (angiotensin II) keeps filtering going when pressure is low; squeezing the afferent arteriole lowers it. Between about 80 and 200 mmHg the kidney keeps its flow steady by itself; one way is the macula densa sending adenosine to tighten the afferent arteriole.

Clearance

Clearance = urine concentration × urine flow ÷ plasma concentration. Inulin's clearance equals GFR. Creatinine is the everyday marker: when GFR halves, blood creatinine doubles. PAH measures renal plasma flow. A substance cleared faster than inulin is secreted; slower, it's reabsorbed.

Body water

Water is 60% of body weight: 40% inside cells and 20% outside. Of the outside water, a quarter is plasma. Sodium rules outside the cells and potassium inside. Normal saline stays outside the cells and fills the blood vessels; D5W ends up as plain water that goes everywhere.
plain.rn-tubule:
What's tested
  • How salt, water, glucose and bicarbonate get back into the blood
  • What each part of the tubule does
  • How the kidney makes concentrated urine
  • What aldosterone and ADH do
  • Where each diuretic works

Every tubule cell has a lumen side (apical) and a blood side (basolateral). A sodium pump on the blood side keeps sodium low inside the cell, so sodium rushes in from the lumen and carries other things with it.

Proximal tubule: the bulk reabsorber

It takes back about two-thirds of the salt and water and almost all the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. Water simply follows the salt. Glucose rides in with sodium on SGLT2. Those carriers can fill up: when blood sugar goes above about 180–200 mg/dL, the extra glucose spills into the urine. The "-flozin" drugs block SGLT2 on purpose. Acetazolamide works here too, and makes you lose bicarbonate.

Loop of Henle: building the salty medulla

Going down, the tube lets water out but not salt, so the fluid gets more concentrated. Going up, it lets salt out but not water. The thick part pumps salt out with the NKCC2 carrier and makes the fluid dilute. Furosemide blocks NKCC2. The loop and the slow blood flow of the vasa recta keep the deep medulla very salty (up to about 1,200), and urea adds to it.

Distal tubule

It takes back a little more salt through NCC, the carrier thiazides block. Thiazides also make the kidney keep calcium.

Collecting duct: the fine tuning

Principal cells take in sodium through ENaC and put potassium out into the urine. Aldosterone turns this up. ADH puts water channels (aquaporin-2) into these cells so water can leave the urine and the urine gets concentrated. Intercalated cells handle acid: the alpha type pumps out acid, the beta type pumps out bicarbonate.

Amiloride blocks ENaC and spironolactone blocks aldosterone. Both keep potassium in the body, so they can raise it too high.
plain.rn-balance:
What's tested
  • How ADH and thirst keep the blood's water right, and what goes wrong (SIADH, diabetes insipidus)
  • How the body senses and fixes its volume with salt
  • Potassium: what pushes it into and out of cells, and how the kidney gets rid of it
  • Calcium, phosphate and magnesium, and the hormones PTH, vitamin D and FGF23
  • Acids and bases: the four disorders and how the body makes up for each

Water

Blood sodium tells you about water. Low sodium (under 135) means too much water; high (over 145) means too little. ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Sensors in the brain (the OVLT) notice the blood getting salty and release ADH first, then make you thirsty. ADH puts water channels in the collecting duct. A big drop in blood volume also releases ADH, and volume wins over salt. Alcohol turns ADH off.

Too much ADH (SIADH, often from lung cancer) gives low sodium; restrict fluids. No ADH (central diabetes insipidus) gives lots of dilute urine; give desmopressin. Kidneys that ignore ADH (nephrogenic, usually from lithium) don't respond to desmopressin; thiazides help.

Salt and volume

Total sodium sets how full the blood vessels are. When volume is low: sympathetic nerves fire, renin rises, angiotensin II and aldosterone rise, and the kidney keeps salt and water. When the atria are stretched, they release ANP, which makes the kidney dump salt.

Potassium

Almost all potassium is inside cells; normal blood level is 3.5–5.0. Insulin, epinephrine (β2) and alkalosis push it into cells; acidosis, β-blockers, low insulin and broken cells let it out. The collecting duct decides how much leaves in urine: aldosterone and diuretics make you lose more; spironolactone, kidney failure and acidosis make you keep more.

Calcium, phosphate, magnesium

Most calcium is taken back early in the tubule; the distal tubule does the fine tuning under PTH. Loop diuretics make you lose calcium and magnesium; thiazides make you keep calcium. Magnesium is mostly taken back in the thick ascending limb. PTH raises blood calcium and makes the kidney dump phosphate. Active vitamin D, made in the kidney, mainly pulls calcium in from the gut. FGF23 from bone makes the kidney dump phosphate.

Acid and base

The lungs control CO2; the kidneys control bicarbonate. The kidney takes back filtered bicarbonate and makes new bicarbonate each time it gets rid of acid as ammonium or on phosphate. Metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate, as in diabetic ketoacidosis) → fast breathing. Metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) → slow breathing. Respiratory acidosis (too little breathing) or alkalosis (too much, as in an anxious patient) → the kidneys adjust over days.
plain.rn-disease:
What's tested
  • What chronic kidney disease is, its causes and its five stages
  • Azotemia versus uremia
  • What failing kidneys do to the blood, bones, mouth and bleeding
  • Nephritic versus nephrotic kidney disease and their classic examples
  • Infections, stones, cysts and tumors of the kidney

CKD

Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys have been damaged or underperforming for at least 3 months. Diabetes is the top cause, then high blood pressure. Doctors stage it by eGFR: stage 1 is 90 or more (with other signs of damage), 2 is 60–89, 3 is 30–59, 4 is 15–29, and 5 is under 15, which means dialysis or a transplant. A urine albumin test can show damage early. The kidneys keep up until about half the nephrons are gone.

Azotemia and uremia

Azotemia is a lab result: high BUN and creatinine. Uremia is the sick patient: tired, nauseated, itchy, bleeding easily, with bad breath. It comes from wastes building up, some hormones running high, and the kidney's own hormones (erythropoietin, vitamin D) going missing.

What CKD does

Anemia (no erythropoietin), high blood pressure, high potassium, acid buildup and heart disease. Phosphate builds up and active vitamin D falls, so calcium drops and the parathyroids work overtime; the bones, jaws included, lose mineral (renal osteodystrophy). Platelets work poorly, so patients bleed more. In the mouth: dry mouth, odd taste, ammonia breath, pale gums, bruises and gum disease.

Glomerular disease

Nephritic means an inflamed filter: blood in the urine, high blood pressure, little urine. Examples: post-strep glomerulonephritis in kids a few weeks after strep, IgA nephropathy (the most common worldwide, blood in the urine right after a cold), and rapidly progressive disease with crescents. Nephrotic means a leaky filter: lots of protein in the urine, low albumin, swelling and high cholesterol. Minimal change disease is the common one in children; membranous in adults.

Other problems

Kidney infections (pyelonephritis) are usually E. coli, with fever and flank pain. Most stones are calcium. A blocked ureter swells the kidney (hydronephrosis). Adult polycystic kidney disease is dominant and comes with brain aneurysms. Clear cell carcinoma is the common adult kidney cancer; Wilms tumor is the childhood one.
plain.rn-dental:
What's tested
  • The diuretic families, where they act and their side effects
  • How to treat a patient on dialysis safely
  • Which drugs to avoid, adjust or use freely when the kidneys are failing
  • What kidney failure looks like in the mouth and on X-rays, and the transplant patient

Diuretics

Loop diuretics like furosemide block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. They are the strongest, used for fluid overload and pulmonary edema. They make you lose potassium, magnesium and calcium and can damage hearing. Thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide block NCC in the distal tubule. They are used for high blood pressure; they lose potassium but keep calcium, and raise sugar, lipids and uric acid. Spironolactone and amiloride spare potassium, so they can push it too high; spironolactone can cause breast growth in men. Acetazolamide causes acidosis; mannitol pulls water into the urine.

Patients on diuretics get dizzy when they stand up fast and often have a dry mouth. NSAIDs weaken diuretics and blood pressure drugs, and diuretics and NSAIDs both raise lithium levels.

The dialysis patient

Talk to the kidney doctor first. Hemodialysis is done about three times a week through a fistula in the arm, using heparin. Book dental work for the day after dialysis, when the heparin has worn off and the patient feels best. Never put a blood pressure cuff or needle on the fistula arm. These patients bleed more because their platelets don't work well, so plan good local hemostasis. They have more hepatitis B and C.

Drugs

Drugs the kidney clears build up, so use smaller doses or space them out. Avoid NSAIDs, tetracycline and meperidine. Space out amoxicillin, penicillin and cephalexin. Lidocaine, clindamycin, doxycycline and acetaminophen are generally fine. Give dialyzable drugs after the session.

In the mouth

Ammonia breath, dry mouth, odd taste, pale gums, bruises and sometimes white sores (uremic stomatitis). On X-rays the jaw can lose its lamina dura, look like ground glass and show brown tumors, all from overactive parathyroids. After a transplant, patients are immunosuppressed; cyclosporine grows the gums, and erythromycin or clarithromycin can raise its blood level.
plain.he-axes:
What's tested
  • How hormones signal and how the pituitary is controlled
  • Growth hormone and acromegaly
  • Pituitary tumors, diabetes insipidus and SIADH
  • The adrenal gland: Cushing, Addison, Conn
  • Steroid drugs and the adrenal crisis

The big picture

The hypothalamus tells the pituitary what to do, and the pituitary tells the other glands. When a gland makes enough hormone, that hormone turns the hypothalamus and pituitary down (negative feedback). So if the gland itself is broken, its hormone is low and the pituitary hormone is high (they move opposite ways). If the pituitary is broken, both are low.

The front (anterior) pituitary makes GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH. The back (posterior) pituitary only stores ADH and oxytocin, which nerve cells in the hypothalamus make. Dopamine keeps prolactin down.

Growth hormone

GH comes out in bursts, mostly in deep sleep. It works through IGF-1 from the liver to make bones grow. It also raises blood sugar and breaks down fat. Too much in a child makes a giant; too much in an adult is acromegaly: a jaw that keeps growing into an underbite, spaces between the teeth, a big tongue. The test that proves it: GH does not drop after drinking glucose.

Pituitary problems

A big pituitary tumor squeezes the crossing optic nerves, so people lose the outer half of vision in both eyes. The most common hormone-making tumor makes prolactin (no periods, milky discharge). No ADH, or kidneys that ignore it, means lots of watery urine and high blood sodium (diabetes insipidus). Too much ADH holds water and drops sodium (SIADH), often from small cell lung cancer.

The adrenal gland

The outer layers make salt (aldosterone), sugar (cortisol) and sex (androgen) hormones; the center makes epinephrine. Too much cortisol (Cushing, most often from steroid pills): round face, hump, high sugar, thin skin, slow healing. Too little (Addison): tired, low blood pressure, and dark patches in the mouth, because ACTH is high. Too much aldosterone (Conn): high blood pressure and low potassium.

Steroid drugs

Prednisone and similar drugs calm inflammation but shut down the body's own cortisol. That is why you taper them, and why a patient on them can crash under stress. Side effects: thrush, slow healing, weak bones, high sugar, hidden infections. If a steroid patient becomes pale, confused and very hypotensive in the chair, call 911 and give 100 mg hydrocortisone.
plain.he-thyroid:
What's tested
  • How the thyroid makes its hormone and which lab moves which way
  • Too much vs too little thyroid hormone, and the drugs for each
  • Thyroid cancers
  • PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin, and what goes wrong

The thyroid
