The thyroid grabs iodine, sticks it onto a protein in its colloid, and stores the hormone there. It mostly releases T4, which the body turns into the active T3. TSH from the pituitary pushes the thyroid; thyroid hormone pushes TSH back down. So a sick thyroid shows TSH and T4 moving opposite ways.

Too much (Graves disease, an antibody that acts like TSH): thin, hot, shaky, fast heart, bulging eyes; TSH low, T4 high. Children's teeth come in early. Don't load an uncontrolled patient with epinephrine, and know thyroid storm: high fever, very fast pulse, confusion. Call 911.

Too little (Hashimoto, the immune system destroying the gland): tired, cold, slow heart, weight gain; TSH high, T4 low. A big tongue, late teeth, slow healing. Babies born without enough hormone develop cretinism.

The drugs

Levothyroxine (T4) is the replacement: on an empty stomach, morning, away from calcium and iron; it takes weeks to settle, and if TSH stays high the dose goes up. For an overactive gland, methimazole, except early in pregnancy, when propylthiouracil is used. Watch for fever, sore throat and mouth ulcers on these drugs: white cells may have crashed. Radioactive iodine destroys the gland (never in pregnancy). Beta-blockers calm the shaking. Amiodarone is full of iodine and can push the thyroid either way.

Cancer

Papillary is the most common and the gentlest, spreading to neck nodes. Follicular invades vessels and spreads by blood. Medullary comes from C cells, makes calcitonin and runs in MEN 2 families. Anaplastic is fast and deadly.

Calcium

PTH raises calcium: it frees it from bone, keeps it in the kidney, throws out phosphate, and activates vitamin D so the gut absorbs more. Calcitonin lowers calcium, a little. Too much PTH, usually one benign tumor: high calcium, kidney stones, and on dental X-rays the lamina dura disappears and "brown tumors" appear. Too little PTH, often after thyroid surgery: low calcium, twitching and cramps. Kidney failure lowers active vitamin D, so PTH climbs.
plain.he-diabetes:
What's tested
  • What the islet cells make and how insulin gets released
  • Type 1 vs type 2 and the numbers that diagnose them
  • What each diabetes drug does and which ones cause lows
  • Diabetes in the mouth and a low blood sugar in the chair

Insulin and glucagon

Beta cells make insulin, which moves sugar into muscle and fat and stores it. Alpha cells make glucagon, which makes the liver release sugar. Somatostatin from delta cells slows both. When blood sugar rises, it enters the beta cell, makes more ATP, closes a potassium channel, and the cell releases insulin. Sulfonylurea pills close that same channel. C-peptide is made along with your own insulin, so a low C-peptide means your pancreas isn't making much.

The two types

Type 1: the immune system destroys the beta cells, usually in a young, thin person, who needs insulin to live and can go into ketoacidosis. Type 2: the body stops responding well to insulin, usually in an older, heavier person; it starts with lifestyle and metformin. Diabetes is diagnosed by an HbA1c of 6.5% or more, or a fasting sugar of 126 or more. HbA1c shows the average of the last 2–3 months: under 7 is good control; above 7 is poor, with more infections, gum disease and failed implants.

The drugs

Metformin is first: it stops the liver making sugar, doesn't cause lows, but upsets the stomach and is stopped in severe kidney disease. Insulin, sulfonylureas and meglitinides can cause lows and weight gain. GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide) cause weight loss. DPP-4 drugs (gliptins) are mild pills. SGLT2 drugs (gliflozins) dump sugar in the urine, which brings yeast and urinary infections. Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and can worsen heart failure.

In the chair

Diabetes worsens gum disease, and gum disease worsens diabetes. Expect dry mouth, thrush and slow healing. Book mornings and make sure the patient ate. A low blood sugar looks like sweating, shaking, a fast heart and confusion. If awake, give sugar by mouth (juice, glucose gel); if unconscious, give glucagon and call 911.
plain.he-repro:
What's tested
  • Which testicular and ovarian cells answer to FSH and LH
  • The phases of the cycle and what triggers ovulation
  • The hormones of pregnancy and nursing
  • The sex hormone drugs and their big side effects
  • The main tumors and infections of the reproductive tract

Testes and ovaries

In the testis, FSH works on Sertoli cells, which feed developing sperm and make inhibin; LH works on Leydig cells, which make testosterone. The ovary copies this: LH tells theca cells to make androgen, and FSH tells granulosa cells to turn it into estrogen. Someone injecting testosterone shuts off his own LH and FSH, so his testes shrink and his sperm count drops.

The cycle

In the first half, estrogen grows the uterine lining. When estrogen stays high long enough, it flips to triggering a burst of LH, and ovulation follows. In the second half the corpus luteum makes progesterone to ready the lining. No pregnancy: progesterone falls and the lining sheds. After menopause there are no follicles, so estrogen is low and FSH and LH are high.

Pregnancy and nursing

The early embryo makes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over. That's what a pregnancy test detects. The placenta also makes hPL, which fights insulin (gestational diabetes). Oxytocin drives labor. After birth, prolactin makes milk and oxytocin squeezes it out.

The drugs

Birth control pills stop the LH surge. Estrogen drugs, tamoxifen and raloxifene raise the risk of blood clots. Tamoxifen blocks estrogen in the breast but acts like it in the uterus. Aromatase inhibitors stop estrogen being made. Leuprolide, given nonstop, shuts the pituitary down, which lowers testosterone in prostate cancer. Finasteride blocks DHT for an enlarged prostate. Testosterone can harm the liver.

Disease

An undescended testis needs surgery early, but its cancer risk stays. Testicular cancer hits young men and is very curable; seminoma is the most common. BPH grows around the urethra and blocks urine; prostate cancer grows at the edge and spreads to bone. HPV 16 and 18 cause cervical cancer at the transformation zone; 6 and 11 cause warts. In the mouth, pregnancy brings swollen gums and pyogenic granulomas.
plain.he-heme:
What's tested
  • The blood cells and what each does
  • How the immune system is organized and where its cells mature
  • Anemias and what they do to the tongue
  • The four leukemias and the main lymphomas
  • What a dentist should notice and do

Blood cells

Red cells carry oxygen; platelets start clots; white cells fight infection. Of the white cells, neutrophils are the most common and go after bacteria first; lymphocytes are B, T and NK cells; monocytes become macrophages; eosinophils fight parasites and allergy; basophils carry histamine.

Immune organs

B cells mature in the bone marrow and T cells in the thymus: those two are the primary organs. Lymph nodes, the spleen and the tonsils are secondary organs, where the cells meet germs. In the spleen, T cells wrap around the small arteries (the PALS). NK cells kill cells that hide their MHC I "ID badge."

Anemias

Low iron (small red cells) and low B12 or folate (big red cells) both make the tongue smooth, red and sore, with cracked mouth corners. B12 lack also causes numbness. Sickle cell disease makes red cells sickle and block vessels; keep visits short and the patient warm, hydrated and oxygenated.

Leukemias

Acute leukemias are full of immature blasts and move fast; chronic ones have more mature cells and move slowly. AML is the adult acute one (Auer rods); ALL is the child's. CML has the Philadelphia chromosome and is treated with imatinib. CLL is the old person's slow leukemia with smudge cells. Leukemia crowds out normal marrow: anemia, bleeding gums and infections, and the gums can swell with leukemic cells.

Lymphomas

Hodgkin lymphoma has Reed-Sternberg cells, starts in central nodes and spreads in order; it is very curable. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are mostly B-cell, scattered, and often outside nodes. Burkitt grows very fast and can start in a child's jaw. MALT lymphoma grows from long-standing inflammation, such as Sjögren in the salivary glands. Myeloma punches holes in bone, jaws included.

For the dentist

Swollen, bleeding gums, tiny red spots and pale tissue need a blood count and a referral. Check counts before surgery on a patient with leukemia.
plain.mg-giphys:
What's tested
  • The GI hormones: who makes them, what releases them, what they do
  • How saliva and stomach acid are made and controlled
  • How the gut moves, and how the pancreas and bile digest food
  • Where each nutrient is absorbed, and the two kinds of diarrhea

The messengers

Gastrin (stomach G cells) turns acid up; protein and stretch release it, and acid shuts it off through somatostatin. CCK (I cells) answers fat and protein: it squeezes the gallbladder, calls for pancreatic enzymes and slows the stomach. Secretin (S cells) answers acid in the duodenum by calling for bicarbonate. GIP and GLP-1 tell the pancreas to release insulin. Motilin starts the "housekeeper" waves between meals. Ghrelin makes you hungry. Histamine and somatostatin act on neighbors; VIP and NO relax muscle.

Saliva and acid

The parotid is the biggest gland, but the submandibular makes most resting saliva. Saliva starts out like plasma; the ducts pull out salt but not water, so it ends up watery (hypotonic). Both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves turn it on. In the stomach, parietal cells pump acid with the H+/K+ pump and make intrinsic factor for B12. ACh, gastrin and histamine turn the pump on; histamine boosts the other two. The vagus runs the "thinking about food" phase.

Movement

Pacemaker cells (Cajal) set slow waves; muscle contracts when spikes ride on them. Segmentation mixes, peristalsis pushes. Fat empties from the stomach slowest. Between meals the migrating waves clear out bacteria. Eating triggers colonic mass movements (gastrocolic reflex). If the LES can't relax, that's achalasia.

Digestion

Enteropeptidase switches on trypsin, and trypsin switches on the other proteases. Only single sugars are absorbed. Fat travels in micelles made with bile salts and leaves the gut cell as chylomicrons into lymph. Bile salts are recycled from the terminal ileum, which is also where B12 is absorbed; iron and calcium go in at the duodenum.

Diarrhea

Secretory diarrhea (cholera) keeps going even when fasting: the toxin opens chloride channels. Osmotic diarrhea (lactose intolerance) stops when you stop eating the cause. Sugar-and-salt drinks work because the sodium-glucose carrier still works.
plain.mg-gianat:
What's tested
  • Which artery feeds each part of the gut, and where gut pain is felt
  • Portal hypertension's shortcut veins, the pectinate line, the abdominal wall and hernias
  • How to tell each part of the gut apart under the microscope, plus the mouth, salivary glands and liver

Blood supply and pain

Celiac trunk: stomach to the middle of the duodenum (pain in the upper belly). SMA: the rest of the small bowel to two-thirds of the way across the transverse colon (pain at the navel). IMA: the rest of the colon down to the pectinate line (pain low in the belly). Organ pain is vague until the inflamed organ touches the body-wall lining, which is why appendicitis moves from the navel to the right lower belly. A bleeding ulcer on the back of the duodenum hits the gastroduodenal artery.

Portal hypertension and the wall

When the liver is scarred, portal blood detours: esophageal varices (left gastric to azygos), caput medusae (around the navel) and rectal varices. Above the pectinate line the anal canal is painless and drains to the liver; below it, it hurts and drains to the body's veins. Hernia rule: "MDs don't LIe": medial to the inferior epigastric vessels is direct, lateral is indirect (through the deep ring, the common kind). Below the arcuate line, only transversalis fascia lies behind the rectus. The umbilicus is T10. Diaphragm holes: IVC T8, esophagus T10, aorta T12.

Under the microscope

Esophagus: flat, non-keratinized lining; skeletal muscle on top, smooth at the bottom. Stomach: pits and glands, no villi; parietal cells make acid, chief cells make pepsinogen. Duodenum: Brunner glands. Jejunum: tallest folds. Ileum: Peyer patches. Colon: no villi, lots of goblet cells. Filiform papillae have no taste buds. Parotid is all serous, sublingual mostly mucous.

Liver

Zone 1 sits by the incoming blood and gets the most oxygen; zone 3, by the central vein, gets the least and is damaged first by low blood flow and acetaminophen. Kupffer cells are the liver's macrophages; Ito cells store vitamin A and make scar. The gallbladder wall has no submucosa.
plain.mg-gipath:
What's tested
  • Reflux, ulcers and H. pylori; celiac, Crohn and ulcerative colitis; colon cancer and C. diff
  • Hepatitis, cirrhosis, iron and copper overload, acetaminophen, gallstones
  • Treating a patient with liver disease safely; the main GI drugs

Gut diseases

Reflux can erode the palate side of the upper teeth and, over years, turn the lower esophagus into Barrett lining, which can become adenocarcinoma. H. pylori survives acid by making ammonia with urease and causes most ulcers; NSAIDs cause the rest by removing protective prostaglandins. Celiac disease flattens the villi; it can cause mouth ulcers and enamel defects. Crohn disease can hit anywhere from mouth to anus, goes through the whole wall and skips around; ulcerative colitis starts in the rectum, stays in the lining and is continuous. C. diff colitis follows antibiotics such as clindamycin; it is treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Jaw osteomas plus extra teeth can mean Gardner syndrome, which leads to colon cancer.

Liver

Hepatitis A and E come from food and water and clear up; B and C come from blood and can last for years, leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer. B has a vaccine; C doesn't but can be cured. Hemochromatosis piles up iron; Wilson disease piles up copper. Acetaminophen overdose kills the cells around the central vein; N-acetylcysteine is the antidote. A scarred liver makes fewer clotting factors and the big spleen traps platelets.

In the dental chair

Before surgery on a patient with cirrhosis, check the INR and platelets. Use acetaminophen at a lower dose and skip NSAIDs. Keep local anesthetic doses modest.

Drugs

PPIs shut off the acid pump for good (take them before breakfast); H2 blockers are weaker. Antacids work fastest but bind tetracyclines. Misoprostol protects against NSAID ulcers but can't be used in pregnancy. Ondansetron blocks serotonin to stop nausea; metoclopramide blocks dopamine and speeds the stomach but can cause movement problems. Loperamide slows the gut without reaching the brain. Methotrexate for Crohn disease can cause mouth sores.
plain.mg-bone:
What's tested
  • The three cartilages and the three bone cells
  • How osteoclasts are switched on (RANKL) and off (OPG), and how PTH and vitamin D control calcium
  • The bone diseases and their mouth findings, and the bone drugs with their jaw risk (MRONJ)

Cartilage and bone

Cartilage has no blood supply, so it heals poorly. Hyaline cartilage covers joints, elastic cartilage shapes the ear, and fibrocartilage (discs, menisci, the TMJ disc) has no outer layer. Cartilage uses type II collagen; bone uses type I. Osteoblasts build bone, osteocytes sense load, and osteoclasts dissolve bone with acid. Osteoblasts make RANKL to switch osteoclasts on and OPG to block it. PTH works on osteoblasts, not directly on osteoclasts.

Growth and calcium

Skull bones, the upper jaw and most of the lower jaw form straight from tissue (intramembranous); long bones form from a cartilage model (endochondral). Low calcium releases PTH, which pulls calcium from bone, keeps it in the kidney and activates vitamin D in the kidney. Too little calcium causes tingling and cramps; too much causes stones, bone pain, belly pain and confusion.

Diseases

Brittle bone disease (OI) is a type I collagen problem: fractures, blue whites of the eyes, weak see-through teeth. Achondroplasia (FGFR3) gives short limbs. In osteopetrosis, osteoclasts can't dissolve bone, so it is dense but breaks, and a jaw infection after extraction is a real risk. Missing collarbones and many extra unerupted teeth suggest cleidocranial dysplasia. Paget disease remodels bone chaotically: a growing jaw, spaced teeth, loose dentures and "cotton wool" X-rays. Osteoporosis is too little normal bone; osteomalacia is soft, poorly mineralized bone from low vitamin D.

Drugs and the jaw

Bisphosphonates stick to bone and kill the osteoclasts that eat them. Denosumab blocks RANKL; its effect fades fast if stopped. Teriparatide builds bone and isn't linked to jaw necrosis. Jaw necrosis (MRONJ) is most likely with high-dose IV drugs for cancer plus an extraction, so do the dental work before the drug starts.
plain.et-ada:
What's tested
  • The five principles in Code order, their one-word meanings and the duty each states: patient autonomy (1), nonmaleficence (2), beneficence (3), justice (4), veracity (5)
  • Naming the principle and Code section a scenario turns on, and the ethical answer
  • How the Code is built: principles (aspirational), the Code of Professional Conduct (binding on members) and advisory opinions (interpretations); ethics versus law
  • The classic cases: records and transfer, impaired colleagues, abandonment, postexposure duties, abuse reporting, patient selection and HIV, emergency care, justifiable criticism, split fees, amalgam removal, insurance and fees, advertising and specialty claims

Three parts

The ADA Code has principles (the ideals), a Code of Professional Conduct (the rules ADA members must follow, or face discipline) and advisory opinions (how the rules apply to real situations). Ethics often asks more of you than the law does.

The five principles, in order

  • 1. Patient autonomy (self-governance): involve patients in decisions and keep their information private. Send records to a new dentist when asked, even if the patient still owes you money.
  • 2. Nonmaleficence (do no harm): stay current, refer when needed, don't work impaired, and don't abandon a patient in the middle of treatment. Help an impaired colleague get treatment and report them to the dental society's assistance committee. After a needlestick, tell the patient and send them for care.
  • 3. Beneficence (do good): serve the community, regulate your own profession, and report suspected abuse as the law requires.
  • 4. Justice (fairness): don't turn patients away because of race, gender, disability or HIV status; arrange emergency care even for people who aren't your patients; don't badmouth other dentists' work (but report gross or repeated bad work); never split fees.
  • 5. Veracity (truthfulness): no removing healthy amalgams to "detox," no misleading ads, no fudging insurance claims or dates, no unnecessary treatment, and say when you profit from a product you recommend.

How to answer a scenario

Find the duty at stake, name the principle, then pick the answer that protects the patient while staying honest and fair. Answers that hold records for payment, refuse patients with HIV, disparage colleagues or bend a claim are always wrong.
plain.et-pro:
What's tested
  • Informed consent: what must be disclosed, the reasonable-patient standard (Canterbury v. Spence), decision-making capacity, informed refusal and implied consent
  • Who consents for a minor or for an adult who lacks capacity
  • Confidentiality and HIPAA: what's protected, when you may share without authorization, the patient's rights, and the duty to warn (Tarasoff)
  • Records and the medical history: what to record and how to correct an entry
  • The duty to report suspected child abuse and neglect and its signs; disclosing errors; whistle-blowing
  • Infection control and bloodborne pathogens as professional duties: standard precautions, OSHA's rules, transmission risks and what to do after an exposure
  • Ethical reasoning: valid and sound arguments, the common fallacies and the main moral theories

Consent

Before treatment, tell the patient what's wrong, what you plan, its risks and benefits, the other options (including doing nothing) and the cost, so they can choose. The signature only records that the talk happened. Since Canterbury v. Spence, you disclose what a reasonable patient would want to know. A patient can say no (document it), but can't make you give care below the standard. Capacity means they understand, see that it applies to them, can weigh the options and can state a choice.

Children

A parent or legal guardian consents for a child; a grandparent or babysitter can't unless they have legal authority. Ask the child to agree too.

Privacy

HIPAA protects any health information that identifies a patient, spoken, written or electronic. You may share it for treatment, payment and running the practice, and when the law requires (such as abuse reports); for most other uses you need written permission. Patients can get copies of their records. If a patient seriously threatens a specific person, the duty to protect that person (Tarasoff) outweighs confidentiality.

Records

Never change or backdate a record; cross out an error with one line, date and initial it. Check the medical history every visit.

Reporting

If you suspect child abuse (bruises of different ages, a torn lip frenum, a story that changes), you must report it; you don't need proof, and an honest report is legally protected. Tell patients about your mistakes.

Infection control

Treat every patient with standard precautions. After a needlestick, wash, report right away and start HIV medicine within hours if needed. Hepatitis B is the most contagious by needlestick (about 30%), then hepatitis C (about 2%), then HIV (about 0.3%); only hepatitis B has a vaccine, which employers must offer free.

Reasoning

A valid argument's conclusion must follow if its premises are true; a sound one is valid with true premises. Watch for slippery slopes, straw men and attacks on the person. Utilitarians judge by results; Kantians by duty and respect for persons.
plain.eb-ask:
What's tested
  • The 5 A's in order (ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess) and what each step does
  • Building a PICO(T) question and picking P, I, C, O and T out of a case; background versus foreground questions; the four kinds of clinical question and the design that best answers each
  • Where to search: TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library
  • Naming the design from a short description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good and bad at
  • The evidence pyramid, and literature review versus systematic review versus meta-analysis versus clinical practice guideline (GRADE, AGREE)
  • Efficacy versus effectiveness, the study-context continuum, practice-based research networks and the three gaps between evidence and practice

The big picture

Evidence-based dentistry means deciding with three things together: good research, your own clinical skill, and what the patient wants. The 5 A's are the steps: ask a clear question, acquire (find) the evidence, appraise (judge) it, apply it with your patient, then assess how it went.

Asking a good question

PICO(T) keeps a question focused: who the patient is (P), what you're thinking of doing (I), what you're comparing it with (C), the result you care about (O), and over how long (T). Only "which is better?" questions (foreground questions) fit PICO; simple fact questions such as "what causes dry socket?" (background questions) don't need it.

Finding the evidence

Start with TRIP, then PubMed's Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library of systematic reviews.

Telling the designs apart

  • Case report or series: describes patients, with no comparison group.
  • Ecological: compares whole groups, such as cities.
  • Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time; gives prevalence.
  • Case-control: starts with people who have the disease and looks back; good for rare diseases; gives an odds ratio.
  • Cohort: starts with an exposure and follows people forward; gives incidence and relative risk; good for rare exposures.
  • Randomized controlled trial: people are randomly put into groups; the best single study for "does this treatment work?"

The pyramid

Lab and animal studies sit at the bottom (very controlled but far from real patients), then case reports and expert opinion, then the observational designs, then RCTs, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with clinical practice guidelines on top. A systematic review searches for every study in a planned, repeatable way; a meta-analysis also pools their numbers; a plain literature review has no method and reflects the author's picks.

Ideal versus real world

Efficacy is whether a treatment works in a perfect study setting; effectiveness is whether it works in ordinary offices with ordinary patients. Evidence also has to reach practice: if it doesn't exist yet, that's a knowledge gap; if dentists haven't heard of it, a knowing gap; if they know but don't use it, a knowing-to-doing gap.
plain.eb-appraise:
What's tested
  • Internal versus external validity, and the three threats to validity: bias, confounding and chance
  • The kinds of bias and what randomization, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis do about them; what to check in an RCT
  • Standardization versus calibration, inter- versus intra-examiner reliability, precision versus accuracy, incidence versus prevalence
  • Types of data, mean versus median, and standard deviation
  • Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a 2×2 table, and which one a screening or a confirming test needs
  • Relative risk, odds ratio, absolute risk and the number needed to treat; reading a ratio with its 95% confidence interval
  • p-values, type I and II errors, power, and statistical versus clinical significance

Can you trust the study?

Internal validity means the study was done right; external validity means its results apply to your patients. Three things spoil a result: bias (a built-in tilt, such as people misremembering the past), confounding (a hidden third factor, such as brushing habits in a soda study) and chance (the luck of who was sampled).

A good trial

People are put into groups at random, nobody knows who got the real treatment (blinding), and everyone is counted in the group they were assigned to, even if they quit (intention to treat).

Measuring

Standardization means everyone uses the same tools and rules; calibration means examiners practice on the same patients until their scores agree. Precision is getting the same answer each time; accuracy is getting the right answer. Incidence counts new cases over time; prevalence counts everyone who has it now. For skewed numbers, the median is a better middle than the mean.

Tests

Sensitivity is how well a test catches people who have the disease: good for screening, and a negative result rules the disease out. Specificity is how well it clears people who don't: wanted before something you can't undo, and a positive result rules the disease in. How much a positive or negative result means (PPV, NPV) depends on how common the disease is.

Risk numbers

A relative risk or odds ratio of 1 means no difference, above 1 more risk, below 1 less risk. Case-control studies give odds ratios; cohorts and trials give relative risks. The NNT is how many people you treat for one to benefit (1 ÷ the absolute risk reduction): smaller is better.

Significance

p below 0.05 is "significant"; a ratio's confidence interval that includes 1 is not. A type I error is a false alarm; a type II error misses a real effect; power, the chance of finding a real effect, grows with bigger samples. A significant result can still be too small to matter to patients.

hy.hn-neck:
What's tested
  • Spinal nerve parts, white vs gray rami, and the sympathetic and parasympathetic layout (thoracolumbar vs craniosacral, the four head ganglia)
  • Horner syndrome: the four signs and why each happens
  • Boundaries and contents of the posterior and anterior triangles; CN XI in the posterior triangle; the cervical plexus at the nerve point
  • Suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles and their nerves; ECA branches; carotid sheath, sinus and body
  • Root of the neck: subclavian parts and branches, phrenic and vagus, thoracic duct; thyroid and parathyroid relations and the nerves at risk in thyroid surgery
  • Deep cervical fascia, the retropharyngeal and danger spaces, and how infection reaches the mediastinum

1 Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and flushing from a cervical sympathetic lesion

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • To the head: presynaptic fibers from T1–T2 ascend the trunk and synapse in the superior cervical ganglion; postsynaptic fibers ride the internal and external carotid arteries (periarterial plexuses) to the dilator pupillae, superior tarsal muscle, sweat glands and vessels.

Horner syndrome (cervical sympathetic chain cut or compressed, classically by an apical lung, or Pancoast, tumor): ptosis (superior tarsal muscle, so the droop is partial), miosis (unopposed sphincter pupillae, so the pupil is small), anhidrosis and flushing (warm, red skin) on the same side.

2 Nerves at risk in thyroid surgery and the carotid sheath and its neighbors

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

External carotid branches (SALFOPSM): superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, and the two terminal branches, superficial temporal and maxillary. The internal carotid has no branches in the neck. The carotid sinus (dilation of the proximal ICA) holds baroreceptors; the carotid body (at the bifurcation) holds chemoreceptors; both report through the carotid sinus branch of IX, so pressure on the sinus can slow the heart. The carotid sheath holds the common/internal carotid (medial), IJV (lateral) and vagus (posterior, between them), with the deep cervical nodes along the IJV; the sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, in the prevertebral fascia. The IJV begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. Key nodes: jugulodigastric (tonsil, back of the tongue) and jugulo-omohyoid (tongue).

  • Thyroid: isthmus over tracheal rings 2–4, inside the pretracheal fascia (so it moves with swallowing). Superior thyroid artery (ECA) runs with the external laryngeal nerve (injury: can't raise pitch, weak monotone voice); inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk) is close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (injury: hoarseness). A thyroid ima artery is present in about 10%. Superior and middle thyroid veins go to the IJV, the inferior to the brachiocephalic veins. The four parathyroids sit on the back of the lobes; removing them causes hypocalcemia and tetany.

3 Root of the neck: subclavian branches, phrenic nerve, thoracic duct and the superior thoracic aperture

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

The superior thoracic aperture (T1, first ribs, manubrium) passes the trachea, esophagus, great vessels, vagus and phrenic nerves, thoracic duct and the lung's cupula (a stab wound here can cause a pneumothorax). The brachial plexus and subclavian vessels go over the first rib to the axilla instead.

  • Thoracic duct: from the cisterna chyli to the left venous angle; drains everything except the right upper quadrant, which the right lymphatic duct drains. Injury leaks chyle (chylothorax).

4 Posterior triangle: CN XI and the cervical plexus at the nerve point

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • CN XI crosses it superficially on the levator scapulae, so a lymph node biopsy here can cut it: the shoulder droops and the patient can't shrug (trapezius). The SCM is often spared because its branch leaves earlier.
  • Cervical plexus (C1–C4 ventral rami) cutaneous branches emerge at the nerve point (Erb's point) at the middle of the SCM's posterior border, the site of a cervical plexus block: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–C3; skin over the parotid and the angle of the mandible, which is not trigeminal), transverse cervical (C2–C3; front of the neck), supraclavicular (C3–C4).

hy.hn-skull:
What's tested
  • Bones of the neurocranium and viscerocranium; sutures, bregma, lambda and the pterion over the middle meningeal artery
  • Fontanelles and skull fractures (basilar fractures leak CSF)
  • Contents of the three cranial fossae and the foramina with what passes through each

  • The cavernous sinus, beside the sella, drains backward through the superior petrosal (to the transverse/sigmoid) and inferior petrosal (to the IJV) sinuses. It receives the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins and connects to the pterygoid plexus by emissary veins through the foramen ovale.

1 Parotid: what runs through it, the duct opposite the maxillary second molar, IX–otic–auriculotemporal secretion, Frey syndrome

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Secretomotor path: inferior salivatory nucleus → IX → tympanic nerve and plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → synapse in the otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve (V3) → gland. VII passes through but gives it no secretory fibers. Frey syndrome: after parotid surgery, cut parasympathetic fibers regrow into the sweat glands of the overlying skin (great auricular and auriculotemporal territory), so eating causes sweating and flushing of the cheek. A parotid tumor with facial weakness suggests malignancy.

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Bell palsy (lower motor neuron): the whole half of the face, forehead included; the eye won't close (dry eye, corneal risk), the mouth droops and drools. An inferior alveolar injection placed too far back, into the parotid, can numb VII for a few hours with the same picture.

3 Orbit: blow-out fracture, extraocular muscle actions and nerves, accommodation and glaucoma

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Blow-out fracture: a blow to the eye raises orbital pressure and breaks the thinnest walls, most often the floor (into the maxillary sinus), then the medial wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid). Signs: the inferior rectus is trapped (can't look up, double vision), numbness of the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip (infraorbital nerve), sunken eye.

4 Sensory supply of the face, scalp layers and lacrimal secretion

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

S-C-A-L-P: skin; dense connective tissue with vessels held open when cut (scalp wounds bleed freely); epicranial aponeurosis (frontalis and occipitalis); loose connective tissue, the "danger zone" where blood and pus spread and emissary veins lead into the skull; pericranium. Fluid in the loose layer can't spread back or to the sides but can run forward into the eyelids (black eyes). Supply: in front of the ears V, behind them C2–C3 (greater and lesser occipital); arteries from the ECA (superficial temporal, occipital, posterior auricular) and ICA (supraorbital, supratrochlear).

1 Muscles of mastication: actions, the lateral pterygoid as the opener, jaw deviation toward a V3 lesion

Study guide + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

The digastric, geniohyoid and mylohyoid help open the jaw. A V3 motor lesion wastes the masseter and temporalis on that side, and on opening the jaw deviates toward the lesion, pushed by the working lateral pterygoid of the other side.

  • The disc splits the joint into a superior compartment (gliding: disc and condyle slide forward onto the eminence) and an inferior compartment (hinge: condyle rotates under the disc). Small opening is rotation; wide opening adds translation, pulled by the lateral pterygoid. Behind the disc is the vascular, innervated retrodiscal tissue.

3 Pharynx: all X except the stylopharyngeus, gag reflex, piriform recess and tonsillar bed

Study guide + review guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Constrictors (superior, middle, inferior) insert into the posterior midline raphe; all X through the pharyngeal plexus, which lies mainly on the middle constrictor (IX sensory, X motor, sympathetic vasomotor). The superior constrictor attaches to the pterygomandibular raphe, shared with the buccinator, the landmark for an inferior alveolar block. The cricopharyngeus (lowest inferior constrictor) is the upper esophageal sphincter; a Zenker diverticulum bulges just above it.
  • Sensation: nasopharynx V2, oropharynx IX, laryngopharynx X. Gag reflex: IX in, X out. Swallowing: oral stage voluntary; pharyngeal and esophageal stages reflex.

4 Clefts, tongue development and neck cysts

Study guide + review guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Groove 1 becomes the external acoustic meatus; membrane 1 the tympanic membrane. Grooves 2–4 are buried by arch 2 as the cervical sinus; if it persists, a lateral cervical (branchial) cyst or fistula appears along the anterior border of the SCM, often in a young adult.

The front two-thirds of the tongue come from arch 1 (two lateral lingual swellings over the tuberculum impar), so general sensation is V3 (lingual nerve); taste there runs in the chorda tympani (VII). The back third comes from the hypopharyngeal eminence of arches 3 and 4: IX, with X at the base. Tongue muscles come from occipital myotomes and bring XII with them (the palatoglossus, a palate muscle, is X). The thyroid grows down from the foramen cecum along the thyroglossal duct, in front of the hyoid. A thyroglossal duct cyst is in or near the midline and rises with swallowing and tongue protrusion; a leftover piece can form a pyramidal lobe or a lingual thyroid.

Study guide + slides · 2 questions in the bank

  • Canine guidance: in a lateral excursion only the canines touch. Canines have the longest roots and the best crown-to-root ratio, sit in dense bone, and when only they touch, fewer elevator muscles fire.
  • Group function: several working-side teeth share the guidance, ideally the canine, the premolars and sometimes the MB cusp of the first molar, with nothing touching on the nonworking side.

Study guide + recording · 1 question in the bank

  • Centric relation (CR): the condyles in their most anterosuperior position against the posterior slopes of the articular eminences, on the thinnest avascular part of the discs. It is set by the joints and muscles, not the teeth, it is reproducible, and it is the musculoskeletally stable position (older definitions said "most retruded").
  • About 90% of people have a slide from CR contact into MIP (about 1–1¼ mm); only about 10% close straight into MIP.

Mandibular movement is set by a posterior determinant (the TMJ: condylar guidance, fixed; the dentist cannot change it) and an anterior determinant (anterior guidance, variable). The nearer a tooth is to one of them, the more that one shapes its cusps.

Slides + recording · 1 question in the bank

  • A protrusive record sets the condylar inclination; lateral records set the Bennett angle. A cast mounted in CR can be closed into MIP, but a cast mounted in MIP can never find CR.

5 TMD etiology and conservative care; occlusal trauma, mobility and wear

Slides + recording · 1 question in the bank

  • Occlusion matters in two ways: an acute change (a high crown) triggers protective co-contraction and muscle pain; orthopedic instability (the joints and the teeth not stable at the same time, with a CR-to-MIP discrepancy greater than about 3–4 mm) loads the joint. Bruxism is centrally mediated; occlusion does not start it.
  • Primary occlusal trauma: excessive force on a normal periodontium. Secondary: normal or excessive force on a reduced periodontium. Signs: increasing mobility, a widened PDL space, fremitus. Trauma does not start gingivitis or periodontitis or cause attachment loss, and it is reversible; adjust the occlusion after the infection is treated.

1 Phases of the nerve action potential, refractory periods, and how hyperkalemia, tetrodotoxin and local anesthetics change it

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Hyperkalemia depolarizes the resting membrane, which inactivates Na+ channels and lowers excitability (dangerous for the heart). Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from outside, so threshold is never reached. Local anesthetics cross the axon membrane in their uncharged form, then the charged form blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from the cytoplasmic side. In inflamed, acidic tissue more of the drug is charged outside the nerve and less gets in, so the block is weaker.

3 Nernst equilibrium potentials (a tenfold gradient gives about 60 mV) and the resting potential

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

Bulk solutions are electrically neutral; only a thin layer of charge at the membrane is separated (the membrane acts as a capacitor, ion channels as resistors). The equilibrium potential of an ion is the voltage that balances its concentration gradient: E = (61.5/z) log([out]/[in]) at body temperature, so a tenfold gradient gives about 60 mV (the class used ±60 mV). E(K+) is about −90 mV and E(Na+) about +60 mV. At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+ through leak channels, so the resting potential (about −70 mV) sits close to E(K+). The Na+/K+ pump keeps the gradients; its own electrogenic current adds only a few millivolts.

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Oncogenes: a mutated proto-oncogene (normally pro-growth) becomes overactive ("stepping on the gas"); one mutated copy is enough. Activated by amplification (HER2/ErbB2 in breast cancer), a point mutation that leaves the protein always on (RAS), translocation making a fusion protein (BCR-ABL, chronic myeloid leukemia), or insertion next to a strong promoter.
  • Tumor suppressors ("removing the brakes"): both copies must be lost, Knudson's two-hit hypothesis. RB (retinoblastoma), p53 (stops the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; abnormal in over half of cancers), APC (colon).
  • An inherited first hit is in every cell, so cancer comes earlier and more often. High-risk HPV (types 16 and 18) causes oropharyngeal and cervical cancer: its E6 protein degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB.

3 Replication enzymes, leading and lagging strands, and telomerase

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Replication is semiconservative (each daughter has one old and one new strand) and happens in S phase. It starts at origins (one in bacteria, many in eukaryotes) and runs both ways from each. Polymerases add only to a free 3′-OH, so new DNA grows 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made away from it in short Okazaki fragments, each also built 5′ → 3′.

4 Transcription: σ and promoters, the lac operon, the three eukaryotic polymerases and epigenetic switches

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

The lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA share one promoter and operator. Negative control: the lacI repressor binds the operator; allolactose (from lactose) pulls it off. Positive control: when glucose is low, cAMP rises and the CAP–cAMP complex binds upstream, bends the DNA and recruits polymerase. Transcription is highest with lactose present and glucose absent; glucose and lactose together give only low expression (catabolite repression).

2 Km, Vmax, kcat and catalytic efficiency, and how enzymes lower activation energy

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Michaelis-Menten: v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Km is the [S] that gives half of Vmax; a low Km means tight binding (high affinity). At low [S] the rate is first order in substrate; at saturating [S] it is zero order and approaches Vmax, which rises with the amount of enzyme. kcat (turnover number) = Vmax / [enzyme]: substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second at saturation. kcat/Km is catalytic efficiency at low [S]; its ceiling is the diffusion limit (about 10^8–10^9 per molar per second). The ES complex reaches a steady state.

  • Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A. PKA is two regulatory and two catalytic subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits (four sites in all) and frees the active catalytic ones. Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down (caffeine blocks it). Study guide · 1 question in the bank

Made in the adrenal cortex (glomerulosa: aldosterone; fasciculata: cortisol; reticularis: androgens) and the gonads. The first and rate-limiting step, in mitochondria, cleaves cholesterol's side chain to make pregnenolone. Most steps use cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases, which need O2 and NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway). Carriers: transcortin (corticosteroid-binding globulin) holds about 75% of cortisol and albumin most of the rest; SHBG binds testosterone and estradiol and sets how much is free.

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Gram stain: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol (decolorizer) → safranin. The alcohol step decides it: a thick peptidoglycan wall holds the violet (gram-positive, purple); a thin wall under an outer membrane lets it wash out, and the counterstain makes it pink (gram-negative). Shape and arrangement (cocci in clusters or chains, rods, spirals) complete the first identification.

1 Tuberculosis: airborne spread, the caseating granuloma and why treatment takes months

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Pathogenesis: alveolar macrophages eat the bacilli, which block phagolysosome maturation and grow inside; they later escape by killing the cell (necroptosis). CD4 Th1 cells make IFN-γ (driven by IL-12), which activates macrophages to acidify and make ROS and NO. The result is the caseating granuloma. Defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ loop, HIV, malnutrition, age and immunosuppression allow disease or reactivation of latent infection.
  • Why treatment takes months, with several drugs at once: bacilli hide in granulomas; the waxy envelope is very poorly permeable (intrinsic resistance); slow, drug-tolerant persisters; and single drugs select resistance (streptomycin alone failed within a year). Penicillins don't work. A vaccine (BCG) exists.

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Mycoplasma: smallest free-living bacteria, no cell wall (sterols stiffen the membrane), so β-lactams and vancomycin are useless; use macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones. M. pneumoniae: "walking," atypical pneumonia in children and young adults (peak 5-15 years), droplets, slow onset, dry cough, patchy infiltrates; P1 adhesin binds sialic acid; CARDS toxin strips cilia; can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Bell palsy and cold-agglutinin hemolysis. PCR is the most sensitive test; culture takes weeks. M. genitalium: sexually transmitted urethritis, often silent.
  • Rickettsia: tiny obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria that stain poorly; infect endothelial cells, escape the phagosome and spread on actin tails, causing vasculitis, leaky vessels and possibly DIC. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii, dog and wood ticks): fever, headache, myalgia, then a petechial rash starting at the wrists and ankles that spreads inward and reaches the palms and soles; about 23% fatal untreated. Treat with doxycycline at once; confirmation (rising titers in convalescent serum) comes too late to wait for. Murine typhus (R. typhi, rat fleas) is milder and spares palms and soles.

3 Fluoride's three actions and why it spares lactobacilli

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Fluoride works three ways: forms fluorapatite, which resists acid (critical pH about 4.5); promotes remineralization of incipient lesions; and inhibits the bacterial glycolytic enzyme enolase, so less acid and less energy.
  • Fluoride does not inhibit lactobacilli, so its antibacterial effect matters mostly in early, noncavitated lesions dominated by S. mutans.

4 Plaque formation sequence and which organism goes with which lesion

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

StageWhat happens
1. Acquired pellicleWithin minutes a film of salivary glycoproteins, mucins, immunoglobulins and enzymes (under 1 µm thick) coats a clean tooth. Gp340 is the key receptor.
2. Reversible attachmentPioneer bacteria carried by saliva are held by weak, long-range forces (van der Waals).
3. Irreversible adhesionAdhesins on the pioneers bind pellicle receptors. The pioneers are commensal Gram-positive streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. oralis, S. mitis) and Actinomyces.
4. CoaggregationSecondary colonizers bind bacteria already attached, often through lectin-like adhesins. F. nucleatum is the bridge between early colonizers and the Gram-negative late colonizers.
5. MaturationThe matrix thickens, oxygen falls and Gram-negative anaerobes such as P. gingivalis (tertiary colonizers) settle in.
6. DispersalCells detach, often by degrading their own adhesins, and seed new sites.

2 Ester versus amide metabolism and allergy; prilocaine and articaine

Every local anesthetic has a lipophilic aromatic ring, an intermediate chain (ester or amide link) and a hydrophilic amine. Naming trick: amides have an "i" before "-caine" (lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine, bupivacaine); esters do not (procaine, benzocaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine, cocaine).

True amide allergy is very rare; reactions are usually to the preservative methylparaben or to sodium bisulfite, the antioxidant in cartridges with a vasoconstrictor. No cross-allergy between the classes.

3 Local anesthetic systemic toxicity

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

LAST (local anesthetic systemic toxicity), usually from intravascular injection or overdose: the CNS goes first: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness, twitching, then seizures, then CNS depression; at higher levels the heart: hypotension, arrhythmia, arrest. Potency tracks toxicity; acidosis makes it worse. Treatment: stop injecting, airway, oxygen, a benzodiazepine for seizures, and 20% lipid emulsion (the "lipid sink").

  • NMDA receptor: a coincidence detector. It needs glutamate (and glycine) plus depolarization to push out its Mg²⁺ block; it lets in Ca²⁺, the trigger for long-term potentiation. Ketamine blocks it.
  • MAC (minimum alveolar concentration): the inhaled concentration at which 50% of patients do not move to a surgical incision. Lower MAC = more potent; potency rises with lipid solubility. 1 Trigeminal neuralgia and the upper- versus lower-half causes of head and facial pain

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

"Upper-half" pain (above the eyes) is mostly primary headache, glaucoma, giant cell arteritis or pseudotumor; "lower-half" pain is most often dental, then TMD and burning mouth; sinus disease (overdiagnosed), cardiac pain referred to the jaw, atypical facial pain and trigeminal neuralgia can be either. Red flags: thunderclap onset, new headache after 50, papilledema, fever, visual loss.

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Gate control: large Aβ touch fibers excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn that damp Aδ and C input; rubbing a bumped elbow helps.

3 Taste and smell pathways and tongue innervation

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Taste fibers go to the nucleus of the solitary tract → VPM → gustatory cortex (anterior insula and frontal operculum), all on the same side. Flavor combines smell (I), taste (VII, IX, X) and texture and temperature (V). Smell is the one sense with no thalamic relay: receptor neurons → olfactory bulb (mitral and tufted cells) → piriform cortex, amygdala and entorhinal cortex, which is why smells call up emotion and memory. Loss of smell (anosmia) follows head trauma that shears the fibers at the cribriform plate, infections and aging, and is an early sign of Parkinson and Alzheimer disease.

1 Antiseizure drugs and their oral side effects; managing a seizure in the chair

Study guide + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

A seizure in the chair: stop treatment, clear instruments, protect the patient from injury (nothing in the mouth), time it, give oxygen; if it lasts 5 minutes, call EMS and give a benzodiazepine (for example midazolam intranasal, buccal or IM). Ask about triggers, control and missed doses before treating.

2 Multiple sclerosis: presentation, diagnosis, treatment and the trigeminal neuralgia link

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Diagnosis: a typical demyelinating event plus dissemination in time and space and no better explanation. MRI shows periventricular plaques (gadolinium-enhancing = active, new); CSF shows oligoclonal bands and a raised IgG index; evoked potentials are slowed.
  • Dental: trigeminal neuralgia in a patient under 40 or on both sides suggests MS; patients on immunosuppressants or long steroids may need infection precautions; keep visits short and cool.

3 Alzheimer pathology and drugs; Parkinson drugs and dental care

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Dental: short morning visits, involve the caregiver and confirm consent, aggressive prevention (fluoride) as self-care slips; cholinesterase inhibitors can slow the heart and increase saliva, while many other drugs dry the mouth.

4 Obstructive sleep apnea and oral appliances; narcolepsy; the circadian clock

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Obstructive sleep apnea: airway collapse with continued breathing effort; loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headache, daytime sleepiness. Risks: obesity (strongest), male over 50, postmenopause, thick neck, retrognathia or micrognathia, crowded oropharynx, alcohol and sedatives. Diagnosed by polysomnography. Treatment: weight loss, avoid sleeping supine, CPAP (first line), and a mandibular advancement oral appliance for snoring and mild to moderate OSA, or moderate to severe OSA when CPAP is refused or not tolerated (best in thin patients whose OSA is worse supine). Avoid benzodiazepines.

5 Reward circuitry and drugs of abuse; antipsychotics; LTP

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Reward runs on dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (the mesolimbic pathway). Every drug of abuse raises dopamine there. Cocaine blocks the dopamine (and norepinephrine and serotonin) transporters; amphetamine reverses them. Opioids act on mu receptors (Gi/o) of GABA interneurons, releasing VTA dopamine neurons from inhibition. Alcohol boosts GABA-A and blocks NMDA; nicotine acts on α4β2 nicotinic receptors; marijuana on CB1 (anandamide). Addiction: tolerance, craving, withdrawal, use despite harm; genetic risk is polygenic. Treatment: behavioral therapy (CBT, contingency management, 12-step), nicotine replacement and varenicline, naltrexone or disulfiram for alcohol, methadone, buprenorphine or naltrexone for opioids. Dental: no epinephrine within 24 hours of cocaine use (arrhythmia, hypertensive crisis); methamphetamine causes rampant caries; for patients recovering from opioid use, plan non-opioid analgesia.

1 Clearance: the formula, inulin = GFR, PAH = RPF, creatinine and GFR, and clearance ratios

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Inulin: freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR (the gold standard).
  • Creatinine: made by muscle at a steady rate and freely filtered, with a little secretion, so it slightly overestimates GFR; it's the clinical marker (eGFR also uses cystatin C). Plasma creatinine varies inversely with GFR: if GFR halves, plasma creatinine doubles at steady state.
  • Clearance ratio (Cx / Cinulin): = 1, filtered only; > 1, filtered and secreted (PAH, organic acids and bases); < 1, filtered and reabsorbed (Na+, Cl−, urea) or not filtered. Glucose and albumin normally have a clearance of 0.

2 Afferent versus efferent arteriole resistance, angiotensin II, prostaglandins and autoregulation

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Regulators: sympathetic nerves constrict both arterioles and lower RBF and GFR; angiotensin II constricts the efferent more and holds GFR up when perfusion falls; prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) dilate the arterioles and protect flow in hemorrhage or heart failure (NSAIDs remove this protection); low-dose dopamine dilates.

3 Body fluid compartments (60–40–20), plasma osmolarity, fluid shifts and IV fluids

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • 60–40–20: total body water is 60% of body weight; ICF 40%; ECF 20%. The ECF is 3/4 interstitial fluid and 1/4 plasma. In a 70-kg man: TBW 42 L, ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, plasma 3.5 L.
  • Plasma osmolarity ≈ 2[Na+] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; normal about 275–290 mOsm/kg. At steady state ICF and ECF osmolarity are equal; water moves until they match.

4 Filtration barrier and juxtaglomerular apparatus

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus: the macula densa (tubule cells at the end of the thick ascending limb, where the tubule touches its own glomerulus) senses NaCl; JG (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall secrete renin; extraglomerular mesangial cells lie between them.

1 What each segment reabsorbs and which transporter and diuretic belong to it

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Early proximal tubule: the apical Na+/H+ exchanger secretes H+, which reclaims filtered HCO3− with the help of carbonic anhydrase; HCO3− leaves basolaterally on a Na+-HCO3− cotransporter. Glucose enters with Na+ on SGLT2 and leaves on GLUT transporters.
  • Intercalated cells (about 40%): α-intercalated cells secrete H+ (apical H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase, which also reabsorbs K+) and return HCO3− to the blood through the basolateral Cl−/HCO3− exchanger AE1; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− through apical pendrin.

2 Glucose transport maximum, glycosuria and SGLT2 inhibitors

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Glucose transport maximum (Tm): the carriers saturate. Once the filtered load passes Tm (plasma glucose above about 180–200 mg/dL, the renal threshold), the excess is excreted – glycosuria with an osmotic diuresis. SGLT2 inhibitors (the "-flozins": empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) cause glycosuria on purpose to treat type 2 diabetes; watch for genital yeast infections, UTIs, volume loss and euglycemic ketoacidosis.

3 Countercurrent multiplication, urea recycling and ADH's actions

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Urea recycling: ADH makes the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts permeable to water but not urea, so urea concentrates in the duct; in the inner medullary collecting duct ADH also inserts urea transporters, urea diffuses into the interstitium and supplies much of the inner medulla's osmolarity. Some urea re-enters the thin limbs and is recycled.

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • K+ secretion rises with a high-K+ diet, aldosterone, alkalosis and high tubular flow or Na+ delivery (loop and thiazide diuretics → hypokalemia). It falls with acute acidosis, low aldosterone, K+-sparing diuretics and low GFR. NSAIDs blunt renin release and, with CKD, ACE inhibitors or spironolactone, can cause hyperkalemia.

1 CKD stages, causes, azotemia versus uremia, and CKD mineral and bone disorder

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Uremia comes from three things: retained products the kidney should excrete (nitrogen wastes), normal products in excess (hormones such as PTH), and loss of products the kidney makes (erythropoietin, calcitriol). Failing excretion also retains Na+ and water and causes hyperkalemia.
  • CKD mineral and bone disorder: falling GFR retains phosphate → FGF23 rises and calcitriol falls → less Ca2+ absorbed → plasma Ca2+ falls → secondary hyperparathyroidism (seen from stages 3–5) → renal osteodystrophy: bone resorption, demineralized jaws and brown tumors.

2 Nephritic versus nephrotic syndrome and the classic glomerular diseases

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Post-streptococcal GN: children, 1–4 weeks after group A strep throat or skin infection; cola-colored urine, edema, hypertension, low C3; hypercellular glomeruli with subepithelial "humps". Most children recover; adults more often progress.
  • Membranous nephropathy: the classic most common nephrotic syndrome in adults (ages 30–50); subepithelial immune deposits; slowly progressive.

3 Pyelonephritis, casts, stones and renal tumors

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Acute pyelonephritis: bacterial infection of the kidney and pelvis, usually ascending, most often E. coli. Fever, chills, flank pain, dysuria and frequency; WBC casts place it in the kidney. Complications: pyonephrosis, papillary necrosis, sepsis.

1 The patient on long-term steroids in the chair: a suppressed axis, the adrenal crisis and 100 mg hydrocortisone, and why steroids are tapered

Recording + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Why a taper: an outside steroid suppresses CRH and ACTH, and the cortex goes into rest. Stopped abruptly, it cannot answer: adrenal insufficiency. Taken in the morning, like the natural peak, it disturbs sleep less.
  • A patient on long-term steroids (about 20 mg prednisone a day for 3 weeks or more) should be assumed to have a suppressed axis. For routine care under local anesthesia: the usual morning dose, a morning appointment, and good anxiety and pain control. A long or stressful surgery, an infection or trauma, or a missed dose can trigger an adrenal crisis; extra steroid for a big procedure is set with the physician.
  • Adrenal crisis: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, abdominal pain, loss of consciousness, shock. Stop, call 911, lay the patient supine with legs raised, give oxygen and 100 mg hydrocortisone IV or IM, and monitor vitals.

Neoplastic cells replace the marrow and spill into the blood. 4 Motility: slow waves, the migrating motor complex and motilin, and achalasia

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Interstitial cells of Cajal set slow waves, the basic electrical rhythm (about 3/min in the stomach, 12/min in the duodenum). A slow wave alone doesn't contract muscle; contraction happens when spike potentials fire on top of it, and nerves and hormones decide how often that happens. Swallowing is voluntary, then a medullary reflex (soft palate up, epiglottis down, UES relaxes), then primary peristalsis, with secondary peristalsis clearing what's left; the LES relaxes through vagal VIP and NO. In achalasia, those inhibitory myenteric neurons are lost, so the LES can't relax: dysphagia to solids and liquids and a "bird's beak" on barium swallow.

5 Saliva: isotonic primary saliva made hypotonic by the ducts, and dual autonomic control

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

The parotid is the largest gland and is purely serous (amylase); the submandibular makes about 60-70% of resting saliva and is mixed; the sublingual makes about 5% and is mostly mucous. Acinar cells make primary saliva that is isotonic to plasma. The ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, but they let little water through, so final saliva is hypotonic. The faster it flows, the less time the ducts have, so high-flow saliva is closer to plasma and richest in HCO3-. Unusually, both autonomic divisions stimulate saliva: parasympathetic (copious, watery; blocked by atropine) and sympathetic (small volume, protein-rich). Saliva lubricates and buffers, starts starch digestion (α-amylase) and fat digestion (lingual lipase), and defends the mouth (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA, mucins).

5 Liver histology: the acinus zones, Kupffer and stellate cells, and the gallbladder wall

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

Three ways to draw the lobule: the classic lobule (hexagon around a central vein, portal triads at the corners; blood flow), the portal lobule (triangle around a triad; bile flow) and the hepatic acinus (diamond between two central veins; the metabolic unit). In the acinus, zone 1 (periportal) gets the most oxygen; zone 3 (centrilobular) gets the least and has the most CYP450, so it is hit first by ischemia, acetaminophen and alcohol. Blood runs from triad to central vein; bile runs the other way, from canaliculi between hepatocytes to the ducts of the triad. Sinusoids have fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium over the space of Disse; Kupffer cells are the resident macrophages; stellate (Ito) cells store vitamin A and, when activated, lay down the collagen of fibrosis. The gallbladder has simple columnar epithelium that concentrates bile, a smooth muscle coat, and no muscularis mucosae or submucosa.

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

C. difficile colitis follows antibiotics (clindamycin is the classic one, also cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones) and PPIs: toxins A and B, watery diarrhea, pseudomembranes. Treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin and avoid antimotility drugs. Diverticulosis (outpouchings, mostly sigmoid, low-fiber diets) can bleed painlessly; diverticulitis gives left lower quadrant pain and fever. Hirschsprung disease: neural crest cells fail to reach the distal colon, the aganglionic segment can't relax, and the colon above it dilates (delayed meconium). Colorectal adenocarcinoma is among the top causes of cancer death and usually follows the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (APC, then KRAS, then p53). Syndromes a dentist may spot first: Gardner syndrome (an APC variant of familial adenomatous polyposis: jaw osteomas, supernumerary and impacted teeth, odontomas, epidermoid cysts; colon cancer is nearly certain without colectomy) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11: hamartomatous polyps and dark macules on the lips and buccal mucosa). GISTs arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal (c-KIT).

3 Osteoclast biology: RANKL, OPG and M-CSF, and PTH acting through osteoblasts

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Coupling: osteoblasts and osteocytes make M-CSF and RANKL; RANKL binds RANK on precursors and makes osteoclasts. OPG is the osteoblast's decoy receptor that soaks up RANKL. Estrogen raises OPG, lowers RANKL and speeds osteoclast apoptosis, which is why bone loss accelerates after menopause. Osteoclasts have no PTH receptors: PTH acts on osteoblasts, which raise RANKL. Continuous PTH resorbs bone; intermittent PTH builds it.

4 Intramembranous vs endochondral ossification; cartilage types and collagen types

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Intramembranous ossification turns mesenchyme straight into bone: the skull vault, maxilla, most of the mandible and most of the clavicle (and an extraction socket heals the same way). Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model: long bones, vertebrae, pelvis, skull base. The growth plate runs reserve → proliferation → hypertrophy → calcification → ossification; estrogen closes it in both sexes. The mandibular condyle has its own secondary cartilage growth site. Remodeling never stops: activation, resorption (weeks), reversal, formation and mineralization (months).

5 Calcium balance: hypocalcemia after thyroid surgery and the osteoporosis risk factors

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Hypocalcemia (after parathyroid removal in thyroid surgery, vitamin D deficiency, CKD): perioral tingling, muscle cramps and tetany (Chvostek and Trousseau signs), long QT, cataracts; in children, enamel hypoplasia. Hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism, cancer): stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychiatric moans, constipation and weakness; hyperparathyroidism in the jaws shows loss of the lamina dura and brown tumors. Treat severe hypercalcemia with IV saline, then a bisphosphonate, denosumab or calcitonin.

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Code of Professional Conduct: specific conduct that is required or forbidden, adopted by the ADA House of Delegates. It is binding on ADA members, and a violation can bring censure, suspension or expulsion.
  • 4.A Patient selection: dentists may use reasonable discretion, but may not refuse a patient because of race, creed, color, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin or disability. A patient with HIV, HBV or HCV is treated on the same basis as anyone else: refer only if another practitioner's skills or equipment are needed, and consult the physician if treatment might seriously compromise the patient's health.

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • 2.D Personal impairment: practicing while impaired by alcohol or drugs is unethical. Urge an impaired colleague to seek treatment; with first-hand knowledge that a colleague is practicing impaired, report it to the dental society's professional assistance committee. A dentist with a disease that could endanger patients limits their practice on a physician's advice.
  • 4.C Justifiable criticism: tell patients their present oral health status without disparaging prior work, and check with the previous dentist where possible; a difference of opinion is not mistreatment. Report gross or continual faulty treatment to the reviewing agency the local or state society designates.

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • 5.B Representation of fees: waiving a copayment without telling the insurer is overbilling; raising a fee because the patient has insurance is unethical; the full fee is the fee charged a patient without benefits. 1 Informed consent and refusal: what to disclose, Canterbury's reasonable-patient standard, capacity and consent for minors

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Three court cases built it. Schloendorff (1914): every adult of sound mind has the right to decide what is done to their own body. Salgo (1957): the first use of the words "informed consent." Canterbury v. Spence (1972): disclose every risk that a reasonable person in the patient's position would find significant to the decision (the reasonable-patient standard), not just what other doctors customarily disclose.

2 Bloodborne pathogens: transmission risks, the steps after a needlestick, and OSHA's hepatitis B vaccine rule

Review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard: a written exposure control plan; engineering controls (sharps containers, self-sheathing needles) and work-practice controls (no two-handed recapping); PPE at no cost; the hepatitis B vaccine offered free within 10 working days of assignment (a refusal is signed); free, confidential follow-up after an exposure; and yearly training.
  • Risk of infection after a needlestick from an infected source: HBV about 30% (6–30%), HCV about 2%, HIV about 0.3%. HBV survives on dry surfaces for at least a week. There is a vaccine for HBV, but none for HCV or HIV.
  • After an exposure: wash with soap and water (flush the eyes or mouth with water), don't squeeze the wound or use bleach, report at once, and test the source with consent. HIV prophylaxis starts as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72.

3 Confidentiality, HIPAA and the duty to warn

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • PHI may be shared without written authorization for treatment, payment and health care operations, and where the law requires it (abuse reports, public health, court orders). Other uses, such as marketing or a patient's photo on social media, need written authorization.

Tarasoff (1976): a therapist had a duty to protect an identifiable person whom his patient had threatened to kill. Confidentiality gives way to a serious, foreseeable threat to someone else.

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Child abuse and neglect: dentists are mandated reporters in every state. Report a reasonable suspicion (proof isn't needed) to child protective services or the police. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability, and in most states failing to report is itself an offense.
  • More than half of physical abuse injuries are to the head, face, mouth or neck. 1 Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values: calculating them and choosing a test for screening or confirming

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • PPV = a/(a+b) and NPV = d/(c+d). Predictive values change with prevalence: where a disease is rarer, PPV falls and NPV rises. Sensitivity and specificity don't change with prevalence.

2 Reading relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio and NNT with their confidence intervals and p-values; type I and II errors and power

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Relative risk (risk ratio) = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed, from cohorts and RCTs. 1 means no difference, above 1 a harmful effect, below 1 a protective one (0.87 means 13% lower risk). A hazard ratio reads the same way over time.
  • The 95% confidence interval is the range of plausible true values. For a ratio, an interval that includes 1 is not significant (HR 0.92, CI 0.83–1.02); for a difference, one that includes 0. A narrower interval is a more precise estimate.
